# Interview question coverage

The library contains **121 distinct question families across 15 topics**. The
initial 40 covered common screens and a narrow leadership core. The expansion
adds operational, organizational, product, technical, and contemporary leadership
decisions. Counts describe editorial coverage, not how many questions any one
candidate should practice or an exhaustive survey of employer interviews.

## Topic inventory

| Topic | IDs | Count | What these questions examine |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Common/recruiter](common.md) | C01–C07, C09–C10 | 9 | Professional narrative, motivation, choices, range-first negotiation, and candidate questions |
| [Behavioral](behavioral.md) | B01–B11 | 11 | Evidence of contribution, judgment, conflict, learning, and explicit decision-quality criteria |
| [Management fundamentals](management.md) | M01–M10 | 10 | Work through others, feedback, development, performance, and team functioning |
| [Staff/principal IC](staff.md) | T01–T05 | 5 | Technical depth, influence, adoption, and enabling others |
| [Executive](executive.md) | E01–E05 | 5 | Business-level strategy, resources, organizational systems, and accountability |
| [Delivery/execution](delivery.md) | DL01–DL08 | 8 | How commitments become feasible work and how plans change |
| [Reliability/operations](operations.md) | O01–O08 | 8 | Service risk, incident response, operational learning, and preparedness |
| [Product/business](product.md) | P01–P08 | 8 | Customer problems, discovery, adoption, and business constraints |
| [Managing managers/change](organization.md) | G01–G08 | 8 | Leadership through managers, organizational transitions, and durable ownership |
| [Talent decisions](talent.md) | HR01–HR08 | 8 | Consistent people decisions and their consequences |
| [Technical strategy](technical-strategy.md) | TS01–TS09 | 9 | Shared technical direction, investment, complexity, governance, and technical decision quality |
| [Culture/inclusion/ethics](culture.md) | K01–K08 | 8 | Who can participate, how power operates, and what behavior is rewarded |
| [Distributed work](distributed.md) | W01–W08 | 8 | Communication systems across locations, schedules, and access needs |
| [Personal leadership](personal-leadership.md) | LQ01–LQ08 | 8 | Self-management, relationships, learning, trust, and career decisions |
| [AI judgment](ai.md) | AI01–AI08 | 8 | Adoption under uncertainty, verification, learning, and accountable use |
| **Total** | | **121** | |

The 1 October review removed C08 (routine availability/location/travel/authorization)
from the preparation bank and added B11/TS09. IDs remain stable; C08 is not reused.
Practical facts still belong in a user-owned preparation checklist when needed.
See [the question-by-question review](review.md) for the reasoning and open gaps.

## Boundaries that prevent duplicate questions

Similar stories can support different questions; their evaluation target must
change. A variant changes wording, not the card count. A profile adaptation
changes relevant scope, not the underlying competency.

| Adjacent questions | Difference in what the listener needs to understand |
| --- | --- |
| B06 prioritization / DL02 deadline / E03 allocation | Personal/team choices among work / renegotiating a specific commitment / allocating organizational capacity |
| B09 crisis / O01 incident | Behavior under pressure / service mitigation, coordination, and operational control |
| B02 failure / O03 postmortem / P08 experiment | Personal accountability / organizational learning after service failure / interpreting evidence from a product hypothesis |
| M04 development / G01 developing managers | Helping an individual grow / improving another manager's ability to lead through their team |
| M08 hiring / HR02 panel disagreement | Designing and running a hiring approach / deciding when interview evidence and panel judgments conflict |
| M10 promotion / HR04 calibration | Supporting one person's development and case / consistent comparisons and access across people and teams |
| T03 migration / TS03 platform product | Completing a technical transition / discovering and sustaining a useful internal product |
| T02 tradeoff / TS04 decision process | Reasoning about one technical choice / making multi-party architecture decisions without permanent deadlock |
| E04 org design / G03 interfaces / G06 reorganization | Choosing organizational structure / clarifying everyday decision rights / carrying out a structural transition |
| M05 performance / HR06 harmful high performer / K04 conduct | Addressing delivery or capability expectations / separating output from harmful behavior / responding to a conduct concern with appropriate care and process |
| B03 disagreement / W06 remote conflict / K08 dissent | Resolving a substantive disagreement / repairing a communication breakdown across distance / ensuring disagreement can influence decisions before authority closes them |
| C05 growth / LQ05 new-domain learning / LQ07 scope | A relevant development area / a concrete method of learning unfamiliar work / evidence and boundaries for increasing responsibility |
| E05 metrics / AI02 productivity evidence | General decision-useful engineering measurement / distinguishing AI adoption effects from confounding and selection bias |
| B11 decision quality / B02 failure / B08 changing mind | Explicit criteria for a good decision / reconstructing one disappointing episode / updating a belief when evidence changes |
| TS09 technical decision quality / T02 tradeoff / TS04 decision process | Technical criteria and their limits / applying judgment in one actual choice / resolving multi-party disagreement with accountable closure |

## Choose by responsibilities, then by the actual loop

All candidates benefit from a professional introduction and concrete examples.
The following are selection lenses, not mandatory interview curricula. Use the
job's scope and recruiter guidance; a small company may combine several roles.

| Profile or interview | Useful emphasis |
| --- | --- |
| Recruiter screen | Relevant C cards and a short B01 example; seek the budgeted range first through C07; logistics are checklist facts |
| Early/mid-career IC | B, bounded DL/O/P/W examples, and T02; assess actual contribution rather than authority |
| Senior/staff/principal IC | T and TS, cross-team DL/O/P/K/W, and relevant AI judgment; people authority remains optional |
| First-time manager | M01/M03/M06 plus transferable DL/K/W evidence; explicitly label situational plans |
| Experienced EM | M, DL, O, HR, K, W; product and technical criteria matched to responsibilities |
| Director/manager of managers | G, HR, E03/E04/E05, dependencies, manager capability, and change adoption |
| Executive | E and G, business/product choices, resource and talent systems, risks, and AI investment where relevant |
| Product-adjacent engineering leader | P and shared decision-making; engineering leadership does not automatically establish product ownership |
| Reliability/platform leader | O, TS03/TS05, DL04/DL06, and customer/consumer evidence |

## Coverage limits and future additions

This is a broad foundation, not “every possible interview question.” Coding,
system-design problems, detailed domain knowledge, portfolio tasks, and company
or industry-specific scenarios need separate banks. The AI questions address
leadership and judgment; they do not certify model safety or technical expertise.

Add another family when it introduces a distinct decision, evidence requirement,
or evaluation target. Add a variant when only wording changes. Add a profile
adaptation when only scope changes. Future prioritization should use actual
interview loops and reviewer feedback rather than an arbitrary total.

For every major competency, explicitly check whether the bank lets a candidate
explain what good looks like, demonstrate it in an experience, and reason through
a relevant scenario. Not every competency needs three separate cards: a distinct
target can be a variant or probe. Retain a standalone family only when preparing
it helps clarify judgment or improve a substantive answer. Screen logistics do
not meet that criterion. Track proposed additions and unresolved overlaps in
[the content review](review.md), rather than padding categories to equal counts.

All anchors remain research-informed editorial proposals. The
[evaluation guide](evaluation.md#calibration-before-product-use) describes the
independent calibration still needed before automated grading is trusted.

# Personalization and answer evaluation

This is a proposed content evaluation method for interview rehearsal. It grades
what an answer demonstrates, keeps factual support separate, and identifies the
next useful improvement. It does not grade the person or establish that they
can perform the job.

## Inputs before drafting or evaluating

1. **Question and format:** card ID, exact wording, historical/situational
   variant, principle/concept, negotiation, or role-play; recruiter screen or
   deeper interview; and any known time allowance.
2. **Target context:** responsibilities, company stage, industry constraints,
   required capabilities, and the actual interview criteria if supplied.
3. **Profile facts:** accepted roles, dates, scope, contribution, collaborators,
   decisions, outcomes, metrics with definitions/timeframes, and evidence IDs.
4. **Experience inventory:** user-described episodes, including failures,
   feedback, uncertainties, and examples of work through others.
5. **User choices:** career goals, boundaries, compensation preferences,
   logistics, accessibility preferences, and what they consent to discuss.
6. **Answer transcript:** the user's words, with sentence/segment references.
   Text-only practice can use typed answers; this content does not require
   recording, microphone access, or live interview assistance.

Missing profile facts should produce a focused request or a marked draft slot.
They must not be filled by inventing achievements, tools, teams, metrics, or
authority. A role-specific example can be narrower than the target role when the
candidate clearly states that boundary.

## Keep four kinds of statement separate

| Kind | Treatment |
| --- | --- |
| Accepted profile fact | Reference the source ID and preserve its scope and qualification |
| New user recollection | Attribute to the user; request confirmation before any canonical reuse |
| Hypothetical intention | Evaluate the reasoning; never present it as past experience |
| Evaluator inference | Label as interpretation and show the answer passage that supports it |

New statements are **unverified**, not automatically false. Missing corroboration
is not proof of fabrication. A contradiction with an accepted fact triggers
clarification: the accepted fact may also need correction. Company assumptions
must be similarly labeled; a public job ad does not establish internal causes.

Generated stories and feedback do not update Candidate Profile facts, fit
scores, or readiness assessments. Any later profile promotion requires its own
explicit review flow. This document proposes content behavior; it does not add
that flow to the product.

## Evaluate in two separate passes

**Pass 1: factual and privacy support.** Identify each material factual claim and
mark it `supported`, `new_user_statement`, `needs_clarification`, or
`hypothetical`. Show the source or exact conflict. Flag confidential details for
redaction without penalizing the candidate for preserving confidentiality.
Unavailable exact numbers can become an honest qualitative outcome; avoid
plausible-looking estimates supplied by the evaluator.

**Pass 2: answer content.** Use only the dimensions on the selected question
card. An outcome does not erase the quality of the decision made with the
information available. A confident tone does not add evidence. For situational
questions, substitute assumptions, action sequence, contingencies, and checks
for historical outcomes.

For principle questions such as B11 and TS09, assess the stated criteria, the
reasoning and limits that make them useful, and an example or counterexample
that demonstrates application. Do not demand a historical outcome when the
question asks for a definition. If the candidate only tells a story, probe for
the criterion; if they only recite a framework, probe where it would fail.
For negotiation, assess informed preparation and response choices separately
from leadership competence or the ultimate salary obtained.

## Scoring anchors

Each question has three dimensions with a weak and a strong anchor. The proposed
0–3 scale adds intermediate levels consistently:

| Result | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `not_observed` | No fair opportunity or usable transcript: interruption, format exclusion, unresolved question ambiguity, or a protected disclosure boundary; no numeric value |
| 0 | After a fair opportunity and needed clarification, an attempted answer supplies no relevant content or explicitly demonstrates the weak behavior |
| 1 | Relevant assertion or partial detail, but the listener cannot yet follow the reasoning or action |
| 2 | Concrete, role-appropriate evidence meeting the core intent; a material limitation or follow-up remains |
| 3 | Meets the card's strong anchor, with sufficient relevant detail and appropriate limits; not maximum length or drama |

Anchors are content expectations, not mandatory phrases. Every numeric value
needs an answer passage and a reason. A missing transcript cannot receive zero.
Do not total these dimensions into a leadership score, percentile, role level,
or hiring probability. For C07, assess information seeking, package clarity,
and response to pressure under the range-first coaching default. Never score
the amount demanded, private minimum, personal constraints, or willingness to
walk away as better or worse. A deliberate user-chosen exception is not a
competency failure. C08 is retired: routine logistics are user-declared checklist
facts, not scored interview preparation content.

For LQ08, assess whether the professional decision and tradeoffs are understandable;
do not rank the person's career priorities. Apply the same boundary whenever
an expanded card involves work hours, personal support, private information, or
access needs. Serious conduct scenarios assess responsible role-appropriate
handling, not whether the candidate recites a predetermined disciplinary sequence.

For AI answers, distinguish current local observations from forecasts and
published results in other settings. Tool enthusiasm, adoption rate, and generated
volume are not quality dimensions unless the question explicitly asks about a
defined outcome they help explain.

Do not add a dimension merely because another question uses it. STAR
(situation, task, action, result) can help organize experiential answers, but it
is unnecessary for an introduction, salary discussion, or hypothetical plan.
Learning and changed behavior are useful where relevant; an unrelated moral at
the end is not required.

## Role adaptation

Use the card's profile inputs and target context to choose evidence. Expectations
change with responsibilities, rather than rewarding larger numbers by default.

- An IC can demonstrate influence within one team; staff expectations may
  require adoption across teams when that is part of the role.
- A first-time manager can demonstrate mentorship, coordination, feedback, or
  a situational exercise. Label this transferable evidence and leave formal
  people-management experience unestablished.
- An EM should explain team outcomes and their own management actions. A
  director should additionally explain how managers and teams gained autonomy.
- An executive should connect decisions to the business and constraints,
  explain shared ownership with peers, and examine system effects. A CTO role
  defined as a senior IC needs the corresponding IC criteria instead.
- A return from management to IC work is a legitimate choice. Gaps, nonlinear
  careers, disability accommodations, or lack of impressive employers are not
  negative quality signals.

## Useful evaluator output

Return a short, evidence-linked assessment:

```text
Question: B02, historical failure example; target: staff IC
Answer type: historical / situational / principle / negotiation / preference / mixed
Content dimensions:
  responsibility: 2 — segment 3 names the missed dependency
  decision analysis: 1 — segment 4 says "we underestimated it"; no explanation yet
  changed practice: not_observed — not asked before the interruption
Factual support:
  outcome claim in segment 6: new_user_statement, no accepted source yet
What works: one concrete episode and a clear personal decision
Next improvement: explain what you knew when you committed to the date
Follow-up: which signal would make you decide differently now?
Readiness of this answer: needs_detail
```

Readiness labels apply only to this answer: `ready_to_rehearse`, `needs_detail`,
`needs_clarification`, or `not_assessable`. An answer can be ready to rehearse
while new factual claims remain clearly marked for confirmation. Do not present
the readiness label as a statement that the candidate is ready for the role.

Give at most two high-value improvements at once. Prefer a probe that helps the
user recover their real experience over replacing their answer with a fabricated
ideal. If asked to draft a revision, retain their meaning and voice, mark missing
facts, and let the user decide whether the wording is accurate.

## What not to reward or punish

Do not reward invented precision, exaggerated individual ownership, performative
humility, named frameworks, incessant availability, or a rehearsed answer that
does not address the prompt. Do not punish brevity, speech differences, an
accent, imperfect grammar, disclosure boundaries, small-company scope, or an
honest lack of direct experience. Understandability matters only to whether the
listener can follow the content; ask a clarification before inferring absence.

One respectful disagreement can be well reasoned or poorly reasoned. One
termination, rewrite, reorganization, or decision to stop a project can be sound
or unsound. Evaluate evidence and context instead of matching a preferred act.

## Calibration before product use

The [OPM anchor guidance](https://www.opm.gov/frequently-asked-questions/assessment-policy-faq/structured-interviews/how-do-i-develop-a-customized-rating-scale-for-structured-interviews/)
supports using question-specific examples and subject matter experts. Our scale
still needs independent calibration:

1. Have experienced IC, management, and executive interviewers review cards
   against actual job responsibilities and acceptable alternatives.
2. Build an independently authored response set: strong, partial, vague,
   defensible unconventional, unsuccessful-but-sound, successful-but-unsound,
   first-time manager, confidential, and ambiguous examples.
3. Have at least two humans assess it independently before seeing model output.
   Examine dimension-level disagreement and revise unclear anchors. Use held-out
   answers after revisions; do not claim validation from training examples.
4. Test factual checks with unsupported metrics, ambiguous ownership,
   conflicting dates, and new truthful user recollections. Test invariance by
   varying verbosity, grammar, accent markers, names, and employer prestige
   while preserving substantive content. Verify interruptions stay unassessed.
5. Compare model feedback with independent human feedback, including whether
   it helps improve truthful answers. Record errors, role coverage, and limits.
   Set acceptance thresholds before product grading is enabled.

The [worked examples](examples.md) are author-created illustrations and review
fixtures. They demonstrate intended semantics; they do not establish model
accuracy, fairness, coaching efficacy, or interview success.
guidance.overview:
# Interview preparation content library

Research draft, revised 1 October 2026. This library defines interview questions,
strong-answer guidance, profile adaptations, and evaluation criteria for later
practice. It does not change the current InterviewPrep generator or enable a
practice feature. The numeric anchors are editorial proposals, not validated
predictors of hiring outcomes.

## What makes an answer good?

A good answer addresses the question, makes the candidate's actual contribution
understandable, explains judgment in context, and uses honest evidence. For an
experience question, the listener should understand the situation, the choice,
the action, what happened, and what changed afterward. A disappointing outcome
can accompany a strong answer; a successful outcome can conceal poor judgment.

There is no single ideal leadership persona or universal script. A candidate
should be able to explain a defensible choice and its limits. Different company
needs can make different choices appropriate. These are our working criteria,
derived from the [research](sources.md), rather than a rubric endorsed by the
authors.

## Read the content

| Resource | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| [Research and source ledger](sources.md) | Author viewpoints, disagreements, books, reading coverage, and attribution limits |
| [Evaluation and personalization](evaluation.md) | Profile inputs, observable scoring anchors, evidence checks, and feedback format |
| [Coverage map](coverage.md) | All 121 question families, topic boundaries, and role-based selection |
| [Content review and open judgments](review.md) | Question-by-question walkthrough, coverage weaknesses, and proposed changes |
| [Common and recruiter questions](common.md) | C01–C07 and C09–C10: narrative, motivation, transitions, growth, range-first compensation, direction, and candidate questions; C08 retired |
| [Behavioral questions](behavioral.md) | B01–B11: achievement, failure, disagreement, feedback, ambiguity, priorities, influence, change, pressure, pushback, and decision quality |
| [Management questions](management.md) | M01–M10: management motivation, technical involvement, delegation, development, performance, feedback, one-to-ones, hiring, team health, and promotion |
| [Staff and principal IC questions](staff.md) | T01–T05: technical leadership, tradeoffs, technical debt, code-review conflict, and multiplying others' impact |
| [Executive questions](executive.md) | E01–E05: strategy, entering a role, resources, organization design, and measurement |
| [Delivery and execution](delivery.md) | DL01–DL08: commitments, deadlines, recovery, dependencies, process, releases, stopping work, and decision bottlenecks |
| [Reliability and operations](operations.md) | O01–O08: incidents, reliability investment, learning, on-call, rollbacks, recovery, communication, and security risk |
| [Product and business judgment](product.md) | P01–P08: discovery, assumptions, customer demands, adoption, collaboration, economics, and experiments |
| [Managing managers and organizational change](organization.md) | G01–G08: manager development, skip-levels, interfaces, succession, integration, reorganization, transitions, and change adoption |
| [Talent decisions](talent.md) | HR01–HR08: onboarding, hiring calibration, potential, promotion fairness, compensation, harmful behavior, retention, and reductions |
| [Technical strategy](technical-strategy.md) | TS01–TS09: standards, build/buy, platforms, architectural decisions, capacity, complexity, exploration, long-term investment, and technical decision quality |
| [Culture, inclusion, and ethics](culture.md) | K01–K08: candor, participation, opportunity, conduct, incentives, norms, ethical requests, and dissent |
| [Distributed work and communication](distributed.md) | W01–W08: async/sync, time zones, proximity bias, decision records, meetings, conflict, belonging, and accessibility |
| [Personal leadership and career judgment](personal-leadership.md) | LQ01–LQ08: managing up, difficult managers, boundaries, support, learning, trust repair, scope growth, and career tradeoffs |
| [AI judgment and leadership](ai.md) | AI01–AI08: adoption, productivity evidence, code verification, learning, product evaluation, agent authority, factual reliability, and workforce planning |
| [Worked answers and evaluation examples](examples.md) | Synthetic examples, weak-to-strong revisions, and evaluator edge cases |

All 121 cards contain an intent, answer target, personalization inputs, acceptable
alternatives, probes, failure modes, question-specific anchors, and provenance.
They span 15 topics. The original 40 were a starter set and the next 80 expanded
topic coverage. The content review retired one logistics card and added two
explicit decision-quality questions. Counts are an inventory, not an acceptance
target. Variants and role adaptations do not count as extra cards.
The [coverage map](coverage.md) explains adjacent topics and selection.
These are reusable question families, not a claim to cover every employer's loop.
Technical coding, system-design exercises, industry-specific expertise, and legal
eligibility advice require separate content.

## Personalize to the actual profile and role

Select evidence before drafting prose. Use the role's responsibilities rather
than equating a title or headcount with seniority. An early-career candidate can
use a smaller project with clear ownership; someone changing tracks can state
the boundary between transferable experience and work they have not yet done.

| Target | Emphasize in the same generic question | Do not manufacture |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Individual contributor (IC) | Personal decisions, collaboration, delivery, and learning within actual scope | Organization ownership from participation in a large project |
| Staff/principal IC | Technical direction, ambiguous work across teams, adoption, and enabling others | Direct reports, hiring authority, or people-management experience |
| Engineering manager (EM) | Team outcomes, expectations, coaching, delivery, and work through others | Personal authorship of every team result |
| Director / manager of managers | Multiple teams, manager development, dependencies, and durable operating practices | Executive budget or business authority the candidate did not have |
| Executive | Business context, resource allocation, organizational systems, peer alignment, and accountability | Revenue causality, transformation success, or financial authority without evidence |

Preferences, availability, compensation boundaries, and private career context
are user-owned choices. They are not leadership competencies to grade. Profile
facts, new recollections, hypothetical plans, and evaluator interpretations must
remain distinct; see [evaluation](evaluation.md).

## Suggested first preparation set

Start with C01–C03, C05, C09–C10, B01–B04, and B06. Add M03/M05/M06/M09 for
management, T01/T02/T04/T05 for staff ICs, or E01–E05 for executives. Ask the
recruiter what the actual loop evaluates before selecting the rest. A first-time
manager should also prepare M01 and explicitly identify transferable examples.

Build a small evidence inventory rather than memorizing the whole bank. Each episode
can serve several questions, but the selected angle must answer the question
being asked. Practice follow-ups that expose ownership and reasoning; polishing
an unsupported story does not make it usable.

Also prepare explicit criteria for judgment: B11 asks what makes a decision
good; TS09 applies that question to technical choices. A principle answer needs
a defensible position, its limits, and an example or counterexample. A story
alone does not necessarily explain the principle. C07 defaults to obtaining the
employer's budgeted range before volunteering a candidate number; it does not
grade the person's salary requirement or willingness to risk an opportunity.

## What still needs validation

The library is ready for content review and rehearsal design. Before automated
grading is presented as reliable, experienced interviewers need to calibrate
anchors against independently written responses, diverse communication styles,
and actual role expectations. [Evaluation](evaluation.md#calibration-before-product-use)
defines that work. No candidate responses or private profile facts are included
in this repository content.

# Content review and open judgments

Reviewed 1 October 2026 after the candidate-facing content critique. All 120
original answer targets, question-specific anchors, and failure modes were
examined. This records current editorial judgments, not a reconstruction of
unrecorded doubts during the original research or independent rubric validation.

## What the critique revealed

The library was organized around topic coverage, with much of the definition of
good judgment implicit in experience and scenario answers. Explicit criteria
were uneven: M09 asks what makes a team healthy, O03 asks what makes an incident
review useful, and W04 asks what makes a decision record useful, but there was
no equivalent question about a good decision or a good technical decision.
Logistics also passed the selection boundary despite offering little substantive
preparation value. Salary advice treated several tactics as equally useful
without recommending an information-seeking default.

The repair belongs in question selection and canonical answer guidance. The
atlas copies those sources; changing only its appearance would preserve the
editorial defect. Counts describe coverage and must never become a target that
justifies filler or equal-sized categories.

## Changes made

- Retired C08; availability, location, travel, and authorization remain
  user-owned checklist facts. Its ID is preserved as retired, not recycled.
- Rewrote C07 to seek the employer's budgeted range firmly and persistently
  before volunteering a candidate number. Pressure, vague bands, package
  ambiguity, and refusal now have explicit preparation guidance. The final
  choice remains with the candidate.
- Added B11, “What makes a decision a good decision?”, and TS09, “What makes
  a technical decision a good technical decision?”, with separate criteria
  and application probes.
- Added principle/concept answers to evaluation. A definition question needs
  criteria, limits, and application; it should not be forced into a success story.
- Added synthetic C07 pressure-handling dialogue and B11/TS09 principle answers
  with counterexamples. There are now 17 families with worked illustrations.

## Doubts that remain

These are content review judgments, not claims that the original authors agree.

1. **How much of this bank matters for a particular loop?** M&A integration,
   reductions, incident response, platform design, and agent authority are useful
   in specific roles. They should not make a universal preparation curriculum.
2. **Are neighboring cards genuinely distinct?** Several have different targets
   but can use the same episode. Preserve that distinction in evaluation, while
   avoiding repetitive practice. The walkthrough flags the closest overlaps.
3. **Are principles explicit enough?** Decision quality is now covered. Good
   management, staff-level contribution, engineering quality, and organizational
   effectiveness still deserve an explicit concept-to-example coverage review.
4. **Do the answer targets overprescribe process?** “Context, options, evidence,
   owner, checks” is useful but can become a checklist response. A strong answer
   must choose material criteria and explain a position; every answer need not
   mention every safeguard or prove that a formal process was used.
5. **How much attribution is direct?** Sources include direct interview guidance,
   extrapolated practices, selected passages, and book overviews. Book listings
   are reading paths, not evidence of complete-book research. Our anchors remain
   editorial even when the interview theme comes directly from an author.
6. **Where do authors disagree?** Chemistry versus content, technical involvement,
   potential versus demonstrated work, and deciding versus delegating have real
   tensions. Accountable delegation and abdication must not be conflated. The
   source ledger records the decisions rather than implying consensus.
7. **How trustworthy is evaluation?** Three dimensions per card are a convenient
   draft convention, not evidence that every competency has exactly three parts.
   Only 14 original question families have worked examples. Neither those
   illustrations nor numeric anchors validate automated grading. Independent
   calibration, unconventional sound answers, and unsuccessful sound decisions
   remain necessary before product use.

## Question-by-question walkthrough

“Keep” means useful preparation content, not a mandate to practice it. “Select”
means choose it for actual responsibilities or a known interview. “Overlap”
identifies an adjacent target to keep distinct. A row is an editorial review
note; the owning card contains the full answer and rubric.

### Common and recruiter

| ID | Question | Review judgment |
| --- | --- | --- |
| C01 | Tell me about yourself | Keep: relevant contribution and direction; avoid resume recitation or a prescribed persona. |
| C02 | Why this role and company? | Keep: informed interest; do not require manufactured passion or insider knowledge. |
| C03 | Why are you leaving? | Keep: concise truthful transition; overlaps C06 but should not demand private disclosure. |
| C04 | What strength would you bring? | Keep: capability plus mechanism; use B01 evidence without repeating the same answer. |
| C05 | What are you improving? | Keep: genuine development with changed behavior; avoid a strategically harmless fake weakness. |
| C06 | Explain this transition or gap | Select when relevant: transferable capability; a gap is not a competency defect. |
| C07 | Compensation expectations | Revised: employer range first, professional persistence, clear package, and truthful response to pressure. |
| C08 | Availability, location, travel, authorization | Retired: checklist facts do not justify a substantive preparation card or scoring dimensions. |
| C09 | What do you want next? | Keep: responsibilities and environment; overlaps career choice LQ08, with a forward-looking target. |
| C10 | Questions for the employer | Keep: due diligence that changes the candidate's decision; not a performance of enthusiasm. |

### Behavioral

| ID | Question | Review judgment |
| --- | --- | --- |
| B01 | Meaningful accomplishment | Keep: actual contribution and useful effect; achievement alone cannot establish decision quality. |
| B02 | Failure or regretted decision | Keep: responsibility and original information; do not require an eventual triumphant outcome. |
| B03 | Disagreement with a colleague | Keep: represent both positions fairly and reach a decision; distinguish from hierarchy in B10. |
| B04 | Difficult feedback received | Keep: examination and response; accepting every criticism is not the ideal answer. |
| B05 | Working through ambiguity | Keep: diagnosis and bounded progress; avoid rewarding either indefinite research or certainty. |
| B06 | Competing priorities or saying no | Keep: real opportunity cost and communication; overlaps DL02/E03 at different scopes. |
| B07 | Influence without authority | Keep: shared context and adoption; persuasion theater or a circulated document is insufficient. |
| B08 | Changing your mind | Keep: evidence changed a belief; the original choice need not have been wrong. |
| B09 | Crisis or sustained pressure | Select a relevant example; separates general coordination from O01's operational response. |
| B10 | Pushback on a leader | Keep: proportionate dissent and limits; close overlap with K08 should not produce duplicate practice. |
| B11 | What makes a decision good? | Added: explicit criteria, uncertainty, timing, outcomes, and learning; tests the model behind the stories. |

### Management fundamentals

| ID | Question | Review judgment |
| --- | --- | --- |
| M01 | Why management and your approach? | Keep: role understanding and demonstrated principles; an explicit “good manager” variant is worth reviewing. |
| M02 | How technically involved? | Keep: context-dependent engagement; reject a universal coding percentage. |
| M03 | Delegating important work | Keep: authority, support, and retained responsibility; distinguish delegation from avoidance. |
| M04 | Helping someone grow | Keep: their goals and capability; do not make the manager the author of another person's success. |
| M05 | Underperformance | Keep: expectations, causes, direct dialogue, and accountability; no universal disciplinary script. |
| M06 | Difficult feedback role-play | Keep and exercise interactively later; a generic monologue does not prove responsive judgment. |
| M07 | Useful one-to-ones | Keep, lower priority than actual hard decisions; ritual and fixed cadence are not the outcome. |
| M08 | Building a hiring process | Select for hiring responsibility; distinguish process design from a disputed hiring decision in HR02. |
| M09 | Healthy and effective team | Keep: already an explicit good-looks-like question; balance purpose, capability, candor, and sustainability. |
| M10 | Employee upset about promotion | Keep: individual expectations and fair next actions; HR04 evaluates the broader calibration system. |

### Staff and principal IC

| ID | Question | Review judgment |
| --- | --- | --- |
| T01 | Significant technical project | Keep: depth, direction, contribution, and adoption; needs a challenging technical follow-up rather than generic polish. |
| T02 | Difficult technical tradeoff | Keep: application in one real choice; TS09 now supplies explicit technical decision criteria. |
| T03 | Debt or large migration | Keep: costs, transition, adoption, retirement; scope is broader than one rewrite story. |
| T04 | Harsh review and junior engineer | Keep: concrete scenario combining technical standards with care; strong direct interview relevance. |
| T05 | Making others effective | Keep: enabling capability and avoiding a permanent bottleneck; do not reward unlimited glue work. |

This track is thin relative to management. Role archetypes, senior-versus-staff
expectations, choosing leverage, and strategy through influence need a focused
follow-up; larger scope or more meetings cannot stand in for staff contribution.

### Executive

| ID | Question | Review judgment |
| --- | --- | --- |
| E01 | Develop and evaluate strategy | Keep: diagnosis and consequential choices; explicitly ask what makes a strategy good as a variant. |
| E02 | First 90 days | Keep: targeted learning with proportionate urgency; a rigid calendar is weak preparation. |
| E03 | Resource allocation | Keep: business objective, alternatives, and opportunity cost; must use actual financial authority. |
| E04 | Change the organization | Keep: system diagnosis and design; G06 concerns carrying out the transition. |
| E05 | Engineering value | Keep: a measure informs a decision; no business-causality claim from proximity alone. |

Executive breadth is useful but incomplete. CEO/board partnership, functional
mandate, financial literacy, and executive-team conflict need role-specific
research. They should not be silently represented by generic manager answers.

### Delivery and execution

| ID | Question | Review judgment |
| --- | --- | --- |
| DL01 | Estimates and commitments | Keep: basis, confidence, dependencies, and revision; no false precision. |
| DL02 | Fixed deadline, insufficient capacity | Keep: essential outcome and feasible choices; overlaps B06's prioritization at a different target. |
| DL03 | Project recovery | Keep: change a diagnosed cause; changing the date or demanding effort is insufficient. |
| DL04 | Multi-team dependencies | Select cross-team work: feasible agreements and usable ownership, not coordination heroics. |
| DL05 | Process improving delivery | Keep: problem, adoption cost, and observed benefit; no framework compliance scoring. |
| DL06 | Release readiness | Keep: consequences and relevant proof; distinguish from operational capability in O06. |
| DL07 | Stopping after investment | Keep: future value and responsible closure; useful test of sunk-cost reasoning. |
| DL08 | Slow execution versus blocked decisions | Keep: trace actual waiting; do not assume every delay is a decision problem. |

### Reliability and operations

| ID | Question | Review judgment |
| --- | --- | --- |
| O01 | Organizing incident response | Select operational responsibility: mitigation, roles, and verified recovery. |
| O02 | Reliability versus features | Keep for service leaders: user consequences and explicit tradeoffs; no universal target. |
| O03 | Useful incident review | Keep: already defines good practice; prioritize changed behavior over action-item counts. |
| O04 | On-call overload and toil | Select: diagnosis, relief, and durable shared capability; resilience is not unlimited availability. |
| O05 | Risky rollout and rollback | Select: actual state and recovery mechanisms; “we can roll back” is not enough. |
| O06 | Operational readiness | Select: ownership and proven mechanisms; overlaps DL06 but has a post-release operating target. |
| O07 | Incident communication | Select: verified audience-useful updates; can be a follow-up to O01 when the loop is short. |
| O08 | Security vulnerability | Select: risk and expert partnership; general leadership preparation cannot certify security expertise. |

### Product and business judgment

| ID | Question | Review judgment |
| --- | --- | --- |
| P01 | Request without a clear problem | Keep: clarify outcome while respecting real urgency and product authority. |
| P02 | Direct customer learning | Select where expected: behavior and sampling limits; engineers need not invent research ownership. |
| P03 | Testing a risky assumption | Keep: material uncertainty and evidence that can change a decision. |
| P04 | Conflicting customer demands | Select commercial exposure: commitments, value, and continuing cost. |
| P05 | Shipped feature unused | Keep: verify measurement and diagnose before adding code; delivery differs from value. |
| P06 | Engineering/product/design decisions | Keep: shared outcomes and accountable closure; avoid one preferred operating-model script. |
| P07 | Technical choice and business viability | Keep at appropriate scope: explain a mechanism and bound causal claims. |
| P08 | Experiment challenges your idea | Keep, or pair with P03: interpretation and stopping; close overlap with B08's belief update. |

### Managing managers and change

| ID | Question | Review judgment |
| --- | --- | --- |
| G01 | Developing another manager | Select managers of managers: their capability and team effects; not M04 with bigger numbers. |
| G02 | Skip-levels without undermining managers | Select: listening, follow-up, and one usable responsibility chain. |
| G03 | Decision rights between teams | Keep for cross-team leadership: decisions and interfaces rather than reporting lines. |
| G04 | Key-person dependence | Keep: practical transfer and tested continuity; declaring a backup is insufficient. |
| G05 | Acquired organization integration | Specialist selection: acquisition purpose and obligations; low general preparation priority. |
| G06 | Carrying out a reorganization | Select: transition and continuity; E04 owns the design choice. |
| G07 | Managing former peers | Select for this transition: fairness and changed mandate; belongs near first-time management. |
| G08 | Skeptical or exhausted people during change | Keep: understand history and capacity; do not require enthusiasm as evidence of adoption. |

### Talent decisions

| ID | Question | Review judgment |
| --- | --- | --- |
| HR01 | New-hire effectiveness | Keep for managers: useful work and independence; W07 is the remote-access variant/extension. |
| HR02 | Interviewer disagreement | Select hiring authority: evidence and resolution; M08 concerns the process. |
| HR03 | Potential without experience | Keep for people decisions: transferable evidence and feasible support; charisma is not potential. |
| HR04 | Promotion fairness across teams | Select calibration responsibility: opportunity access and consistent expectations. |
| HR05 | Compensation fairness with limited budget | Select actual authority: relevant data and feasible correction; no invented formula. |
| HR06 | Harmful high performer | Keep for managers: output does not excuse harm; K04 owns initial reporting and process. |
| HR07 | Important person wants to leave | Keep: listen, offer honest options, respect the choice, and plan continuity. |
| HR08 | Significant capacity reduction | Select an actual loop/role need: human consequences and commitment reset; not a routine universal question. |

### Technical strategy

| ID | Question | Review judgment |
| --- | --- | --- |
| TS01 | Standards versus autonomy | Keep: shared costs and proportionate exceptions; uniformity is not inherently good. |
| TS02 | Build, buy, or reuse | Keep: fit and whole-life obligations; avoid comparing unlike cost models. |
| TS03 | Useful internal platform | Select platform responsibilities: consumer value, burden, adoption, and ownership. |
| TS04 | Architecture disagreement | Keep: substantive evidence and closure; differs from defining technical quality in TS09. |
| TS05 | Scaling bottleneck | Select technical depth: actual workload and diagnosis; fashionable architecture is not a result. |
| TS06 | Unnecessary complexity | Keep: preserve behavior and avoid exporting burden to consumers. |
| TS07 | Emerging technology | Keep: bounded comparison and operating implications; strong overlap with AI01 when AI is the example. |
| TS08 | Temporary versus durable investment | Keep: horizon, real exit cost, and future ownership; can deepen a T02 episode. |
| TS09 | What makes a technical decision good? | Added: explicit technical fit, whole-system costs, risk, and evolving context. |

### Culture, inclusion, and ethics

| ID | Question | Review judgment |
| --- | --- | --- |
| K01 | Candor and high standards | Keep: practical routes and actual responses; slogans are not evidence. |
| K02 | More inclusive participation | Keep a concrete episode: barrier, intervention, and effect; intent alone is weak. |
| K03 | Opportunities and enabling work | Keep for work allocation: access, support, credit, and sustainability. |
| K04 | Harmful behavior reported | Keep: responsible initial handling; not a universal legal or disciplinary script. |
| K05 | Values versus rewards | Keep: inspect consequential incentives rather than rewriting slogans. |
| K06 | Different working norms | Keep as a practical scenario: actual requirements versus style preferences. |
| K07 | Questionable customer-data use | Select relevant scope: purpose, authorization, and safer alternatives with expertise. |
| K08 | Disagreement improving a decision | Keep: decision environment and dissent; B03/B10 evaluate the candidate's particular disagreement. |

### Distributed work and communication

| ID | Question | Review judgment |
| --- | --- | --- |
| W01 | Async versus meeting | Keep: purpose and channel fit; no async-only dogma. |
| W02 | Fairness across time zones | Select distributed responsibility: real burden and decision access, not availability scoring. |
| W03 | Hybrid proximity bias | Select hybrid work: information and opportunity patterns; overlaps K02 with a location mechanism. |
| W04 | Useful decision record | Keep: already asks what good looks like; conclusion, status, ownership, and findability. |
| W05 | Useful recurring meeting | Lower priority but useful: intended outcome and total cost; routine logistics alone are not enough. |
| W06 | Conflict through remote messages | Select if relevant, or use as B03 follow-up: missing context and substantive repair. |
| W07 | Remote newcomer context | Review possible HR01 variant: distinct value depends on distributed-access and relationship barriers. |
| W08 | Language and access needs | Keep substantive participation expectations; do not grade accent, speed, or personal disclosure. |

### Personal leadership and career judgment

| ID | Question | Review judgment |
| --- | --- | --- |
| LQ01 | Managing up amid ambiguity | Keep: clarify real conflicts and workable options; “managing up” alone is not a mechanism. |
| LQ02 | Problematic manager decisions | Keep, with B10 overlap: work impact and bounded response, not diagnosing character. |
| LQ03 | Sustainable work under excess demand | Review B06/B09 overlap: select the sustainability target rather than repeating prioritization. |
| LQ04 | Seeking support and challenge | Useful optional reflection: changed thinking and retained responsibility, not name-dropping. |
| LQ05 | Learning unfamiliar responsibilities | Keep: gaps, application, feedback, and limits; course attendance is insufficient. |
| LQ06 | Repairing trust after a broken commitment | Keep: concrete repair and sustained behavior; an apology does not prove restoration. |
| LQ07 | Readiness for broader responsibility | Select career/scope discussions: evidence and operating changes; tenure is not readiness. |
| LQ08 | Consequential career tradeoff | Optional reflection with C09 overlap: make judgment understandable without grading priorities. |

### AI judgment and leadership

| ID | Question | Review judgment |
| --- | --- | --- |
| AI01 | Introducing AI assistance | Select a real role need; overlaps TS07's technology adoption, with permissions and human review. |
| AI02 | Productivity effect | Keep for AI leadership: baseline, task selection, downstream work, and inference limits. |
| AI03 | Reviewing AI-generated code | Keep for relevant engineering work: understanding and independent proof; ownership remains human. |
| AI04 | Learning without shaming skepticism | Select team adoption: supported capability, not compulsory enthusiasm. |
| AI05 | AI product quality | Select product responsibility: task-specific failures and independent evaluation; no demo-only evidence. |
| AI06 | Agent data and tool authority | Select agent responsibility: purpose, permissions, execution boundaries, and containment. |
| AI07 | Guesses becoming facts | Keep where generated material is used; provenance and consequential reuse, with strong AI05 overlap. |
| AI08 | Workforce and investment uncertainty | Select executive planning: scenarios and full-work effects; no vendor-uplift-to-headcount shortcut. |

AI is contemporary but should not dominate a role that does not own these
decisions. Forecasts need continual review; this bank establishes neither a
universal productivity effect nor a staffing prediction.

## Proposed next content work

These are review proposals, not additional cards already present:

- Explicitly define a good manager and good staff/principal contribution, then
  link those criteria to existing episodes and scenarios.
- Strengthen executive mandate, CEO/board partnership, and financial tradeoffs
  where the target role calls for them.
- Expand the new decision-quality illustrations into independently written
  historical answers and unconventional but sound alternatives. Test C07
  against a disclosed range, persistent refusal, and candidate-chosen exceptions.
- Resolve flagged overlaps using actual interview loops; keep different
  judgment targets even when they share one evidence episode.
- Calibrate the draft anchors independently before using them for automated
  feedback. Do not optimize for a predetermined question count.

# Research and source ledger

Initial research checked on 30 September 2026; decision-quality and negotiation
follow-up checked on 1 October 2026. Will Larson and Michael Lopp are the
central references. Additional contemporary engineering leaders supply concrete
practices and useful counterpoints. Older publications remain included where
they explain a current practice; dates are visible rather than treating all
advice as recent.

## Findings and tensions

The following is our synthesis. Each source below records the narrower author
claim that informed it. Question wording, profile mappings, scoring dimensions,
numeric anchors, and sample answers are ours unless explicitly stated otherwise.

| Perspective | Implication for our content | Limit or tension |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Larson: assess the skills the particular role needs | Ask for evidence of relevant judgment; use role-specific criteria | A polished story alone cannot establish actual performance |
| Lopp: concrete professional stories and reflection | Probe decisions, feedback, growth, and candidate curiosity | His reflection questionnaire explicitly has no right answer or grade |
| Fournier: management includes delivery and people work | Separate manager contribution from coding and architecture | First-time managers need transferable evidence, not an invented management history |
| Hogan: make feedback and delegation concrete | Ask what was communicated, agreed, supported, and revisited | Naming a framework is weaker than demonstrating its use |
| Reilly: staff work includes enabling others | Value coordination, adoption, and shared capability | Helping everyone can become an unrecognized burden rather than sustainable leadership |
| Majors: management is a distinct career track | Accept an intentional IC career or a return to it | Do not treat management as the default definition of advancement |
| Huston: team success must be sustainable | Look for team capability and health alongside delivery | Constant availability is not a useful leadership quality proxy |
| Buriticá and Turnbull: technical collaboration includes care and standards | Examine how candidates handle review conflict and power | Kindness does not require accepting defective code |
| Skelton/Pais: team interfaces and consumer burden matter | Examine decision rights and platform usefulness | Framework vocabulary is not evidence of judgment |
| Torres: discovery and evaluation need explicit assumptions | Ask what evidence would change a product or AI decision | A promising demonstration cannot establish general usefulness |
| Edmondson: candor and accountability can coexist | Examine routes for questions, concerns, and dissent | Silence alone does not reveal someone's psychological state |
| Osmani: AI assistance still needs human judgment | Examine learning, verification, and ownership | His broad productivity claims are not our assumed baseline |
| METR: productivity estimates depend on task selection and study design | Require bounded inference from local AI evidence | One study does not establish a universal speedup or slowdown |
| Google SRE and GitLab: operating practices need clear ownership and communication | Examine response roles, decision records, and work access | Specific company policies and thresholds are examples, not hiring rules |
| Structured-interview methodology | Anchor feedback to observable answer content | A structured format does not automatically validate our rubric |

Five tensions require explicit editorial decisions:

1. **Chemistry and polish.** Lopp's older screening essay uses conversational
   impressions. Larson warns about accidentally assessing polish. We evaluate
   understandable, relevant content; we do not score eye contact, accent,
   enthusiasm, pauses, social similarity, or whether someone asks a question
   before time runs out.
2. **Potential versus demonstrated experience.** Fournier discusses hiring
   first-time managers; Larson's loop design emphasizes demonstrated skills.
   We label transferable evidence separately and allow situational exercises.
   A hypothetical plan never becomes evidence that the candidate has done it.
3. **Hands-on leadership.** Majors and Larson discuss technical currency and
   changing expectations. We require alignment with the actual role, not a
   fixed coding percentage for every manager. Inspecting important work and
   prescribing every implementation detail are different behaviors.
4. **Deciding versus delegating.** Lopp's R07 criticizes a delegated decision
   described as escaping its consequences, whereas Hogan's H02 explains useful
   delegation. We distinguish clear authority and retained accountability from
   avoidance; we do not turn either essay into an absolute rule about who must
   make every decision.
5. **Decision quality versus hindsight.** L10 distinguishes decisions from
   outcomes; L21 explains why designs can reasonably fall behind a changing
   quality bar. We examine original reasoning and current fit separately, and
   still use subsequent evidence to test assumptions. A good-looking process
   is not immunity from learning or consequences.

## Source records

Coverage labels: **article** means the author article was read; **selected
chapter/talk** means identified passages were read, not the whole work; **overview** means
only the author's or publisher's description was reviewed. An overview does not
support detailed claims about unread chapters. Where a date is not listed, the
page was verified but its original publication date was not established here.

### Will Larson

- **L01 — [Getting to yes](https://lethain.com/getting-to-yes/)** (2021; article).
  Begin manager hiring with shared role expectations and essential skills.
  Used for role selection and M01.
- **L02 — [Designing interview loops](https://lethain.com/designing-interview-loops/)**
  (2018; article). Explicit skill rubrics and opportunities to demonstrate them;
  avoid accidentally assessing presentation polish. Used for evaluation design.
- **L03 — [Interviewing senior engineering leaders](https://lethain.com/interviewing-senior-eng-leaders/)**
  (2020; article). Exercises can reveal leadership judgment through editing,
  analysis, and feedback. Used for M06 and E04. We do not adopt backchannel checks.
- **L04 — [Interviewing engineering executives](https://lethain.com/interviewing-eng-executives/)**
  (2023; article). Examine executive skills, company challenges, functional
  expertise, and historical behavior. Used for executive question selection.
- **L05 — [Getting an engineering executive job](https://lethain.com/getting-engineering-executive-job/)**
  (2023; article). Clarify motivation, prepare relevant experiences, and learn
  the company's needs. Used for C02 and executive adaptations.
- **L06 — [Interviewing for staff-plus roles](https://staffeng.com/guides/interviewing-staff-plus-roles/)**
  (article/guide). Staff loops vary; understand format and prepare relevant work
  deep dives. Used for T01 and preparation selection.
- **L07 — [Diagnosis for strategy](https://lethain.com/diagnosis-for-strategy/)**
  (22 February 2025; article). Investigate facts, perspectives, and constraints
  before choosing a solution. Used for B05 and E01.
- **L08 — [Is this strategy any good?](https://lethain.com/is-this-strategy-any-good/)**
  (27 March 2025; article). Evaluate strategy through impact and refinement;
  learning costs matter. Used for B08 and E01.
- **L09 — [Good engineering management is a fad](https://lethain.com/good-eng-mgmt-is-a-fad/)**
  (26 October 2025; article). Management expectations change; execution, team,
  ownership, and alignment remain useful concerns. Used for M02 and M09.
- **L10 — [Inspected trust](https://lethain.com/inspection/)**
  (2021; article). Inspect important interpretations; distinguish decisions
  from outcomes. Used for B02, T02, and E04.
- **L11 — [Measuring engineering organizations](https://lethain.com/measuring-engineering-organizations/)**
  (2023; article/book chapter). Measures serve different decisions and
  stakeholders. Used for E05; no individual output leaderboard is prescribed.
- **L12 — [Your first 90 days as CTO or VP Engineering](https://lethain.com/first-ninety-days-cto-vpe/)**
  (article/book chapter). Learn business and organizational context; adapt
  onboarding to urgency and company size. Used for E02.
- **L13 — [Roadmap decisions rather than dates](https://lethain.com/decisions-not-dates/)**
  (11 August 2026; article). Unresolved decisions and dependencies can constrain
  execution; make them explicit and use exploration to resolve them. Used for
  DL08. We do not assume that every delay is a decision problem.
- **L14 — [Moving from an orchestration-heavy to leadership-heavy management role](https://lethain.com/orchestration-heavy-leadership-heavy/)**
  (19 July 2025; article). Selecting problems and solutions can be a distinct
  responsibility from orchestrating execution. Used for P01/LQ05; the actual
  role determines whether this responsibility belongs to the candidate.
- **L15 — [How to create software quality](https://lethain.com/quality/)**
  (16 June 2024; selected article sections on quality, context, and complexity).
  Quality expectations depend on the system and its consequences. Used for
  DL06/TS06; no universal test count or release procedure is prescribed.
- **L16 — [How should we control access to user data?](https://lethain.com/user-data-access-strategy/)**
  (7 February 2025; article/public strategy chapter). Access controls must fit
  legitimate workflows and support auditable decisions. Used for K07/AI06;
  the essay's hypothetical thresholds are not universal requirements.
- **L17 — [Performance & Compensation (for Eng Execs)](https://lethain.com/performance-compensation-process-exec/)**
  (3 September 2023; selected sections on competing goals, levels, and
  calibration). People processes involve fairness, feedback, cost, and time
  tradeoffs. Used for HR04/HR05/HR06; not a universal compensation formula.
- **L18 — [Running your engineering onboarding program](https://lethain.com/engineering-onboarding-programs/)**
  (6 March 2023; selected introduction and program-role sections). Onboarding
  needs ownership and an ongoing program adapted to new hires. Used for HR01;
  no fixed duration is required.
- **L19 — [Engineering's role in Mergers & Acquisitions](https://lethain.com/engineering-in-mergers-and-acquisition/)**
  (27 February 2023; selected evaluation and integration sections). Engineering
  should understand the acquisition thesis, technical risks, and integration
  consequences. Used for G05; not legal or investment guidance.
- **L20 — [Writing an engineering strategy](https://lethain.com/eng-strategies/)**
  (13 February 2023; selected diagnosis, guiding-policy, decision-rights, and
  transition sections; follow-up checked 1 October 2026). Technical choices
  should connect to the organization's circumstances and shared direction.
  Used for TS09; his example approval processes are not universal requirements.
- **L21 — [Managing technical quality in a codebase](https://lethain.com/managing-technical-quality/)**
  (17 October 2020; selected opening, problem, and lightweight-intervention
  sections; follow-up checked 1 October 2026). Requirements and appropriate
  quality investment change as a company changes. Used for TS09; a design's
  current limitations do not alone prove that its original choice was unsound.

### Michael Lopp

- **R01 — [The Sanity Check](https://randsinrepose.com/archives/the-sanity-check/)**
  (2007; article). A screen explores professional history, communication, and
  candidate questions. Used for C01/C10, with the chemistry limits above.
- **R02 — [Your Professional Growth Questionnaire](https://randsinrepose.com/archives/your-professional-growth-questionnaire/)**
  (2018; article). Reflect on strengths, growth, feedback, failures, and desired
  next work. Explicitly not a graded questionnaire. Used for C04/C05/C09/B04.
- **R03 — [Act Last, Read the Room, and Taste the Soup](https://randsinrepose.com/archives/act-last-read-the-room-and-taste-the-soup/)**
  (2018; article). Hear other perspectives before anchoring decisions; inspect
  without solving everything yourself. Used for B03/B07/M03.
- **R04 — [A Performance Question](https://randsinrepose.com/archives/a-performance-question/)**
  (2018; article). Performance concerns should receive clear feedback and a
  chance for dialogue before formal escalation. Used for M05, not legal advice.
- **R05 — [Barely Treading Water](https://randsinrepose.com/archives/barely-treading-water/)**
  (19 May 2026; article). Admit overload, seek candid help, reprioritize,
  delegate, and communicate refusals. Used for B06/B09.
- **R06 — [The Update, The Vent, and The Disaster](https://randsinrepose.com/archives/the-update-the-vent-and-the-disaster/)**
  (2010; article). One-to-ones offer listening and learning beyond status.
  Used for M07. We adapt rigid cadence recommendations and do not adopt mood
  classifications as an interview-scoring method.
- **R07 — [Seven Decisions](https://randsinrepose.com/archives/seven-decisions/)**
  (11 November 2025; article; follow-up checked 1 October 2026). Examines
  explainable rationale, decision context, and choices that avoid discomfort or
  responsibility. Used for B11. Its categories are reflective observations,
  not a validated hierarchy or a prohibition on accountable delegation.

### Other contemporary leaders

- **H01 — Lara Hogan, [The Feedback Equation](https://larahogan.me/blog/feedback-equation/)**
  (2018; article). Separate observations from judgments, explain impact, and
  invite response or action. Used for M06/B04.
- **H02 — Lara Hogan, [Delegation is an art](https://larahogan.me/blog/delegation-is-an-art/)**
  (2022; article). Agree outcomes, support, and escalation conditions while
  giving the delegate room to choose the approach. Used for M03.
- **H03 — Lara Hogan, [What are you optimizing for?](https://larahogan.me/blog/what-are-you-optimizing-for/)**
  (2019; article). Explore another person's priorities rather than assuming
  shared goals. Used for B03/B07/M10.
- **H04 — Lara Hogan, [When to delegate, when to say no](https://larahogan.me/blog/when-to-delegate-when-to-say-no/)**
  (2022; article). Consider the work and the person's circumstances when
  prioritizing or delegating. Used for B06/M04.
- **H05 — Lara Hogan, [Why can't they just...? Revisited](https://larahogan.me/blog/why-cant-they-just-revisited/)**
  (22 April 2026; article). Understand legitimate concerns, share constraints,
  and distinguish what people can control or influence. Used for G08/LQ01;
  raising a problem does not require already knowing the solution.
- **H06 — Lara Hogan, [AI 'aha' team meetings](https://larahogan.me/blog/ai-aha-team-meetings/)**
  (20 March 2026; article). Peer learning can make AI experimentation and
  mistakes discussable. Used for AI04. A meeting is one option, not a required
  learning style or a reason to pressure people to disclose mistakes publicly.
- **H07 — Lara Hogan, [Recognition and rewards at work](https://larahogan.me/blog/what-you-recognize-and-reward/)**
  (6 March 2023; selected introductory principle). What an organization
  recognizes and rewards communicates its priorities. Used for K05; detailed
  reward-system design on our card is editorial synthesis.
- **F01 — Camille Fournier, [Ask the CTO: How do I hire managers?](https://www.oreilly.com/content/ask-the-cto-how-do-i-hire-managers/)**
  (2016; article). Direct interview guidance: probe delivery, mentoring,
  process, hiring, goals, and conflict with examples or role-play. Used for
  M01/M04/M07/M08/M10. Our cards paraphrase themes, not her full question list.
- **TR01 — Tanya Reilly, [Being Glue](https://www.noidea.dog/glue)**
  (2018 talk; selected author-transcript sections on glue, promotion, and track
  choice). Coordination work enables teams but can
  become an unfair or career-limiting burden. Used for T05.
- **TR02 — Tanya Reilly, [The Staff Engineer's Path](https://www.noidea.dog/staff)**
  (author overview). Describes big-picture thinking, project execution, and
  enabling others. Used to organize the IC family; full book not read here.
- **TR03 — Tanya Reilly, [How to make a big technical change](https://www.noidea.dog/blog/getting-there-from-here)**
  (2018; article). A migration requires adoption work and a completion measure,
  not only a new implementation. Used for technical change; we do not prescribe
  the essay's suggestions to intentionally degrade an old service.
- **TR04 — Tanya Reilly, [Delegation means not answering all the questions](https://www.noidea.dog/blog/delegation-means-not-answering-all-the-questions)**
  (2018; article). Redirect decisions to their owner rather than intercepting
  communications and visibility. Used for enabling others.
- **J01 — Charity Majors, [The Engineer/Manager Pendulum](https://charity.wtf/p/the-engineer-manager-pendulum)**
  (2017; article). IC and management careers can alternate; management is a
  distinct profession. Used for C09/M01; technical-currency advice is contextual.
- **U01 — Cate Huston, [The Engineering Leader, chapter 14: What Good Looks Like](https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/the-engineering-leader/9781098154059/ch14.html)**
  (2024; selected chapter). Sustainable team functioning, feedback, growth, and
  healthy conflict matter more than a leader's constant availability. Used for
  B01/M09. Public publisher preview linked; selected chapter read separately.
- **U02 — Juan Pablo Buriticá and James Turnbull, [Engineering Leadership: The Hard Parts, chapter 9](https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/engineering-leadership-the/9781098175627/ch09.html)**
  (January 2026; selected passage, “Navigating code-review drama”). A harsh
  review scenario tests care, actual code assessment, and coaching; Turnbull
  explicitly describes using it in senior-engineer interviews. Used for T04.
- **D01 — Sarah Drasner, [Engineering Management for the Rest of Us](https://www.engmanagement.dev/)**
  (2022; author overview). Frames leadership around people and learned practice.
  Supplementary reading; no detailed card criteria attributed to the unread book.

### Additional topic research

- **DM01 — Dan McKinley, [Choose Boring Technology](https://mcfunley.com/choose-boring-technology)**
  (30 March 2015; article; follow-up checked 1 October 2026). Technology costs
  include operations and cognitive burden across the organization; novelty
  needs a reason that existing options cannot serve well. Used for TS09.
  Familiar tools are a contextual default, not an absolute ban on innovation;
  examples from 2015 are not current product recommendations.
- **TP01 — Matthew Skelton and Manuel Pais, [Team Topologies: Key Concepts](https://teamtopologies.com/key-concepts)**
  (official concept guide). Team interfaces, cognitive load, and platforms as
  products inform G03/TS03. We do not require candidates to memorize team types
  or treat the model as universally appropriate; full book not read here.
- **OS01 — Addy Osmani, [Leading Effective Engineering Teams in the Age of GenAI](https://addyo.substack.com/p/leading-effective-engineering-teams-c9b)**
  (19 March 2025; selected opening and leadership sections). Human judgment,
  learning, and verification remain important alongside AI assistance. Used
  for AI01/AI03; the essay's broad productivity claims are not adopted as facts.
- **ME01 — METR, [We are Changing our Developer Productivity Experiment Design](https://metr.org/blog/2026-02-24-uplift-update/)**
  (24 February 2026; research update). Selection effects, changing tasks, and
  concurrent work complicate productivity estimates; the authors caution
  against a reliable current uplift estimate from their new data. Used for
  AI02. Earlier results from a specific setting are not generalized to all teams.
- **GI01 — GitLab, [Communication handbook](https://handbook.gitlab.com/handbook/communication/)**
  (live organizational handbook checked 30 September 2026; selected async,
  written conclusions, availability, and clear-communication sections). Inform
  W01/W04/W05/W08. One company's policies are examples, not universal standards.
- **AE01 — Amy Edmondson, [Leading in Tough Times](https://www.hbs.edu/recruiting/guides-and-stories/leading-in-tough-times)**
  (22 November 2022; Harvard Business School author discussion). Psychological
  safety supports candor and participation alongside accountability. Used for
  K01/K08; no personality or psychological diagnosis is inferred from answers.
- **PT01 — Teresa Torres, [Assumption Testing](https://www.producttalk.org/assumption-testing/)**
  (18 October 2023; selected introduction, assumption types, and testing
  sections). Test the assumptions behind options rather than only asking
  whether people like a solution. Used for P02/P03/P08.
- **PT02 — Teresa Torres, [AI Evals: A Hands-On Guide for Product Teams](https://www.producttalk.org/ai-evals/)**
  (2 September 2026; selected opening and correctness sections). Define useful,
  context-specific output and inspect errors rather than delegating correctness
  to the model provider. Used for AI05/AI07. Her interview-coach example concerns
  customer-discovery interviews; application to job interviews is our extrapolation.
- **SR01 — Google, [SRE Workbook: Example Error Budget Policy](https://sre.google/workbook/error-budget-policy/)**
  (2018; public example). Balance reliability and feature work through explicit
  expectations and decisions. Used for O02; example thresholds are not mandates.
- **SR02 — Google, [SRE Workbook: Incident Response](https://sre.google/workbook/incident-response/)**
  (2018; selected response-role discussion and incident cases). Coordination,
  mitigation, and communication require deliberate ownership. Used for O01/O07;
  incident process should fit the organization's scale and risk.
- **PC01 — Marty Cagan, [Meaningful Transformation](https://www.svpg.com/meaningful-transformation/)**
  (14 May 2020; article). Product outcomes depend on collaboration, trust, and
  real decision authority. Used for P06/G08; we do not require every organization
  to adopt a single product operating model.

### Negotiation

- **N01 — Patrick McKenzie, [Salary Negotiation: Make More Money, Be More Valued](https://www.kalzumeus.com/2012/01/23/salary-negotiation/)**
  (23 January 2012; selected first-number and package sections; follow-up
  checked 1 October 2026). Argues for avoiding a premature candidate anchor
  and examining the package. Used narrowly for C07, with the user-requested
  employer-range-first default. This older tactical reference supplies no
  current salary data. We do not adopt its claims about universal leverage,
  risk-free negotiation, market conditions, or artificial form-entry numbers.

### Evaluation methodology

- **A01 — US Office of Personnel Management, [Developing a customized rating scale](https://www.opm.gov/frequently-asked-questions/assessment-policy-faq/structured-interviews/how-do-i-develop-a-customized-rating-scale-for-structured-interviews/)**
  (agency guidance). Behavioral anchors are question-specific and need subject
  matter expert involvement. Used for calibration methodology, not an assertion
  that this content has been validated or is an official hiring instrument.

## Attribution on question cards

**Direct interview guidance** means a source discusses interviewing for that
question/theme. **Practice extrapolation** means a leadership practice has been
translated into a question and answer criteria. **Editorial synthesis** means
the wording and target are chiefly our proposal, with a source providing limited
context. Even direct guidance does not make our numeric anchors author-approved.

No source establishes a universal “correct” answer, a validated leadership
score, or a hiring probability. The library intentionally records alternatives
and limits so that an evaluator can distinguish unfamiliar choices from poor
reasoning.

questions.adaptation: Current role, two evidence-backed episodes, target responsibilities, and user-stated direction. IC: technical contribution and collaboration. EM: team delivery and people development. Executive: business problem, organizational responsibility, and peer partnership. Do not merely replace the title while reusing the same claims.
questions.alternatives: A career changer can lead with the connecting capability and acknowledge the transition. A nonlinear career need not be apologized for. Personal context is optional.
questions.answer: Start with the work you do now and the problems you are good at solving. Select one or two relevant experiences, explain your actual contribution, and connect them to the next role. A roughly one-to-two-minute version is useful for rehearsal, not a scoring requirement. Avoid narrating every job or listing unsupported adjectives.

examples.body:
### Staff IC

> I'm a backend engineer, and much of my recent work has been making changes
> across service boundaries easier to deliver. In my current role I led the
> design and rollout of a shared event interface. I owned the compatibility
> plan and worked with the service owners on adoption; they did most of the
> changes in their own services. That experience made me interested in work
> where the technical decision and how teams adopt it matter equally. This
> role appears to have that scope, and I'd like to understand how technical
> direction is shared between staff engineers and the team leads.

**Why it works:** Identifies a capability, a bounded contribution, and a reason
for the next role. It does not imply direct reports or claim every team's result.
**Useful follow-up:** What tradeoff shaped the compatibility plan?

### Engineering manager

> I manage a product engineering team. The part of the role I enjoy most is
> helping people take ownership of delivery while making difficult priorities
> explicit. During a recent launch, I worked with product to reduce the initial
> scope and helped two engineers lead the rollout. They owned the technical
> decisions; I handled expectations, staffing, and coaching. We delivered the
> agreed release, although we still had support work afterward. I'm looking
> for a role where I can keep developing engineers and improve how a team
> turns uncertain requirements into reliable commitments.

**Why it works:** Shows management actions and credits technical ownership.
The unfinished support work provides an honest limit.
**Useful follow-up:** How did reducing scope affect customers and the team?

### Engineering executive

> I lead engineering in a software business where customers need dependable
> integrations. My recent focus has been aligning engineering investment with
> the commitments sales and product make. I partnered with those leaders to
> separate urgent customer work from reusable integration capabilities, and
> changed ownership so teams could make more of those tradeoffs themselves.
> Engineering owned delivery; the commercial results also depended on product
> and sales. I'm interested in this opportunity because it seems to need that
> combination of technical direction and business coordination. I'd want to
> learn whether that is the mandate you actually have in mind.

**Why it works:** Connects organizational work to a business problem while
avoiding a claim of sole commercial causality.
**Useful follow-up:** Which investment did you decline, and why?
