questions.adaptation: Target job description, dated company research, user priorities, and a relevant episode. A first-time leader can explain both the interest and what they need to learn; do not invent management success.
questions.alternatives: Early in a recruiter conversation, state what is promising and what remains unknown. Joining for a specific mission, domain, technical challenge, or working arrangement can all be defensible.
questions.answer: Name a concrete feature of the role or company, explain why it matters to you, and connect a relevant capability to that need. Separate public facts from hypotheses you want to test. For an executive, explain why the business challenge and responsibility appeal, beyond the title. For any role, financial stability and work arrangements can be legitimate motivations too.

questions.alternatives: A short factual explanation can be sufficient. Compensation, relocation, caregiving, health, scope, values, or stability can be legitimate reasons. Private details need not be offered.

Executive: judgment or systems with an actual business connection. Match the strongest truthful example, not the most prestigious employer.
questions.alternatives: A quieter strength such as dependable follow-through or clear written reasoning can be valuable. No heroic or numerical result is required if the effect is concrete.

questions.adaptation: User-selected growth area, episode, received feedback, and actual experiment. IC: e.g. surfacing risk earlier. EM: e.g. delegating decisions. Executive: e.g. inviting dissent before committing. These are possibilities, never inferred weaknesses in the user's profile.
questions.alternatives: A capability the candidate has not yet learned can be discussed honestly, with a credible plan. Progress can be qualitative; claiming to have eliminated the weakness is unnecessary.
questions.answer: Name a real, work-relevant pattern, explain its effect, and show what you have changed. Describe how you check progress and what remains difficult. “I care too much” without a real cost or behavioral change is weak. Do not invent a strategically harmless weakness or demand private disclosure.

> I used to hold onto uncertain work too long before asking for help. In one
> project, that meant our dependency risk reached my manager only when the

questions.variants: Why did you change fields? Why the shorter tenure? What connects these different roles?

questions.adaptation: User-confirmed expectations, location, currency, package structure, and boundaries. Executive or startup packages may need more components clarified; no assumed preference for equity over cash.
questions.alternatives: If a usable employer range is already disclosed, clarify its meaning instead of mechanically asking again. A candidate may choose to state a researched target or a genuine hard boundary; this is an explicit departure from the range-first default. Do not grade their need to keep a process moving or their ultimate compensation preference.
questions.answer: First seek the employer's budgeted range for this role and level before volunteering your own number. Ask firmly and professionally; if they redirect, repeat the request with its purpose: establishing whether the scope and package can fit before anchoring expectations. Clarify base, variable pay, equity, currency, location basis, and level as relevant. A vague “competitive” answer is not a range; a very broad band needs clarification about this hire. Do not reveal your private minimum or salary history by default. If disclosure is refused, make the next step explicit: defer numbers, continue by choice, give a deliberately chosen position, or stop. Persist in seeking the range, while leaving that final tradeoff with the candidate. A disclosed band is information to assess, not an instruction to accept its lower end. Do not invent market ranges, competing offers, or the user's willingness to walk away.

examples.body:
This is a synthetic dialogue illustrating the coaching default, not a candidate's
compensation history or a guarantee that an employer will disclose its range.

Recruiter: “What salary are you looking for?”

Candidate: “Before I give a number, what is the budgeted base range for this
role and level, and how does the rest of the package work?”

Recruiter: “It depends on the person. What would you need?”

Candidate: “I understand there may be flexibility. I'd still like to understand
the range you've budgeted for this hire before setting an expectation. Can you
share that band, or check with the hiring team?”

Recruiter: “We have a broad band spanning several levels.”

Candidate: “Which level are you considering for this role, and what range applies
to that level and location? Is the band base salary or total compensation?”

If they still refuse, the candidate chooses a truthful next step. “I'm not ready
to set a number before understanding the scope and package. Let's clarify those
first and return to compensation” is one option. A deliberate target or a
decision not to continue can also be appropriate; do not invent the user's
leverage, minimum, or willingness to stop.

The useful behaviors are seeking information before anchoring, persisting
professionally, clarifying the actual package, and retaining a plan under
pressure. Length, charm, aggressiveness, and the salary obtained are not rubric
dimensions. If a usable band is already disclosed, do not repeat the opening
mechanically.

questions.adaptation: Episode, scope, contribution, outcome evidence, and target capability. IC: implementation or technical influence. EM: conditions that enabled team delivery and growth. Executive: organizational mechanism and business effect, with shared ownership. Small scope can still supply strong evidence.
questions.alternatives: Preventing a problem, improving maintainability, developing someone, or stopping wasteful work can be accomplishments. Exact metrics are optional when unavailable; identify the observation instead.
questions.answer: Explain the starting problem and why it mattered, identify your responsibility, and describe the key decisions and actions. Connect the result to an observable change for customers, colleagues, or the business. Name collaborators and limitations. A durable improvement can be more instructive than one dramatic launch.

examples.body:
Given synthetic facts: the candidate wrote a rollout checklist after two
missed handoffs; a colleague later used it and noticed a missing approval before
release; no measured reduction in incidents exists.

**Weak answer:** “I'm a great collaborator. I improved our release process and
made everything much more efficient.”

**Truthful revision:** “After two missed handoffs, I wrote a checklist showing
the release steps and their owners. A colleague used it on the next release and
spotted an approval we hadn't completed. I don't have an incident-reduction
measurement, but it made that handoff clearer and caught a missing step.”

**Why this revision helps:** It uses only the supplied facts, establishes
contribution, and bounds the result. It does not convert a qualitative example
into an invented percentage improvement.
