questions.variants: What are you proud of? Describe a project where you made a difference.

questions.adaptation: User-selected episode, contemporary constraints, personal decision, consequences, repair, and later practice. Manager/executive: include effects on others and the operating change. IC: describe detection, technical reasoning, and coordination within actual authority.
questions.alternatives: A small but consequential failure is valid. The candidate can defend part of the original reasoning while recognizing a real limitation. Not every failure has a neat redemption.
questions.answer: Choose a meaningful episode, define the expectation, and state what did not work. Identify your contribution without taking blame for everything. Explain what was knowable at the time, what you missed, how you responded, and what you changed afterward. Distinguish a poor decision from a reasonable decision with a bad outcome.

examples.body:
Sentence labels are for the evaluator illustration, not a recommended speaking style.

> [1] I committed our migration to a date before checking a dependency owned
> by another team. [2] I knew our code path was ready and assumed their
> interface would remain stable; I did not verify that assumption with its
> owner. [3] Their planned change meant our rollout could not use the original
> sequence, and we missed the date. [4] I explained my mistake to the team and
> stakeholders, then worked with the owner on a smaller compatible step.
> [5] For the next rollout, I added an explicit owner confirmation before we
> committed, and we found a conflict early enough to change the sequence.
> [6] That check helps with known dependencies; it does not eliminate every
> integration risk.

| B02 dimension | Proposed result | Answer evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Responsibility | 3 | Sentences 1–4 identify the assumption and its consequence without blaming the other team |
| Decision analysis | 3 | Sentence 2 distinguishes what was known from what was assumed |
| Changed practice | 3 | Sentences 5–6 show a specific later action, observation, and boundary |

**Separate fact check:** In a real session, every episode fact and claimed
outcome would need its own support status. The answer's structure does not prove
the event happened. Missing corroboration alone does not make it fabricated.
examples.title: A failure with accountable reasoning

questions.failures: Fake failure ending in triumph, blaming others exclusively, or hindsight certainty that ignores information available at the time.
questions.intent: Examine accountability, reasoning, and changed practice.
questions.probes: Which signal did you overlook? What would you repeat? What evidence shows that your later approach changed?
questions.provenance: Practice extrapolation from [L10](sources.md#will-larson); no requirement that every unsuccessful outcome imply incompetence.

rubric.strong: Owns a bounded contribution and its consequences
Distinguishes available information, choice, and uncertainty
rubric.weak: Gives only an outcome or hindsight slogan

rubric.strong: Describes a specific repair or later behavior and its limits
rubric.weak: “I learned a lot” without a change

questions.title: Tell me about a failure or a decision you regret
questions.variants: When did you miss a commitment? What would you do differently?

questions.adaptation: Episode, competing goals, decision process, communication, and result. IC: technical options and adoption. EM: process and power dynamics. Executive: peer priorities and enterprise consequences. A manager should explain how they avoided silencing people with formal authority.
questions.alternatives: You can change your mind, compromise, escalate a decision appropriately, or support a decision you still disagree with. Agreement is not mandatory; unresolved disagreement can be described honestly.
questions.answer: Explain the substantive disagreement and the other person's goals fairly. Describe how you checked assumptions, surfaced tradeoffs, and reached or supported a decision. State your authority and how the working relationship and outcome developed. “I convinced them” is not sufficient.

examples.body:
> Product wanted to launch the new workflow at once; I wanted a staged rollout
> because we had limited recovery options. Their concern was a customer
> commitment, not indifference to reliability. I laid out the recovery risk
> and asked which customers needed the new path immediately. We agreed to
> start with those customers and keep the old path available while we learned.
> I gave up a slower internal-only rollout, and product accepted a narrower
> first release. The launch worked for that group, though supporting both
> paths cost more than we initially expected.

**Evaluation:** Represents the other goal fairly, names a compromise, and
acknowledges a cost. Follow up on decision authority and how recovery was tested.
Do not assume “we agreed” means there was no pressure or unresolved concern.
examples.title: Disagreement without a winner narrative

questions.failures: Caricaturing the colleague, winning through rank, avoiding the issue indefinitely, or confusing respect with unconditional agreement.
questions.intent: Understand collaboration under real differences.
questions.probes: What was reasonable in their position? Who had decision authority? What would they say about your handling of it?
questions.provenance: Practice extrapolation from [H03](sources.md#other-contemporary-leaders) and [R03](sources.md#michael-lopp).

rubric.strong: Explains differing goals or evidence without caricature
rubric.weak: Cannot represent the other position fairly

rubric.strong: Uses relevant evidence, tradeoffs, and clear decision authority
rubric.weak: Relies solely on force, avoidance, or persuasion

rubric.strong: Describes respectful handling and what happened afterward
rubric.weak: Ignores effects on people or follow-through

questions.title: Describe a disagreement with a colleague
questions.variants: How did you handle conflicting technical views? Tell me about friction.

questions.adaptation: User-selected feedback, context, reflection, action, and follow-up. IC: work habits or collaboration. EM: impact of management behavior. Executive: how peers or team members could safely challenge you. Do not imply psychological traits from the response.
questions.alternatives: Respectfully rejecting unsupported feedback after investigation can be sound. If formal reviews were absent, use a colleague's comment or a retrospective. Personal or discriminatory criticism need not be treated as a valid development instruction.
questions.answer: State the feedback as a behavior and effect, describe how you clarified it, and explain what you accepted, questioned, or tested. Show a concrete response and how you observed its effect. You need not pretend that criticism felt easy or that every criticism was accurate.
questions.failures: Defensiveness without examination, automatic agreement with no action, or a changed behavior unrelated to the feedback.
questions.intent: Understand how the candidate examines feedback and acts on it.
questions.probes: What did you ask to understand it? What would the giver observe now?
questions.provenance: Practice extrapolation from [H01](sources.md#other-contemporary-leaders); receiving-feedback criteria are our adaptation of the author's feedback practice.

rubric.strong: Identifies the behavior, effect, and relevant context
Clarifies and evaluates the feedback fairly
rubric.weak: Dismisses or accepts without considering evidence

rubric.strong: Describes a relevant change/test or justified disagreement
rubric.weak: Supplies no action or reasoned conclusion

questions.title: Tell me about difficult feedback you received
questions.variants: How have you responded to criticism? What surprised you in a review?

questions.adaptation: Unclear problem, constraints, information sought, decision, and results. IC: technical or product uncertainty. EM: team and delivery uncertainty. Executive: business and organizational diagnosis. Scale the story to actual authority instead of making every ambiguity “strategy.”
questions.alternatives: A reversible experiment, immediate action on a known urgent risk, or pausing for critical information can all be appropriate. Hypothetical answers are permitted when labeled as such.
questions.answer: Distinguish what was known, assumed, and missing. Explain how you found the highest-value information, involved relevant people, and chose a bounded next step. Identify the risk of acting and of waiting, plus how the approach would change as evidence arrived.
questions.failures: Imported solution before diagnosis, indefinite research, or confusing decisiveness with unsupported certainty.
questions.intent: Examine diagnosis and progress with incomplete information.
questions.probes: Which assumption could invalidate the approach? What did you choose not to investigate? What would trigger a change?
questions.provenance: Practice extrapolation from [L07](sources.md#will-larson), extended from strategy diagnosis to other role scopes.

rubric.strong: Names the uncertainty and the evidence needed
rubric.weak: Assumptions and observed facts are indistinguishable

rubric.strong: Chooses a proportionate action given urgency and risk
rubric.weak: No next step or unjustified irreversible commitment

rubric.strong: States a useful check or revision trigger
rubric.weak: No way to notice the approach is wrong

questions.title: Tell me about working through ambiguity
questions.variants: How did you start when the problem was unclear? Describe an uncertain decision.

questions.adaptation: Demand, capacity, decision authority, options, stakeholders, and result. IC: negotiate scope with owners. EM: protect team capacity while making delivery tradeoffs visible. Executive: allocate resources and align peers on opportunity costs. Delegation must account for others' capacity.
questions.alternatives: A bounded exceptional push can be sensible if risks, recovery, and consent are considered. Deferring a high-value item may be necessary. An unpopular refusal can be justified without being confrontational.
questions.answer: Explain the competing obligations and constraints. Show the decision rule, what you delayed, reduced, delegated, or declined, and how affected people learned about it. Describe the consequence and any reconsideration. Do not present habitual overtime as the prioritization method.
questions.failures: “Everything was a priority,” silent missed commitments, passing overload to someone else, or constant rescue work.
questions.intent: Understand prioritization, explicit tradeoffs, and communication.
questions.probes: What stopped getting done? Who disagreed? When would you revisit it?
questions.provenance: Practice extrapolation from [H04](sources.md#other-contemporary-leaders) and [R05](sources.md#michael-lopp).

rubric.strong: Explains a clear choice and its opportunity cost
Uses realistic capacity and proportionate options
rubric.weak: Ignores resource limits or merely transfers overload

rubric.strong: Communicates consequences and a revision path

questions.title: Tell me about competing priorities or saying no
questions.variants: How do you handle too much work? When did you push back on a deadline?

questions.adaptation: Episode, stakeholders, incentives, approach, and observable adoption. IC: technical proposals or cross-team delivery. EM: dependencies and support. Executive: peers with legitimate competing objectives. Keep formal mandate separate from voluntary agreement.
questions.alternatives: Adjusting the proposal, running a small pilot, finding a willing partner, or using appropriate decision escalation can work. Not every party needs to be enthusiastic for a clear agreement to be effective.
questions.answer: Name the problem, the other groups' priorities, and why participation would matter to them. Show how you built a shared understanding, clarified a decision, and made the work feasible. Explain what you changed in response to others. Adoption and follow-through matter more than one presentation.
questions.failures: Manipulation, title-dropping, claiming influence because a document was sent, or ignoring the other team's costs.
questions.intent: Understand collaboration beyond formal control.
questions.probes: What did others gain or give up? What changed because of their input? How did you know agreement became action?
questions.provenance: Practice extrapolation from [H03](sources.md#other-contemporary-leaders); the influence rubric is ours.

rubric.strong: Identifies relevant priorities and constraints
rubric.weak: Treats others as obstacles with no valid needs

rubric.strong: Shows a concrete path to a workable decision
rubric.weak: Describes only pressure or generic persuasion

rubric.strong: Provides follow-through evidence and bounded contribution

questions.title: How have you influenced people without authority?
questions.variants: Describe cross-functional alignment. How did you get another team to help?

questions.adaptation: Original decision, new evidence, decision authority, revision, and effect. IC: design or implementation. EM: process or team approach. Executive: investment or strategy. Explain costs of reversal for people who depended on the original plan.
questions.alternatives: A partial update, a decision to stop learning expensively, or maintaining a view after serious examination can be discussed; the last option needs a different example if the interviewer specifically asks for an actual change.
questions.answer: Explain the original belief and why it was reasonable, the information that challenged it, and how you tested its importance. Describe the revised choice, communication, and consequences. State remaining uncertainty. Updating a plan is not automatically an admission that the original decision was poor.
questions.failures: Change for fashion or authority alone, denying the earlier view, or claiming flexibility without naming a revised decision.
questions.intent: Examine learning and revising a position responsibly.
questions.probes: What made the evidence persuasive? What would change your view again?
questions.provenance: Practice extrapolation from [L08](sources.md#will-larson).

rubric.strong: Explains why the prior choice made sense then
rubric.weak: Original view has no understandable basis

rubric.strong: Shows how evidence altered a key belief or constraint
Describes implementation, communication, and remaining limits

questions.title: Tell me about changing your mind
questions.variants: When did evidence overturn your view? When did you stop a project?

questions.adaptation: Incident or overload episode, authority, choices, stakeholders, and follow-up. IC: safe mitigation and technical communication. EM: roles, workload, and team support. Executive: business decisions, resources, and peer coordination. Do not imply expertise from a crisis the candidate only observed.
questions.alternatives: Seeking help, handing leadership to a better-suited person, or stopping unsafe work can be strong actions. Visible stress or a calm voice does not determine quality. Not every emergency could have been prevented.
questions.answer: Name the immediate risk, your role, and the initial priorities. Explain how work, decisions, and communication were coordinated. Distinguish immediate mitigation from later diagnosis. Describe recovery and what changed so the same problem was less likely or easier to handle.
questions.failures: Hero story with no coordination, unsafe shortcuts, blaming tired people, or leaving recurring overload untreated.
questions.intent: Examine risk management, coordination, and sustainable recovery.
questions.probes: What did you deliberately avoid doing? How did you know recovery was real? Who needed support afterward?
questions.provenance: Editorial crisis application of [R05](sources.md#michael-lopp), whose topic is leadership overload rather than incident-response procedure. The technical incident criteria are our synthesis.

rubric.strong: Takes proportionate action based on actual risk
Establishes useful roles, help, and communication
Describes recovery checks and a relevant follow-up change
rubric.weak: Treats exhaustion or temporary mitigation as completion

questions.title: Describe handling a crisis or sustained pressure
questions.variants: What did you do when delivery was in trouble? How did you respond to an incident?

questions.adaptation: Real episode or explicitly hypothetical scenario, facts, authority, communication, and outcome. IC: raise technical/product risk. EM: protect delivery and people. Executive: challenge peer or CEO decisions with business consequences. Do not prescribe jurisdiction-specific legal processes.
questions.alternatives: Privately challenging then supporting a legitimate decision, escalating a serious concern, or declining an action can be defensible. Use proportionate channels and acknowledge retaliation risks without inventing them.
questions.answer: Explain the concern and its evidence, the leader's constraints as you understood them, and how you raised options and consequences. Describe decision authority and what happened next. Distinguish an ordinary preference disagreement from a safety, integrity, or policy concern that needs different handling. “Disagree and commit” is not a universal answer.
questions.failures: Uncritical obedience, theatrical confrontation, or invoking ethics to dismiss a reasonable disagreement without examining facts.
questions.intent: Understand independent judgment, constructive challenge, and limits.
questions.probes: What alternative did you offer? What would have made further escalation necessary? Which part was within your authority?
questions.provenance: Editorial synthesis, informed by the inspection principle in [L10](sources.md#will-larson); this is not an author-supplied ethical interview rubric.

rubric.strong: States a material concern and examines its context
rubric.weak: Pushback has no relevant reason or evidence

rubric.strong: Communicates options through proportionate channels
Distinguishes decision authority from serious constraints

questions.title: When have you pushed back on a leader's decision?
questions.variants: What if you disagree with your manager? Describe raising an important concern.

questions.adaptation: One actual decision, its purpose, authority, available evidence, alternatives, assumptions, consequences, and later learning. An IC can discuss a local choice. A manager can discuss team commitments or development. An executive should account for business and system consequences within actual responsibility; greater seniority does not mean more ceremonial process. A hypothetical counterexample is valid if clearly labeled.
questions.alternatives: Speed, expert intuition, deliberate delay, or a small experiment can each be sound when the candidate explains their basis and limits. A deliberately accepted downside need not invalidate the choice. Useful delegation can improve judgment when authority, support, and accountability are clear; avoiding responsibility is different.
questions.answer: Define quality relative to the purpose, legitimate constraints, plausible alternatives, and information available when deciding. Explain why the chosen option was preferable, what was uncertain, what was given up, and why the amount of investigation and timing suited the stakes. Show how the decision becomes usable action with accountable ownership and a way to learn or revise. Distinguish the quality of reasoning from the eventual outcome: luck can reward weak reasoning or defeat a sound choice. Outcomes still test assumptions; do not use uncertainty to excuse repeated errors or ignore new evidence. Demonstrate the definition with a bounded example or counterexample. There is no requirement to attach a large checklist to every small decision.

examples.body:
Synthetic principle answer:

“A good decision is a defensible choice for the objective and constraints, using
the information we could reasonably obtain at the time. I want to understand
the alternatives, the important downside, and why the timing makes sense. I also
want someone able to carry it out and a way to notice when an assumption fails.
The amount of analysis should fit the stakes. Waiting can be right, but it has
a cost too.

“Suppose we deliberately limit a pilot to a reversible experiment because we
have weak evidence about adoption. Low adoption would be a disappointing result,
but it would not by itself mean the decision to run the pilot was bad. In the
opposite direction, a rollout that ignores a known serious failure path does not
become well judged just because no failure happens that week. I would examine
the original rationale separately from the result, then use the result to
improve the next choice.”

| Dimension | What the answer demonstrates | Useful follow-up |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Decision criterion | Objective, constraints, feasible information, and proportionate timing | Which tradeoff was decisive in an actual decision? |
| Reasoning under uncertainty | A bounded experiment and an explicitly unaddressed risk are different | When would more investigation have been worth its cost? |
| Evaluation and learning | A good outcome is not proof, and contrary evidence still matters | What later evidence changed the policy rather than only one choice? |

These hypothetical cases establish reasoning only. Ask for an actual episode
if the interview also needs evidence of demonstrated behavior.
examples.title: Good reasoning and outcomes are separate questions

questions.failures: “It worked, so it was good”; consensus or confidence as proof; no plausible alternative; indefinite analysis; hindsight reconstruction; reasoning so general that it cannot reject a choice; or a polished process used to excuse harm, ignored constraints, or failure to learn.
questions.intent: Reveal the candidate's explicit criteria for judgment before asking for a success or failure story.
questions.probes: Give a good decision that ended badly and explain why. What could have made a successful decision unsound? What information would have changed your choice? What did you stop investigating, and why? How would you know that you were rationalizing after the result?
questions.provenance: Practice extrapolation from [L10](sources.md#will-larson), which separates process, decisions, and outcomes, and [R07](sources.md#michael-lopp), which explores rationale, context, and avoidance. Criteria and anchors are our synthesis; neither author provides this question's validated grading scheme.

rubric.strong: Gives purpose- and context-specific criteria that can distinguish defensible and unsound choices
rubric.weak: Defines goodness only by outcome or preference

rubric.strong: Explains a material tradeoff, available evidence, uncertainty, and proportionate timing
rubric.weak: Hides alternatives, costs, or unknowns behind confidence

rubric.strong: Separates prior reasoning from results and identifies meaningful action, learning, or revision conditions
rubric.weak: Rewrites history or dismisses all outcome evidence

questions.title: What makes a decision a good decision?
questions.variants: How do you evaluate decision quality? Can a good decision have a bad outcome? Can a successful decision still have been bad? When is waiting a good decision?

questions.adaptation: User motivation, actual responsibility, example, and target expectations. First-time manager: mentorship, coordination, feedback, and the gap to formal management. Experienced manager: changed practices and team effects. Director: how managers make decisions without becoming conduits.
questions.alternatives: Exploration is honest if accompanied by an understanding of the work. An IC career or a return to it remains valid; do not grade interest in management as more ambitious than other choices.
questions.answer: Explain which management responsibilities attract you, what the team should gain, and how you know this work suits you. State a small number of operating principles and demonstrate one in an episode. Address delivery and people development together rather than defining management only as kindness, control, or leaving coding behind.

examples.body:
> I haven't formally managed people yet. As a tech lead, I found that helping
> engineers make their own decisions and improving our planning was work I
> wanted to do more of. I mentored a new colleague through their first rollout
> and coordinated our team's dependencies, but I haven't owned compensation
> or a formal performance process. I'm exploring management because I want
> responsibility for team effectiveness and development, and I'd want clear
> expectations and support as I learn the parts I haven't done.

**Evaluation:** Good role understanding and bounded evidence. Formal management
experience remains unestablished. Do not rewrite “tech lead” as “manager.”
examples.title: A first-time manager with transferable evidence

questions.failures: Title/status motivation alone, slogans without behavior, or treating the manager as the best engineer who approves everything.
questions.intent: Understand motivation, role understanding, and behavior behind a philosophy.
questions.probes: What would you miss about IC work? When did one of your principles need adapting? How would your team describe your behavior?
questions.provenance: Direct management-interview theme in [F01](sources.md#other-contemporary-leaders); role definition informed by [L01](sources.md#will-larson). Answer shape and anchors are ours.

rubric.strong: Describes concrete delivery and people responsibilities
rubric.weak: Confuses management with status or technical control

rubric.strong: Explains a considered reason supported by experience or exploration
rubric.weak: Cannot connect interest to the actual work

rubric.strong: Demonstrates a principle and its contextual limits

questions.title: Why management, and what is your management approach?
questions.variants: Why become a manager? What do you believe a manager is responsible for?

questions.adaptation: Actual team context, technical responsibilities, time tradeoffs, and an intervention example. Small-team EM: possibly hands-on delivery with explicit limits. Director: inspect decisions and develop technical leaders. Manager of managers: retain relevant judgment without bypassing managers.
questions.alternatives: Coding may be expected, optional, or rare. A specific deep dive can be valuable even when normal management work is indirect. The candidate should disclose a mismatch with the advertised role rather than pretending to prefer it.
questions.answer: Define the target role's technical expectations and how you stay able to evaluate important work. Give an example of choosing to engage, coach, or step back. Explain which responsibilities would suffer if you became a critical-path implementer. Do not claim one percentage fits every team.
questions.failures: Blanket “managers never code,” manager as mandatory reviewer of everything, or coding used to avoid difficult people work.
questions.intent: Test alignment with the role and effective allocation of attention.
questions.probes: When did your involvement become a bottleneck? How do you detect a technical issue without owning every implementation?
questions.provenance: Practice extrapolation from [L09](sources.md#will-larson), including changing expectations rather than a timeless coding rule.

rubric.strong: Explains involvement appropriate to this role
rubric.weak: Uses a universal rule despite target responsibilities

rubric.strong: Shows an effective way to inspect or evaluate decisions
rubric.weak: Cannot describe how important work is understood

rubric.strong: Explains when to engage or step back and why

questions.title: How involved should you be technically?
questions.variants: How do you spend your time? How much should a manager code?

questions.adaptation: Assignment, delegate's capacity and interests, constraints, decision rights, checkpoints, and result. EM: task or project. Director: a manager-owned team problem. Executive: a function or strategic initiative, with explicit business constraints. Do not disguise dumping unwanted work as development.
questions.alternatives: Closer support is appropriate for unfamiliar or high-risk work. Reclaiming a task can be defensible if the reason and effect on trust are addressed. Delegation need not wait for perfect readiness.
questions.answer: Explain why the work and person were suitable, define the outcome and authority, and describe the support you agreed. Show how progress and escalation were handled without dictating every step. Explain what the delegate decided and what you remained accountable for. Discuss the result and how the arrangement changed when needed.

examples.body:
> I asked an engineer to lead a rollout they wanted to stretch into. We agreed
> that the outcome was a safe release with a recoverable fallback, not that
> they had to follow my implementation plan. They could choose the sequence
> and coordinate the service owners. I helped secure time from the partner
> team, and we agreed that a compatibility problem or a slip affecting the
> customer commitment should come to me. We reviewed the risks weekly.
> When their pilot exposed a missing assumption, they proposed changing the
> sequence. I asked about the consequences, supported their choice, and
> handled the changed stakeholder expectations. They remained the lead and
> presented the result. My responsibility was making the assignment feasible
> and staying accountable for the commitment.

**Evaluation:** Strong agreement, support, and retained accountability. Probe
whether the engineer's existing workload was reduced and how the rollout ended.
This is still incomplete evidence about the final outcome, even though it
demonstrates the delegation mechanism.

**Director adaptation:** Use a manager-owned team problem and describe manager
decision rights; do not merely substitute “manager” into this story. **Executive
adaptation:** Describe a functional mandate and business constraints using actual
authority. If those examples do not exist, use a labeled situational plan.
examples.title: Delegation with real autonomy

questions.failures: Abdication, delegation without authority, hidden success criteria, or taking back every decision that differs from your preference.
questions.intent: Examine autonomy, support, and accountability.
questions.probes: What could they decide without you? What would cause escalation? What did you change when the first approach failed?
questions.provenance: Practice extrapolation from [H02](sources.md#other-contemporary-leaders). Worked answer: [examples](examples.md#m03-delegation-with-real-autonomy).

rubric.strong: Agrees outcome, authority, and constraints
rubric.weak: No understandable outcome or decision boundary

rubric.strong: Tailors support/checkpoints to readiness and risk
rubric.weak: Leaves the person unsupported or dictates all steps

rubric.strong: Explains retained responsibility and proportionate course correction

questions.title: Tell me about delegating important work
questions.variants: How do you delegate? What did you do when delegated work went off track?

questions.adaptation: Consented/anonymized episode, user actions, opportunities, follow-up, and outcomes. First-time manager: mentorship is transferable evidence. EM: growth within real job expectations. Director: manager judgment and succession. Executive: leaders and systemic access to development. Do not imply everyone should want promotion or management.
questions.alternatives: Supporting depth in an existing role, helping someone change tracks, or recognizing an ill-fitting opportunity can be good development. A promotion is not the only acceptable result.
questions.answer: Explain the person's goals as they expressed them, the opportunity or gap, and the support you supplied. Distinguish giving advice, helping them reason, opening opportunities, and offering feedback. Describe what they did and learned rather than taking ownership of their achievement.
questions.failures: Prescribing a career path, attributing their success to self, or offering a stretch assignment without support or capacity.
questions.intent: Understand individualized development and contribution to others' capability.
questions.probes: What did they want? How did you know the support was useful? Who else received comparable opportunities?
questions.provenance: Editorial development synthesis; opportunity/capacity context informed by [H04](sources.md#other-contemporary-leaders).

rubric.strong: Connects support to the person's stated needs and interests
Describes relevant feedback, learning, or opportunity access
Shows what they learned/did and bounds the manager's contribution

questions.title: How have you helped someone grow?
questions.variants: Describe coaching, mentoring, or sponsorship. How do you develop future leaders?

questions.adaptation: Anonymized episode or scenario, expectations, observations, support, authority, and outcome. First-time manager: label a plan as hypothetical. Director: coach the responsible manager without bypassing them. Executive: examine systemic incentives and inconsistent expectations too.
questions.alternatives: Changing scope, improving support, recognizing role mismatch, formal escalation, or ending employment may be appropriate. Serious misconduct may require immediate action. There is no mandatory number of conversations or universal improvement-plan timeline in this rubric.
questions.answer: Define the gap using observable work and agreed role expectations. Check clarity, resources, workload, and other explanations rather than diagnosing character. Describe direct feedback, the person's perspective, support, follow-up, and what happened. If improvement did not occur, explain the decision and appropriate organizational process without disclosing private details.
questions.failures: Surprise consequences, endless vague coaching, treating disagreement as underperformance, or making a legal conclusion from a mock scenario.
questions.intent: Examine diagnosis, fair expectations, support, and timely accountability.
questions.probes: Did they understand the gap? What part of the environment or your management contributed? What changed the decision?
questions.provenance: Practice extrapolation from [R04](sources.md#michael-lopp), not employment-law guidance or a required process duration.

rubric.strong: Establishes expectations and examines plausible causes
rubric.weak: Labels the person without a work-based gap

rubric.strong: Describes direct dialogue and proportionate support
rubric.weak: No understandable feedback or chance to respond

rubric.strong: Uses observable follow-up and a justified next decision
rubric.weak: Avoids the issue or imposes unexplained consequences

questions.title: How do you handle underperformance?
questions.variants: Describe a difficult performance situation. What if someone repeatedly misses expectations?

questions.adaptation: Scenario facts, manager authority, relevant expectation, and privacy context. EM: report's behavior. Director: a manager's handling of a team problem. Executive: peer or senior leader, recognizing limits of unilateral authority. No invented observation should be added to the scenario.
questions.alternatives: Asking a diagnostic question before stating a request is sound when causes are unknown. Urgent safety issues may require clear immediate direction. Warmth need not mean euphemism.
questions.answer: State a concrete observation, explain the relevant effect, and invite their perspective or propose a clear next action. Check understanding and agree follow-up. Use a respectful, direct opening; avoid a long compliment preamble that obscures the concern. In a role-play, respond to the other person's information rather than delivering a memorized monologue.

examples.body:
Scenario facts: a colleague interrupted two people before they could finish
explaining their concerns in yesterday's planning meeting.

> In yesterday's planning meeting, you started responding while two colleagues
> were still explaining their concerns. We made the decision without hearing
> the rest of their points. I'd like to understand what was happening from
> your perspective. For the next discussion, I want us to let each person
> finish and check that we've understood before responding. What would help
> you do that? Let's revisit it after the next planning meeting.

**Evaluation:** Uses scenario facts, explains impact, invites perspective, and
makes a request. If new information contradicts the scenario, investigate it;
do not give a high dialogue score just for asking a question and then ignoring
the answer. No diagnosis such as “you are arrogant” is supported.
examples.title: Difficult-feedback role-play

questions.failures: Character labels, hearsay as fact, public humiliation, or empathy language without an understandable expectation.
questions.intent: Observe actual feedback behavior rather than only a claim of being candid.
questions.probes: What would you say verbatim? How would you respond if the person disagrees with your facts? What agreement would end the conversation?
questions.provenance: Practice extrapolation from [H01](sources.md#other-contemporary-leaders); direct exercise rationale in [L03](sources.md#will-larson). Worked wording: [examples](examples.md#m06-difficult-feedback-role-play).

rubric.strong: States a specific observation and relevant effect
rubric.weak: Opens with labels or vague disappointment

rubric.strong: Invites and responds to the person's perspective
rubric.weak: Dictates a conclusion and ignores new information

rubric.strong: Establishes a relevant next step and follow-up

questions.title: Give difficult feedback to this person
questions.variants: Role-play a missed commitment. How would you address harmful meeting behavior?

questions.adaptation: Actual routine, participant preferences, example, and follow-up. First-time manager: label proposed cadence as a plan. Director: support managers' judgment. Executive: reports and peer relationships, not a requirement to personally meet every employee every week.
questions.alternatives: Different frequencies, lengths, asynchronous preparation, or walking meetings can work if the agreed needs are met. A quiet conversation is not automatically failure or concealed dissatisfaction. Ask about concerns rather than diagnosing mood from body language.
questions.answer: Explain how you agree the purpose and cadence, make room for the other person's priorities, and follow through on commitments. Show an example where listening led to a useful action or understanding. Keep room for growth and concerns beyond project status; respect personal boundaries.
questions.failures: Solely reading status updates, repeated cancellation, forcing private disclosure, or a meeting ritual without follow-through.
questions.intent: Understand a dependable space for support, feedback, and development.
questions.probes: What changed because of one conversation? How do you avoid solving everything for the person? What happens when you must reschedule?
questions.provenance: Practice extrapolation from [R06](sources.md#michael-lopp). Cadence flexibility and avoiding mood inference are our adaptations.

rubric.strong: Provides space for individual needs, feedback, and growth
rubric.weak: Treats the meeting only as reporting to the manager

rubric.strong: Uses questions and respects the person's choices
rubric.weak: Assumes concerns or imposes only the manager's agenda

rubric.strong: Demonstrates dependable access and relevant follow-through
rubric.weak: Commitments disappear or meetings are routinely neglected

questions.title: How do you run useful one-to-ones?
questions.variants: What happens in your 1:1s? What if the person says everything is fine?

questions.adaptation: Actual hiring authority, role definition, pipeline, process observations, and changes. EM: team role and interviews. Director: manager consistency and resource constraints. Executive: portfolio needs and hiring system. No invented hire count or diversity improvement metrics.
questions.alternatives: Hiring fewer people, changing a poorly scoped role, developing internal talent, or improving retention may solve the underlying need. Candidates with no hiring history can analyze a scenario and state the boundary.
questions.answer: Start with what the team needs someone to do, then define assessment and sourcing around it. Explain manager/recruiter/interviewer responsibilities, candidate communication, and how you detect process problems. Discuss barriers to a broader pipeline and consistent job-relevant criteria. Avoid treating “culture fit” or similarity to current staff as competence.
questions.failures: Hiring as recruiting's problem alone, vague “raise the bar,” unrelated trivia, or treating candidate pedigree as the rubric.
questions.intent: Examine role clarity, shared hiring responsibility, and usable assessment.
questions.probes: Which skill does this interview assess? Where are candidates lost? How would you notice interviewers disagreeing for irrelevant reasons?
questions.provenance: Direct pipeline theme in [F01](sources.md#other-contemporary-leaders); assessment design informed by [L02](sources.md#will-larson). Detailed process and anchors are editorial.

rubric.strong: Defines important responsibilities and corresponding skills
rubric.weak: Cannot connect assessment to actual work

rubric.strong: Clarifies roles, consistent assessment, and candidate information
rubric.weak: Relies on one person or unstructured impressions

rubric.strong: Diagnoses a bottleneck and proposes a measurable change
rubric.weak: Assumes more candidates fixes every problem

questions.title: How would you build and improve a hiring process?
questions.variants: How have you hired? How do you address a weak candidate pipeline?

questions.adaptation: Team context, observations, role, intervention, and outcome. EM: individuals and team practices. Director: dependencies and manager capability. Executive: operating systems across groups. Include customer and stakeholder outcomes where appropriate, not only internal sentiment.
questions.alternatives: Healthy teams can disagree and encounter incidents. Low attrition alone is insufficient; a necessary departure is not automatically failure. Different contexts require different checks.
questions.answer: Define the team's purpose and describe several observable signals: useful delivery, clear ownership, learning, candid feedback, manageable load, and the ability to resolve disagreement. Give an actual intervention and its effect. Explain how you would detect misleading signals such as apparent harmony accompanied by suppressed concerns.
questions.failures: Delivery at any human cost, measuring health by agreement, leader heroics, or interpreting one survey number as a complete diagnosis.
questions.intent: Examine delivery, capability, trust, and sustainability together.
questions.probes: What happens when you are away? Which signal has misled you? What would the least-heard person say about the team?
questions.provenance: Practice extrapolation from [U01](sources.md#other-contemporary-leaders) and [L09](sources.md#will-larson).

rubric.strong: Combines purpose, capability, people, and sustainability
rubric.weak: Equates health with speed or niceness alone

rubric.strong: Uses concrete signals and understands their limitations
rubric.weak: Uses only intuition or one proxy

rubric.strong: Shows a durable improvement in team autonomy or functioning
rubric.weak: Success depends on constant manager intervention

questions.title: What tells you a team is healthy and effective?
questions.variants: How do you build a high-performing team? Can the team work without you?

questions.adaptation: Scenario facts, career expectations, actual criteria, evidence, and decision authority. EM: understand and support the report. Director: examine calibration and coach managers. Executive: inspect system fairness without making an exception solely to keep a favored employee.
questions.alternatives: A promotion, a delayed decision, a role change, or an honest disagreement may follow. Wanting more pay without broader scope is a valid preference; do not assume every concern is about title.
questions.answer: First learn what the person expected, what matters to them, and what information is missing. Clarify criteria, evidence, decision ownership, and constraints. Acknowledge any manager failure to set expectations. Discuss credible next actions without guaranteeing an outcome outside your authority. If the decision was flawed, explain how you would seek correction.
questions.failures: Instant reassurance, promises you cannot keep, dismissing the concern as entitlement, or retention bargaining without examining fairness.
questions.intent: Examine listening, fair expectations, and honest communication.
questions.probes: What if expectations were never documented? What can you actually promise? What would you do if comparable evidence was treated differently?
questions.provenance: Direct role-play theme in [F01](sources.md#other-contemporary-leaders); listening adaptation informed by [H03](sources.md#other-contemporary-leaders). Our scenario and anchors are original.

rubric.strong: Explores the person's expectations and missing context
rubric.weak: Assumes motives and defends the decision immediately

rubric.strong: Explains criteria, evidence, limits, and possible correction
rubric.weak: Uses opaque authority or personal preference

rubric.strong: Agrees realistic next steps within actual authority
rubric.weak: Makes empty promises or offers no path

questions.title: A strong employee is upset about not being promoted. What do you do?
questions.variants: Role-play a promotion conversation. How do you handle retention concerns?

questions.adaptation: Project artifacts the user may describe, technical decisions, personal actions, collaborators, and outcome. Senior IC: substantial bounded contribution. Staff/principal: cross-team direction or ambiguous work when the target role requires it. Organization-wide scope is not mandatory just because the title says “staff.”
questions.alternatives: A project completed by several leads, a migration, or an unsuccessful project with substantial learning can supply useful evidence. Confidential details can be abstracted without replacing them with false specifics.
questions.answer: Explain the problem, constraints, architecture, and the part you owned. Walk through a consequential decision and the alternatives, then describe implementation, coordination, and adoption. Address failures or remaining limitations. Be ready to go deeper than a rehearsed high-level story without claiming sole authorship.
questions.failures: Architecture tour with no ownership, unverifiable scale, or a launch claimed as success without examining use and maintenance.
questions.intent: Understand technical depth and leadership in real work.
questions.probes: Why this design? What did you personally decide? Which operational constraint changed the plan? How did other teams begin using it?
questions.provenance: Direct work-deep-dive preparation in [L06](sources.md#will-larson); our proposed assessment dimensions.

rubric.strong: Explains design choices with relevant technical depth
rubric.weak: Cannot explain a key mechanism or constraint

rubric.strong: Shows consequential direction, execution, or coordination
Describes use, operational outcome, and meaningful limits

questions.title: Walk me through a technically significant project you led
questions.variants: Deep-dive a project. What was your most important technical contribution?

questions.adaptation: Decision, alternatives, evidence, authority, and consequences. Senior IC: component/service tradeoff. Staff/principal: interoperability, adoption, organizational capability, and long-term effects as relevant. Do not turn every answer into a survey of technologies.
questions.alternatives: A familiar technology, a purchased service, deferred work, or a deliberately temporary solution may be sound. An uncommon approach is not weak merely because the evaluator prefers another stack.
questions.answer: State the problem and constraints, compare plausible options, and explain why the chosen compromise fit. Address operational burden, cost, risk, reversibility, and ownership where relevant. Separate what you believed at decision time from the later result. State what would change the choice.
questions.failures: Technology fashion as rationale, impossible certainty, ignoring operating costs, or judging a choice solely by a lucky outcome.
questions.intent: Understand technical judgment under actual constraints.
questions.probes: What did the rejected option do better? What was the riskiest assumption? When would you reverse the decision?
questions.provenance: Editorial technical synthesis; decision/outcome distinction informed by [L10](sources.md#will-larson).

rubric.strong: Compares realistic options against the problem
Explains a proportionate compromise and risk
States checks, limits, or conditions for revisiting it
rubric.weak: Treats the decision as permanently correct

questions.title: Describe a difficult technical tradeoff
questions.variants: Why did you choose this architecture? When did you choose simplicity over flexibility?

questions.adaptation: Current pain, evidence, constraints, proposed change, dependencies, adoption observations, and maintenance responsibilities. Senior IC: bounded cleanup or migration. Staff/principal: shared technical direction and making other teams' change feasible. A manager can evaluate the resourcing, but that is a different contribution.
questions.alternatives: Keeping the old system or stopping a rewrite may be best. A mandate can be appropriate with legitimate authority and support. No credit is given for creating disruption to force adoption.
questions.answer: Define the actual cost or risk of the current system and the desired outcome. Compare repair, incremental change, replacement, and deferral. Explain transition ownership, compatibility, support for adopters, and a way to track completion. Address maintenance during the transition and decommissioning when relevant; a new system's availability is not full adoption.
questions.failures: Rewrite because the old code is disliked, free migration assumptions, abandonment halfway, or optimizing an unused platform.
questions.intent: Examine problem selection, practical transition, and completion.
questions.probes: Who bears transition costs? How will holdouts be supported? What does “done” mean beyond shipping the new system?
questions.provenance: Practice extrapolation from [TR03](sources.md#other-contemporary-leaders), with operational safeguards and alternatives supplied by our rubric.

rubric.strong: Defines an evidence-based reason and compares options
rubric.weak: Cannot connect change to a material cost or need

rubric.strong: Accounts for ownership, support, and transition risks
rubric.weak: Treats other teams' work as free

rubric.strong: Defines adoption and retirement/maintenance outcomes

questions.title: How do you handle technical debt or a large migration?
questions.variants: When should we rewrite? How would you get teams to adopt a shared platform?

questions.adaptation: Scenario facts, review content, technical stakes, authority, and team expectations. Senior/staff IC: assess code, help explain, and work with the reviewer or responsible manager. Principal: support shared standards without making every conflict require their personal intervention. Formal employee discipline is not automatically an IC's responsibility.
questions.alternatives: Pairing, a synchronous discussion, or manager involvement may be sensible. Serious behavior concerns can need escalation. The original patch may require major revision; care does not depend on approval.
questions.answer: Support the junior without pretending the code must be correct. Examine the work and distinguish required corrections from optional preferences. Help them understand the technical issue and reach a workable path. Address the reviewer's behavior appropriately and consider whether review expectations need improvement. Do not turn the response into public punishment.

examples.body:
> I'd first tell the junior that a difficult review doesn't determine whether
> they belong here, and ask what would help them work through it. I would
> then read the patch and review comments. We'd separate issues that must be
> fixed from optional preferences and agree the next technical step. I would
> speak with the reviewer privately about the dismissive comments and their
> effect, while recognizing any valid technical concerns. If the behavior
> were repeated or serious, I'd involve the responsible manager. I'd also
> look at whether our review expectations are clear enough to prevent this
> pattern. Supporting the engineer doesn't mean accepting unsafe code.

**Evaluation:** Covers all three dimensions for a situational answer. It is a
plan, not evidence of an incident handled. Probe the concrete first words and
how the candidate would act if they lacked authority over the reviewer.
examples.title: Care and technical standards

questions.failures: Dismissing distress, rubber-stamping code, public shaming, or excusing harmful behavior because the reviewer is strong technically.
questions.intent: Examine technical standards, care, and responsible handling of power.
questions.probes: What would you say first? How would you identify mandatory fixes? What if the reviewer is technically right? What changes afterward?
questions.provenance: Direct interview scenario theme in [U02](sources.md#other-contemporary-leaders), published in 2026. Scenario wording and anchors are ours. Worked response: [examples](examples.md#t04-care-and-technical-standards).

rubric.strong: Offers respectful support without false reassurance
rubric.weak: Blames or ignores the junior's concern

rubric.strong: Separates actual defects, standards, and preferences
rubric.weak: Accepts/rejects code based on the conflict alone

rubric.strong: Uses proportionate action and improves future collaboration

questions.title: A harsh review has shaken a junior engineer. What do you do?
questions.variants: A senior reviewer gives dismissive feedback. The code also has real defects.

questions.adaptation: Constraint, actions, users/collaborators, effects, and workload boundaries. Senior IC: team enablement. Staff/principal: reusable practices or cross-team capability where relevant. Coordination is technical leadership when it meaningfully enables work, not because every helpful act is senior.
questions.alternatives: A small high-value intervention can be stronger than a large mentoring program. Redirecting decisions to their owner can be better than answering everything. Declining invisible work can preserve capacity.
questions.answer: Identify a recurring constraint on others' work and an intervention such as better interfaces, documentation, coaching, or clear ownership. Describe what changed for others and how they gained capability. Explain what you chose not to absorb, how the work was recognized, and how it avoided making you the permanent coordination bottleneck.
questions.failures: Always being the rescuer, “helped everyone” without effect, invisible overload, or appropriating others' achievements.
questions.intent: Examine useful enablement that does not make the candidate indispensable.
questions.probes: Who can do the work without you now? How do you know it helped? What did you stop doing? Who gets recognition for the enabling work?
questions.provenance: Practice extrapolation from [TR01](sources.md#other-contemporary-leaders) and [TR04](sources.md#other-contemporary-leaders).

rubric.strong: Connects intervention to a recurring need
rubric.weak: Lists helpful activity without a constraint

rubric.strong: Shows others becoming more effective or autonomous
Sets ownership, capacity, and recognition boundaries

questions.title: How do you make other engineers more effective?
questions.variants: How do you scale your impact? How do you handle glue work?

questions.adaptation: Strategy episode, business context, resources, decision authority, peer input, actions, and observations. Director moving to executive: state the boundary of prior authority. CTO defined as technical leader: focus on technical strategy and its business connection without inventing financial control.
questions.alternatives: Stabilization, simplification, cost reduction, selective investment, or stopping initiatives can be valid strategies. Avoid preferring novelty or expansion by default. A strategy may evolve without failing.
questions.answer: Describe the business need and observed constraints, then explain your diagnosis and the few choices that followed. Show what you deliberately did not pursue, how engineering and other functions aligned, and how the actions addressed the diagnosis. Explain evidence of progress and how the strategy was revised. Separate a hypothetical company diagnosis from known facts.
questions.failures: Roadmap presented as strategy, imported playbook, everything a priority, or invented certainty about the prospective employer.
questions.intent: Examine diagnosis, focus, coherent action, and adaptation.
questions.probes: What is the diagnosis? Which choice was hardest? What evidence would invalidate the plan? How much did learning cost?
questions.provenance: Practice extrapolation from [L07](sources.md#will-larson) and [L08](sources.md#will-larson).

rubric.strong: Links context and constraints to a clear diagnosis
rubric.weak: Solutions are disconnected from an observed problem

rubric.strong: Describes focused choices and reinforcing actions
Uses relevant outcomes and a credible revision process

questions.title: How do you develop and evaluate engineering strategy?
questions.variants: Describe a strategy you led. What would your strategy be here?

questions.adaptation: Known employer facts, role mandate, uncertainties, user experience, and hypothetical assumptions. New external executive: avoid importing the previous company's solution. Internal promotion: explain which assumptions still need revisiting. Technical CTO: adapt to actual authority.
questions.alternatives: Immediate mitigation can coexist with learning. A small organization may not need three months of discovery. An incomplete plan with useful questions is stronger than false insider certainty.
questions.answer: Clarify success expectations, learn the business and how work gets done, build peer/report relationships, and test a diagnosis. Identify what might need immediate attention and how you would check that. Propose a small number of initial actions with assumptions and success checks. Adapt the pace to company size and actual urgency instead of a rigid calendar.

examples.body:
> I'd first agree with the CEO and my peers on what success in this role means.
> My initial questions would be how the business earns and spends money,
> which commitments are at risk, and how engineering decisions get made. I'd
> meet the leaders and teams involved, review actual customer and delivery
> evidence, and share observations so people can correct my understanding.
> I would not wait three months to address an urgent known risk, but I'd
> avoid choosing a reorganization before diagnosing the problem. Once we
> agreed on the main constraint, I'd propose a small initial change with
> an owner and a check of whether it helped. The pace would depend on the
> size of the organization and the urgency; this is a starting hypothesis,
> not a promise that I know the company's problems already.

**Evaluation:** Useful learning agenda and uncertainty handling. Still needs
role-specific assumptions and a concrete action once more company facts are
available. Do not add a promised revenue increase to make the plan sound stronger.
examples.title: A context-sensitive entry plan

questions.failures: Preselected reorganization, 90 days of passive observation, or arbitrary promises of improved business metrics.
questions.intent: Examine learning, urgency, relationships, and credible initial action.
questions.probes: What would you ask the CEO? Which evidence would make you act in week one? What would you share as an observation rather than a conclusion?
questions.provenance: Practice extrapolation from [L12](sources.md#will-larson). Worked plan: [examples](examples.md#e02-a-context-sensitive-entry-plan).

rubric.strong: Proposes targeted learning tied to the mandate
rubric.weak: Does not investigate business or expectations

rubric.strong: Distinguishes urgent known risks from uncertain changes
rubric.weak: Always waits or always transforms immediately

rubric.strong: Names proportionate actions and observable success conditions
rubric.weak: Promises change without assumptions or checks

questions.title: What would you do in your first 90 days?
questions.variants: How would you enter this organization? Where would you start?

questions.adaptation: User's actual budget authority, business goals, estimates with assumptions, dependencies, and consequences. Prior director: state whether you proposed or approved spending. Executive: address cash/time constraints and effects beyond engineering. No invented financial metrics.
questions.alternatives: Reducing scope, investing in an enabling system, retaining capability during a contraction, or purchasing a solution can be defensible. A hiring freeze is not automatically poor leadership; cuts require understanding what capacity or risk is being accepted.
questions.answer: Establish the objective, constraints, and reliability of the available financial/workload information. Compare realistic options, including stopping work, and connect costs to expected value and risk. Explain who owns the decision, how affected peers participate, and how you revisit the allocation. Do not claim that adding headcount automatically increases delivery.
questions.failures: Spreadsheet precision without reliable inputs, distributing cuts mechanically without consequences, or treating engineering spend in isolation.
questions.intent: Examine financial reasoning and explicit opportunity costs.
questions.probes: What stops if we choose this? What assumption drives the estimate? How will you know the investment is useful? What if the budget changes?
questions.provenance: Editorial resource-allocation rubric. [L04](sources.md#will-larson) explicitly identifies financial planning as an executive assessment area; it does not supply these anchors.

rubric.strong: Connects allocation to business needs and actual authority
rubric.weak: No objective or understanding of constraints

rubric.strong: Compares options and names material assumptions/risks
rubric.weak: Offers one option with unjustified estimates

rubric.strong: Makes opportunity costs explicit and defines a revision check

questions.title: How do you allocate engineering resources?
questions.variants: How would you cut a budget? How do you decide whether to hire, buy, or build?

questions.adaptation: Actual organization, symptoms, user authority, stakeholder perspectives, options, actions, and outcomes. Historical answer: include what the redesign did not fix. Situational answer: seek missing context before prescribing layers or reporting lines. No universal span-of-control rule.
questions.alternatives: Keeping the structure and changing its operation can be strongest. A reorganization, leadership change, or temporary incident structure may be warranted. Support and inspection can coexist with autonomy.
questions.answer: Define the problem through evidence about work, decisions, accountability, or dependencies. Compare structural change with better expectations, interfaces, or support. Explain authority, manager involvement, disruption risks, transition, and success checks. Show how managers gain usable responsibility rather than requiring your approval for everything.
questions.failures: Reorganization as a first reflex, bypassing managers, optimizing title hierarchy, or declaring success on announcement day.
questions.intent: Examine system diagnosis, organizational design, and leadership capability.
questions.probes: Why would an org-chart change solve this? Who loses clarity during the transition? How do you know your managers can lead without you?
questions.provenance: Editorial organization rubric. [L03](sources.md#will-larson) supports using organization-health exercises; the particular answers are ours.

rubric.strong: Uses evidence and competing explanations
rubric.weak: Prescribes structure without understanding the problem

rubric.strong: Compares options and addresses decision flow and disruption
rubric.weak: Changes reporting lines without examining effects

rubric.strong: Defines manager authority, support, and outcome checks
rubric.weak: Executive remains the necessary decision center

questions.title: When and how would you change the organization?
questions.variants: How do you manage managers? How would you assess a troubled engineering organization?

questions.adaptation: Actual goals, audience, measure definitions, sources, decision, and observed effects. Delivery metrics inform execution; customer and business outcomes inform value. Technical CTO: explain shared ownership with product and business peers. Do not fabricate attribution from correlation.
questions.alternatives: Sparse but useful measures, qualitative evidence, or replacing a misleading metric can be good judgment. Different stages and audiences warrant different views. More dashboards do not imply more control.
questions.answer: Start with the decision and audience, then identify the outcomes and operational signals that inform it. Explain definitions, limitations, and qualitative checks. Connect engineering's contribution to the business without claiming sole causality. Give an example where a measure changed a decision, or a scenario with a clear intended use.
questions.failures: Individual code-output leaderboard, one universal velocity number, business-causality claims without evidence, or metrics no one uses.
questions.intent: Examine decision-useful measurement and business accountability.
questions.probes: Which decision changes if this number moves? How could teams game it? Which important work is invisible? What does the metric not establish?
questions.provenance: Practice extrapolation from [L11](sources.md#will-larson).

rubric.strong: Connects measures to a concrete audience and decision
Defines signals, limitations, and corroborating checks
Explains contribution and resulting decisions honestly

questions.title: How do you know engineering is creating value?
questions.variants: What do you measure? How do you communicate engineering performance to the CEO?

questions.adaptation: Actual forecast, unknowns, contributors, and updates. IC: bounded work. EM: team capacity and dependencies. Director: forecast across teams without treating their estimates as interchangeable.
questions.alternatives: Ranges, milestones, discovery first, or a fixed date with adjustable scope can fit. No estimation technique is mandatory.
questions.answer: Define the outcome and assumptions, separate known work from uncertainty, and involve people doing the work. Explain dependencies, confidence, and what the estimate excludes. Describe when new evidence changes the forecast and how stakeholders learn about it.
questions.failures: False precision, imposed estimates, or silent deadline drift.
questions.intent: Understand how a forecast becomes a shared, revisable commitment.
questions.probes: What assumption mattered most? Who accepted the uncertainty?
questions.provenance: Editorial synthesis; decision dependencies informed by [L13](sources.md#will-larson).

rubric.strong: Connects forecast to scope, capacity, unknowns, and dependencies
Explains agreement and visible uncertainty
rubric.weak: Treats an estimate as unilateral certainty

rubric.strong: Uses new evidence to revise expectations promptly

questions.title: How do you estimate work and make a credible commitment?
questions.variants: How do you forecast a project with significant uncertainty?

questions.adaptation: Commitment, authority, indispensable requirements, and options. IC: surface evidence and proposals. Manager: negotiate team work. Executive: own business tradeoffs with peers.
questions.alternatives: A staged launch, smaller outcome, or missing the date openly can be defensible. Adding people is not automatically helpful.
questions.answer: Establish why the date matters and which outcomes are essential. Present feasible scope, sequencing, capacity, or date options with risks. Obtain the responsible decision, preserve required safeguards, and communicate what will and will not be delivered.
questions.failures: Hidden scope cuts, indefinite overtime, or unsupported promises.
questions.intent: Examine negotiation when a constraint cannot simply be removed.
questions.probes: Which requirement cannot be cut? What does the stakeholder lose?
questions.provenance: Practice extrapolation from [R05](sources.md#michael-lopp) and [H04](sources.md#other-contemporary-leaders).

rubric.strong: Identifies the business reason and essential outcome
Presents realistic alternatives and consequences
Makes the chosen commitment and risks explicit

questions.title: A deadline is fixed and the work will not fit. What do you do?
questions.variants: A promised launch exceeds available capacity.

questions.adaptation: Original commitment, warning signs, interventions, and observed progress. Match recovery ownership to role; supporting a recovery does not make the candidate its sole leader.
questions.alternatives: Canceling, handing off, or accepting a smaller result may be a responsible recovery. Complete success is unnecessary.
questions.answer: Show the signal that revealed trouble, your part in the original plan, and how you distinguished causes. Reset scope, sequencing, ownership, or expectations based on evidence. Explain stakeholder communication, what improved, and what remained unresolved.
questions.failures: Blaming predecessors, changing dates without changing causes, or claiming success because the team worked harder.
questions.intent: Examine diagnosis and recovery rather than rescue heroics.
questions.probes: What did you stop doing? How did you know recovery was working?
questions.provenance: Editorial synthesis using diagnosis in [L07](sources.md#will-larson).

rubric.strong: Identifies a specific constraint using evidence
rubric.weak: Calls the team slow without investigation

rubric.strong: Changes a material cause with clear ownership
rubric.weak: Repeats the failed plan with pressure

rubric.strong: Describes progress, communication, and remaining limits

questions.title: Tell me about recovering a project that was going off track
questions.variants: What did you do when a delivery plan stopped being credible?

questions.adaptation: Dependencies, authority, agreements, and handoff evidence. Staff IC: technical coordination. Director: competing team priorities and capacity. Shared ownership remains explicit.
questions.alternatives: Changing the plan, decoupling, or negotiating a temporary collaboration can beat demanding priority.
questions.answer: Clarify the shared outcome, dependency interfaces, owners, and competing commitments. Agree a feasible sequence and escalation path. Reduce coupling where useful and describe how handoffs and changes remain visible without personally routing every message.
questions.failures: Assuming others' work is free, escalation as intimidation, or becoming the permanent dependency broker.
questions.intent: Examine coordination without pretending to control other teams.
questions.probes: What if the other team cannot commit? Who resolves the tradeoff?
questions.provenance: Practice extrapolation from [TP01](sources.md#additional-topic-research) and [TR04](sources.md#other-contemporary-leaders).

rubric.strong: Identifies interfaces, owners, and competing obligations
Establishes feasible sequencing and resolution rights
Creates visibility and ownership that others can use

questions.title: How do you deliver work that depends on several teams?
questions.variants: A critical dependency has a different priority for its owner.

questions.adaptation: Previous workflow, intervention, actual use, and outcomes. An IC can improve a handoff; a manager can change team planning. Do not infer organization-wide impact from one successful trial.
questions.alternatives: A checklist, fewer meetings, clearer ownership, or keeping a useful existing process can be strong.
questions.answer: Identify the recurring problem and who experienced it. Explain the change, its adoption cost, and how affected people shaped it. Compare observed benefits with overhead and describe adjustment or removal if it did not help.
questions.failures: Framework adoption as the outcome, compliance theater, or efficiency claims without an observable effect.
questions.intent: Understand whether process addresses a real constraint.
questions.probes: Who found it burdensome? What observation would make you stop it?
questions.provenance: Direct process-interview theme in [F01](sources.md#other-contemporary-leaders); our specific criteria.

rubric.strong: Connects change to a recurring delivery problem
rubric.weak: Introduces process because it is fashionable

rubric.strong: Accounts for participation, cost, and practical use
Examines useful outcomes and adjusts overhead

questions.title: Tell me about a process change that improved delivery
questions.variants: When did you remove a process rather than add one?

questions.adaptation: System stakes, evidence, release scope, and responsibility. IC: technical checks and risk communication. Manager: readiness across disciplines. Executive: material business risk, not every checklist item.
questions.alternatives: Limited rollout, delayed launch, or deliberate release with bounded risk may fit. Not every system needs identical gates.
questions.answer: Define the user outcome and failure consequences. Identify relevant verification, operational ownership, rollout controls, and decision authority. Explain residual risk, what blocks release, and how an accepted risk will be monitored and contained.
questions.failures: “Tests passed” as complete readiness, no owner after launch, or silently transferring risk to users.
questions.intent: Examine proportionate quality and release judgment.
questions.probes: What would make you stop the rollout? Who can authorize the risk?
questions.provenance: Practice extrapolation from [L15](sources.md#will-larson); release anchors are editorial.

rubric.strong: Matches checks to consequences and uncertainty
rubric.weak: Uses the same quality bar everywhere

rubric.strong: Covers relevant functional and operational evidence
rubric.weak: Relies on confidence or a single signal

rubric.strong: Makes residual risk, authority, and containment clear
rubric.weak: No explicit risk or release owner

questions.title: How do you decide whether a release is ready?
questions.variants: The team wants to ship, but important risks remain.

questions.adaptation: Investment, changed assumptions, decision role, and closure. IC: recommendation and handover. Leader: portfolio tradeoff and people consequences within actual authority.
questions.alternatives: Continue a bounded experiment, pause, narrow scope, or stop entirely. Persistence is not inherently poor judgment.
questions.answer: Compare future value and cost using current evidence, including obligations to customers and dependent teams. Explain alternatives, who decided, and how work was closed or redirected. Acknowledge sunk effort without using it as the sole reason to continue.
questions.failures: Stopping without transition, rewriting history, or preserving a project solely to protect reputation.
questions.intent: Examine stopping decisions and responsible closure.
questions.probes: What future evidence justified the decision? What obligations remained?

questions.adaptation: Waiting points, evidence, decisions, and effects. IC: technical uncertainty. EM: team sequencing. Director: authority across teams. Do not presume all delays are indecision.
questions.alternatives: Add capacity or change a deadline when execution really is constrained. A prototype is useful only if it answers a relevant question.
questions.answer: Trace where work waits: capacity, dependencies, requirements, technical uncertainty, or decision authority. Make the blocking choice explicit, obtain useful evidence, and name its owner. Explain how you checked whether resolving it improved flow.

examples.body:
Synthetic facts: a staff engineer observed repeated waits for two teams to agree
on an event format. They proposed sample payloads, helped the owners choose an
interface, and observed one integration proceed. No overall delivery-speed
measurement exists.

> The teams were active, but the integration kept waiting on the event format.
> I listed the unresolved compatibility questions and prepared sample payloads
> so both owners could examine the same cases. They agreed the interface and
> recorded which team would handle later changes. The next integration proceeded.
> I can't claim an overall speed improvement from that one observation, but it
> showed this particular wait was a decision dependency rather than a lack of
> implementation effort. I would still examine capacity before applying that
> diagnosis to another delay.

**Evaluation:** Strong on bottleneck evidence and unblocking. Verification has
an honest bounded observation; probe subsequent integrations before claiming a
durable improvement. **EM adaptation:** Explain priority and owner agreements.
**Director adaptation:** Explain recurring authority gaps across teams using a
real example, not by enlarging this story.

questions.failures: More status meetings, blaming effort, or calling every delay a leadership failure without examining the work.

questions.adaptation: Symptoms, authority, responders, and actions. IC: assigned technical contribution. Incident lead: coordination. Executive: business decisions and support without taking over the debugging channel.

questions.answer: Establish impact and urgency, engage appropriate responders, and clarify coordination, technical work, and communication. Prioritize safe mitigation while retaining investigation evidence. Explain escalation, handover, and how recovery is verified.

questions.adaptation: Service objectives, impact, costs, and authority. IC: evidence and options. Manager: capacity choice. Executive: business tolerance and peer alignment. Do not invent a service-level agreement.
questions.alternatives: Context-specific objectives or a simpler policy can work. Some periods justify urgent reliability work; others allow bounded risk.
questions.answer: Establish user expectations, service performance, failure costs, and planned change risk. Compare interventions with feature value. Agree decision rules with relevant owners and revisit them when evidence or business needs change.
questions.failures: Reliability as zero failures at any cost, feature urgency as a permanent exemption, or punitive error budgets.
questions.intent: Examine a deliberate service-risk and product-value tradeoff.
questions.probes: Who sets acceptable risk? What happens when expectations are missed?
