questions.alternatives: A lightweight review fits a small event. Some residual risk may be explicitly accepted instead of generating endless work.
questions.answer: Reconstruct events and information available to responders. Explore contributing system conditions and decisions without hiding accountability. Select meaningful changes with owners, priority, and checks; show what actually changed rather than counting action items.
questions.failures: “Human error” as the complete cause, blame rituals, or a large follow-up list nobody can deliver.
questions.intent: Examine learning that leads to feasible risk reduction.

questions.adaptation: Paging patterns, manual work, support, authority, and observed improvement. IC: propose/implement bounded fixes. Leader: staffing, priorities, and protected recovery time within scope.
questions.alternatives: Reduce service scope, buy support, improve alerts, or change rotation design. Automation is not always the best first intervention.
questions.answer: Understand interruptions, workload, recurrence, and coverage. Provide immediate relief where needed, then reduce underlying failure or repetitive work. Build shared capability, realistic staffing, and escalation without making one person permanently indispensable.
questions.failures: Rewarding exhaustion, redistributing impossible load without reducing it, or blaming responders for asking for help.
questions.intent: Examine sustainable operational responsibility.
questions.probes: What caused the load? Could the system operate without the expert?
questions.provenance: Practice extrapolation from [R05](sources.md#michael-lopp) and [U01](sources.md#other-contemporary-leaders).

Offers feasible immediate support and fair coverage
Reduces causes and develops shared operational capability

questions.adaptation: Change mechanism, data effects, blast radius, and operational constraints. Technical depth depends on role; leaders still need to understand the meaningful limits of reversibility.
questions.alternatives: A carefully prepared one-step change may fit. Some changes require recovery rather than a literal rollback.
questions.answer: Identify affected state, compatibility, and failure signals. Choose rollout stages and decision owners proportionate to risk. Explain what rollback restores, what it cannot restore, and how to verify recovery or use an alternative forward repair.
questions.failures: “We can roll back” without mechanism, untested recovery, or multiplying changes while impact is unclear.
questions.intent: Examine concrete containment and recovery design.
questions.probes: What happens to data already changed? What triggers a stop?
questions.provenance: Editorial synthesis using contextual quality in [L15](sources.md#will-larson).

rubric.strong: Explains material failure paths and affected state
Uses proportionate stages, signals, and ownership
Describes feasible recovery and verification limits

questions.title: How would you roll out and, if necessary, roll back a risky change?
questions.variants: A migration cannot be reversed by redeploying old code alone.

questions.adaptation: Criticality, ownership, known failure modes, and exercise results. IC: service mechanisms. Leader: coverage, investment, and accountability across teams.
questions.alternatives: A modest checklist may fit a low-risk service. Not every organization needs a complex disaster-recovery program.
questions.answer: Establish service expectations and owners. Examine visibility, support knowledge, dependencies, access, capacity, and recovery procedures relevant to the service. Verify critical assumptions through suitable exercises and identify accepted gaps with accountable follow-up.
questions.failures: Backup existence as proof of restoration, undocumented single-person access, or dashboards without response ownership.
questions.intent: Examine sustained operability and recovery preparedness.
questions.probes: When was restoration last exercised? Who can act if the owner is absent?
questions.provenance: Editorial synthesis informed by [SR02](sources.md#additional-topic-research); preparedness checks are ours.

questions.title: How do you know a service is operationally ready?

questions.adaptation: Audience, confirmed facts, communication authority, and update history. IC: supply accurate technical information. Designated owner: communicate through agreed channels; not everyone speaks externally.
questions.alternatives: A brief acknowledgment is useful before a full explanation. Update timing depends on urgency and audience needs.
questions.answer: Coordinate technical and customer-facing owners. Describe known impact, actions, uncertainty, and the next update. Keep public claims consistent with verified evidence, correct mistakes promptly, and distinguish service restoration from complete cause analysis.
questions.failures: Speculative causes, false certainty, no next update, or publishing confidential technical/customer information.
questions.intent: Examine useful, truthful communication under uncertainty.
questions.probes: What if someone promises a recovery time without evidence?
questions.provenance: Practice extrapolation from communication roles in [SR02](sources.md#additional-topic-research).

rubric.strong: Separates verified information, uncertainty, and correction
Addresses audience needs and next steps
rubric.weak: Gives technical detail without user impact

questions.title: How do you communicate during a customer-impacting incident?
questions.variants: What do you say when the cause or recovery time is unknown?

questions.adaptation: Scenario facts, access, role, and available expertise. IC: investigate within authority. Leader: capacity and risk decisions with security owners; do not imply specialist expertise from confidence alone.
questions.alternatives: Disable a feature, patch, apply a temporary control, or accept a well-supported bounded risk through the proper owner.
questions.answer: Clarify affected assets, exposure, exploit plausibility, and uncertainty with responsible security specialists. questions.failures: Dismissing risk to meet a date, panic without assessment, or unilateral external disclosure.
questions.intent: Examine evidence, containment, and appropriate specialist involvement.
questions.probes: What facts change urgency? How will you verify the remedy?
questions.provenance: Editorial security scenario; auditable controls informed by [L16](sources.md#will-larson). This is leadership judgment, not legal procedure.

questions.variants: A potential exploit appears shortly before a major launch.

questions.adaptation: Request, user need, evidence, decision rights, and contribution. IC: ask useful questions and offer options. Product-facing leader: own discovery only if the role actually includes it.
questions.alternatives: Implementing the requested feature may be correct. A contractual or urgent operational constraint can narrow exploration.
questions.answer: Understand who needs what outcome and why the request exists. Investigate relevant evidence and constraints, then compare feasible responses with the product owner. Explain how you avoid dismissing legitimate urgency while making assumptions visible.
questions.failures: Automatic obedience, automatic rejection, or claiming stakeholders cannot understand engineering.
questions.intent: Examine problem discovery before solution commitment.
questions.probes: What would you ask first? Who chooses if options conflict?
questions.provenance: Practice extrapolation from [L14](sources.md#will-larson) and [PC01](sources.md#additional-topic-research).

questions.title: What do you do when a feature request does not explain the problem?
questions.variants: A stakeholder has already chosen the solution.

questions.adaptation: Participants, questions, observations, and resulting choices. Support logs or shadowing can provide evidence. Direct research ownership requires actual participation, not receiving a research summary.
questions.alternatives: Qualitative learning can be useful without statistical representativeness. Partnering with research/product specialists is legitimate.
questions.answer: Explain whom you learned from, what recent behavior or context you explored, and how questions avoided steering answers. Distinguish observations from interpretations and describe a decision the evidence changed, including the limits of the sample.
questions.failures: Leading questions, collecting compliments, or treating one customer's request as evidence about all users.
questions.intent: Examine evidence gathering rather than confident customer intuition.
questions.probes: What surprised you? Which observation contradicted your assumption?
questions.provenance: Editorial discovery question informed by [PT01](sources.md#additional-topic-research).

rubric.strong: Explores concrete customer behavior and context
rubric.weak: Seeks approval of an existing solution

rubric.strong: Separates what was observed from what it may mean
Connects findings to a choice with sampling limits

questions.title: How have you learned about a customer's problem directly?
questions.variants: How do you prevent customer conversations from just validating your idea?

questions.adaptation: Hypothesis, alternatives, user evidence, and decision threshold. IC: feasibility tests. Cross-functional leader: customer, usability, viability, or ethical assumptions with appropriate partners.
questions.alternatives: A prototype, observation, small trial, or technical spike can fit. Some risks need stronger evidence than a quick test provides.
questions.answer: Identify the assumption whose failure matters, the evidence that would change the decision, and a proportionate test. Explain participants, limitations, and how results affect the next investment rather than treating all positive signals as validation.

examples.body:
Situational scenario: a team proposes an automated report because it believes
customers spend substantial time preparing updates manually.

> I'd first check the behavior behind the idea: which customers prepare these
> updates, what information they need, and where the work takes time. I'd ask
> them to walk through a recent update rather than asking if they'd like an
> automated report. If the problem is real, a small manually prepared example
> could help us learn whether the output fits their decision. That would not
> establish demand across the whole customer base or the feasibility of safe
> automation. We'd identify those remaining assumptions before committing to
> the full build, and agree what evidence would change our investment decision.

**Evaluation:** Good problem/assumption distinction and explicit test limits.
Still probe sample selection and a concrete decision criterion. **IC adaptation:**
Own a feasibility test and partner on customer evidence. **Engineering leader
adaptation:** Describe how discovery fits shared priorities and authority.
examples.title: Testing an assumption rather than collecting approval

questions.failures: Building the whole solution first, vanity metrics, or moving the success criterion after seeing results.
questions.intent: Examine whether an experiment resolves consequential uncertainty.
questions.probes: What result makes you stop? Does the test measure the actual assumption?

questions.variants: What would you validate first about this proposed product?

questions.adaptation: Commitments, customer segments, capacity, and decision rights. IC: technical options. Leader: tradeoff discussion. Executive: business accountability shared with peers.
questions.alternatives: A targeted solution, shared capability, workaround, or refusal can be reasonable. One strategic customer can legitimately dominate.
questions.answer: Clarify actual commitments, customer impact, recurring needs, business value, and implementation/support costs. Compare options with commercial and product owners. Communicate a decision and its consequences without inventing authority to cancel promises.
questions.failures: Blanket contempt for sales, prioritizing revenue without costs, or promising everyone a bespoke solution.
questions.intent: Examine prioritization beyond the loudest or largest request.
questions.probes: What is already promised? Who bears the ongoing cost?
questions.provenance: Editorial synthesis; cross-functional outcome focus in [PC01](sources.md#additional-topic-research).

rubric.strong: Examines commitments, affected users, and business stakes
rubric.weak: Assumes all requests are equally important

questions.title: How do you handle conflicting demands from important customers?

questions.adaptation: Intended audience, adoption evidence, limitations, and role. An engineer can investigate technical friction; ownership of product strategy remains distinct from helping diagnose it.
questions.alternatives: Retire the feature, improve discovery, narrow the audience, or accept low usage if it serves a valuable occasional need.
questions.answer: Verify what “not using” means and whether measurement is credible. Explore awareness, access, usability, need, and alternatives with affected customers. Choose a bounded intervention or stopping decision and check whether it changes the intended outcome.
questions.failures: Blaming users, adding features without learning, or equating page visits with durable value.
questions.intent: Examine diagnosis after launch rather than celebrating output alone.

questions.adaptation: Decision, partners, mandate, and outcomes. IC: contribution within a team. Leader: enabling the working relationship. Do not claim sole product ownership from attending planning meetings.
questions.alternatives: Roles can overlap in small teams. Explicit escalation can be useful when a decision exceeds team authority.
questions.answer: Explain the common outcome, each discipline's information and authority, and how disagreement becomes a decision. Use a real example of testing assumptions or changing a plan, then show how implementation and customer results fed back into the collaboration.

questions.adaptation: Available business evidence, contribution, and authority. IC: a bounded cost or constraint. Executive: broader economics. No financial metric is required if the candidate never had access to it.
questions.alternatives: A qualitative mechanism can be useful. Strategic investment may be justified before immediate return is measurable.
questions.answer: Identify the business mechanism: cost to serve, revenue opportunity, retention, capacity, or risk. Explain assumptions and options with responsible business partners. Distinguish expected effects from measured outcomes and describe what would change the choice.

questions.adaptation: Original assumption, test design, results, and personal decision. Technical experiment ownership does not imply responsibility for every subsequent product decision.
questions.alternatives: An inconclusive result can merit another test. Stopping can be the valuable outcome of a well-designed experiment.
questions.answer: State the hypothesis and decision criterion before the test. Explain what happened, possible confounds, and what was actually learned. Describe stopping, changing, or retesting with a specific reason rather than calling every failure a success.
questions.failures: Hiding negative evidence, post-hoc success definitions, or broad conclusions from a weak test.

questions.title: Tell me about an experiment that did not support your product idea
questions.variants: When did customer evidence make you abandon an appealing solution?

questions.adaptation: Manager relationship, expectations, coaching, and effects. Director: actual management of managers. Peer/IC: advice and partnership only; do not present mentoring as formal accountability.
questions.alternatives: Shadowing, role-play, external coaching, or adjusting the manager's scope may help. More direct support can be temporarily needed.
questions.answer: Understand the manager's responsibilities, team context, and development need. Agree an observable goal and support, help them practice judgment, and inspect relevant team effects. Keep ownership with the manager while intervening proportionately if serious risk requires it.

examples.body:
Situational scenario: a new manager approves every small technical decision and
their team waits whenever they are unavailable.

> I'd ask the manager to walk me through decisions that waited and why they
> felt approval was necessary. We'd distinguish real risks from choices the
> team could own. Together we'd agree a small set of decision boundaries and
> how the manager would coach rather than prescribe. I'd support them in
> practicing those conversations and review actual examples afterward. I'd
> check whether the team could decide within those boundaries and whether
> risks remained visible. I wouldn't become the replacement approver; if a
> serious issue required intervention, I'd make its scope and duration explicit.

**Evaluation:** Demonstrates diagnosis, supported ownership, and a useful effect
check. This is a plan, not past management-of-managers experience. **Peer/IC
adaptation:** Offer observations and support to the responsible manager; do not
claim the authority to set their team's management expectations.

questions.title: How do you help a manager become more effective?

questions.adaptation: Reporting relationships, concern, authority, and follow-up. Manager of managers: actual oversight. A staff IC should describe partnering with the responsible people leader rather than claiming this mandate.
questions.alternatives: Direct discussion, mediation, or formal escalation may fit depending on safety and seriousness. Do not promise absolute secrecy.
