questions.title: How do you carry out a reorganization responsibly?
questions.variants: Roles and team boundaries are changing; how do you handle the transition?

questions.adaptation: Previous relationships, new mandate, and experience. First-time manager: transferable evidence plus an explicitly hypothetical plan. Experienced candidate: observable decisions from the actual transition.
questions.alternatives: Relationships need not become distant. Existing friendships can continue with clear professional boundaries.
questions.answer: Acknowledge changed responsibility and agree expectations with the team and your manager. Make access, feedback, and decisions consistent while retaining respectful relationships. Seek support and describe how you would address a difficult disagreement without favoritism.
questions.failures: Acting as if nothing changed, performative harshness, or relying on personal loyalty instead of fair expectations.
questions.intent: Examine role transition, fairness, and boundaries.
questions.probes: What if a friend expects special information? What would you explain to the team?
questions.provenance: Editorial transition question informed by distinct career responsibilities in [J01](sources.md#other-contemporary-leaders).

rubric.strong: Explains expectations and the new mandate
Applies consistent information and decision boundaries
rubric.weak: Uses friendship as an access or decision advantage

rubric.strong: Seeks feedback and develops management capability
rubric.weak: Assumes prior technical success is enough

questions.title: What changes when you become the manager of former peers?
questions.variants: How would you handle a promotion that changes existing relationships?

questions.adaptation: History, mandate, affected people, actions, and adoption observations. Leader: tradeoffs and resources. IC: influence and practical adoption support within scope.
questions.alternatives: Slow down, stop a change, or use a directive for urgent risk if its reason and support are clear.
questions.answer: Investigate past experience, current workload, and what the change is meant to improve. Explain constraints and what people can influence. Reduce competing demands, try feasible steps, and use feedback to adapt rather than equating skepticism with disloyalty.
questions.failures: Motivation speeches without capacity, demanding enthusiasm, or asking people to absorb another unsupported process.
questions.intent: Examine adoption through credible action and legitimate concerns.
questions.probes: Which concern is valid? What will you stop to make room?
questions.provenance: Practice extrapolation from [H05](sources.md#other-contemporary-leaders) and [PC01](sources.md#additional-topic-research).

rubric.strong: Examines history, constraints, and legitimate objections
Makes room and offers concrete supported steps
rubric.weak: Adds change without time or support

rubric.strong: Checks actual use and responds to evidence
rubric.weak: Requires public agreement as proof of adoption

questions.title: How do you lead change when people are skeptical or exhausted?
questions.variants: The team has seen several failed transformations.

questions.adaptation: Role, starting needs, support, and outcomes. IC: buddy or technical onboarding contribution. Manager: expectations and team support. Director: program ownership across teams.
questions.alternatives: Different roles can require different pacing. A useful first contribution need not be a production deployment.
questions.answer: Understand the person's starting context and role. Establish access, learning goals, support relationships, and meaningful early work. Clarify ownership and expectations, then use feedback and observed independence to improve the onboarding experience.
questions.failures: Measuring completion only by courses attended, no support owner, or expecting newcomers to infer everything through trial and error.
questions.intent: Examine capability, context, and belonging beyond a checklist.
questions.probes: Who noticed when the hire was stuck? How did they learn unwritten context?
questions.provenance: Practice extrapolation from [L18](sources.md#will-larson).

rubric.strong: Adapts learning and access to role and starting needs
rubric.weak: Gives every hire an identical checklist

rubric.strong: Establishes expectations, owners, and useful relationships
rubric.weak: Assumes the hire will find help

rubric.strong: Examines practical capability and improves gaps

questions.title: How do you help a new hire become effective?
questions.variants: What would you change about an onboarding program?

questions.adaptation: Hiring mandate, criteria, observations, and decision role. Interviewer: evidence contribution. Hiring manager: accountable decision; panel participation alone is not hiring authority.
questions.alternatives: Hire, decline, or run a focused additional exercise can fit. Unanimity is not inherently required.
questions.answer: Return to agreed requirements and each interviewer's specific observations. Separate evidence from impressions and identify missing or contradictory signals. Apply the agreed decision process, obtaining useful additional evidence only when appropriate rather than repeatedly testing until consensus.
questions.failures: Seniority decides without evidence, “culture fit” as an unexamined veto, or counting votes instead of assessing criteria.
questions.intent: Examine a hiring decision anchored to role criteria.
questions.probes: Which requirement is disputed? Is the objection about demonstrated work or similarity?
questions.provenance: Practice extrapolation from [L01](sources.md#will-larson) and [L02](sources.md#will-larson); our panel scenario.

rubric.strong: Uses relevant agreed role requirements
rubric.weak: Changes requirements to favor a preferred person

rubric.strong: Separates observations, interpretations, and missing signals
Uses accountable resolution and proportionate follow-up

questions.title: What do you do when interviewers disagree about a candidate?
questions.variants: A panel strongly likes someone but the evidence is mixed.

questions.adaptation: Role requirements, adjacent experience, exercises, and support capacity. Hiring leader: actual choice. Candidate changing tracks: honest evidence and development plan rather than invented credentials.
questions.alternatives: Prefer experience for an urgent unsupported role, or invest in potential where support and requirements permit.
questions.answer: Specify which capabilities must exist on entry and which can develop. Examine relevant past behavior and suitable situational work, label remaining uncertainty, and assess available support. Explain a decision without turning a hypothetical answer into proven experience.
questions.failures: Charisma as potential, pedigree as capability, or assuming all risks disappear with a mentor.
questions.intent: Examine transferable evidence and the cost of development.
questions.probes: Which skill transfers? What must be learned, and who will help?
questions.provenance: Direct first-time-manager hiring theme in [F01](sources.md#other-contemporary-leaders), contrasted with demonstrated skills in [L02](sources.md#will-larson).

rubric.strong: Distinguishes entry needs from learnable capabilities
rubric.weak: Treats all gaps as equally disqualifying or irrelevant

rubric.strong: Identifies concrete transfer and residual uncertainty
Assesses development cost, support, and fit to urgency

questions.title: How do you assess potential when someone lacks direct experience?
questions.variants: Would you hire a first-time manager or someone changing domains?

questions.adaptation: Calibration role, criteria, opportunity patterns, and decisions. Manager: evidence and advocacy. Director: consistency across teams; confidential individual details can remain abstract.
questions.alternatives: Different role scopes can warrant different outcomes. A process can be imperfect while specific corrections meaningfully improve it.
questions.answer: Use role-relevant expectations and concrete evidence. Compare responsibilities and contribution, not just visibility or project size. Examine unequal access to opportunities and enabling work, resolve inconsistencies, and communicate decisions and development needs through appropriate channels.
questions.failures: Visibility equals impact, retroactive criteria, or penalizing someone for doing assigned work that the process does not reward.
questions.intent: Examine consistency without pretending contexts are identical.
questions.probes: Who lacks the chance to demonstrate the criteria? How do you assess less-visible work?
questions.provenance: Practice extrapolation from [L17](sources.md#will-larson) and [TR01](sources.md#other-contemporary-leaders).

rubric.strong: Compares evidence against relevant shared criteria
Examines context and unequal demonstration opportunities
Makes accountable decisions and addresses process gaps

questions.title: How do you make promotion calibration fair across teams?
questions.variants: Teams provide very different opportunities and promotion evidence.

questions.adaptation: Actual authority, available comparisons, constraints, and actions. Manager: escalation and clear communication. Executive: budget and policy accountability. Never invent access to peers' private pay data.
questions.alternatives: Staged corrections may be necessary. Equal pay amounts are not automatically the same as a defensible compensation system.
questions.answer: Clarify the organization's compensation principles, relevant data, role scope, and decision authority with responsible specialists. Investigate discrepancies without assuming their cause. Compare feasible corrections and budget tradeoffs; explain what is decided, uncertain, or outside your control.
questions.failures: Unsupported promises, treating budget as an excuse never to investigate, or disclosing others' private compensation.
questions.intent: Examine evidence, tradeoffs, and truthful communication.
questions.probes: Which differences are explained? What can you truthfully promise?
questions.provenance: Practice extrapolation from [L17](sources.md#will-larson); not a compensation or legal formula.

rubric.strong: Uses relevant criteria and data with appropriate expertise
rubric.weak: Assumes a cause from one comparison

rubric.strong: Compares corrections, resources, and continuing constraints
rubric.weak: Offers fairness slogans without feasible action

rubric.strong: Explains decisions and uncertainty while preserving privacy

questions.title: How do you approach compensation fairness under a limited budget?
questions.variants: You discover unexplained pay differences within your organization.

questions.adaptation: Observed behavior, authority, responsible partners, and follow-up. IC: raise concerns and address collaboration within scope. Manager: expectations; serious issues need the appropriate specialist process.
questions.alternatives: Coaching, reassignment, or formal action depends on facts and seriousness. A generic coaching sequence cannot fit every concern.
questions.answer: Establish specific behavior and impact, support affected people, and use appropriate fact-finding and organizational processes. Set clear expectations, follow up, and address recurrence. Explain how technical dependency will be reduced so it does not prevent accountability.
questions.failures: “That's just their style,” trading team safety for output, or prejudging allegations without a responsible process.
questions.intent: Examine whether output is allowed to excuse harmful behavior.
questions.probes: What if the person is indispensable? How do you protect those reporting concerns?
questions.provenance: Editorial scenario informed by behavior/outcome distinctions in [L17](sources.md#will-larson) and care/standards in [U02](sources.md#other-contemporary-leaders).

rubric.strong: Identifies conduct and impact through appropriate inquiry
rubric.weak: Uses labels or dismisses concrete harm

rubric.strong: Applies clear expectations and proportionate follow-up
Supports affected people and reduces obstructive dependency

questions.title: A high performer harms colleagues. How do you respond?
questions.variants: A technically valuable person repeatedly undermines the team.

questions.adaptation: Relationship, expressed goals, feasible options, and authority. Manager: direct conversation. Director: systemic patterns. Do not grade the employee's reasons as more or less loyal.
questions.alternatives: Supporting departure can be the right outcome. A counteroffer may fit but is not the default definition of success.
questions.answer: Listen to the person's goals and constraints without pressuring disclosure. Explain realistic options and limits, respect their decision, and arrange proportionate knowledge transfer. Examine whether their experience reveals a broader problem requiring action.
questions.failures: Guilt, retaliation, impossible promises, or treating retention as winning regardless of the person's interests.
questions.intent: Examine respect, useful learning, and continuity.
questions.probes: What can you actually change? What would you improve even if they leave?
questions.provenance: Editorial synthesis informed by [H03](sources.md#other-contemporary-leaders) and growth reflection in [R02](sources.md#michael-lopp).

rubric.strong: Listens to stated needs and respects boundaries
rubric.weak: Assumes the motivation or demands private detail

rubric.strong: Offers honest feasible choices and respects the decision
Plans handover and investigates broader lessons
rubric.weak: Blames the leaver for organizational dependency

questions.title: How do you respond when an important team member wants to leave?
questions.variants: How do you retain people without making promises you cannot keep?

questions.adaptation: Mandate, constraints, obligations, and role. Executive: allocation accountability. Manager: implementation and support within scope. Situational answers cannot imply prior layoff experience.
questions.alternatives: Other savings, narrower scope, or staged changes can be considered if feasible. No particular employment procedure is prescribed.
questions.answer: Clarify the business constraints and decision authority. Work with responsible people/organizational specialists on decisions and communication. Treat affected people respectfully, protect private information, and reduce commitments to match remaining capacity. Explain support and operational continuity.
questions.failures: Expecting unchanged output, casual disclosure of decisions, or using euphemisms to avoid acknowledging consequences.
questions.intent: Examine humane accountability and a credible remaining operating plan.
questions.probes: Which commitments stop? What can you communicate truthfully before decisions are final?
questions.provenance: Editorial scenario using resource reasoning in [L04](sources.md#will-larson) and sustainable work in [U01](sources.md#other-contemporary-leaders); not legal guidance.

rubric.strong: Explains constraints, authority, and feasible alternatives
rubric.weak: Treats reductions as someone else's problem

rubric.strong: Uses respectful communication and appropriate support/process
Reconciles priorities, continuity, and remaining responsibilities
rubric.weak: Expects the same work with less capacity

questions.title: How would you lead through a significant reduction in team capacity?
questions.variants: Your organization must reduce spending and staffing.

questions.adaptation: Actual variation, costs, authority, and adoption. Staff IC: technical proposal and enablement. Director: capacity and ownership. Participation is not proof of organization-wide governance authority.
questions.alternatives: Diverse tools can be appropriate where coupling is low. A strong default can be enough without a universal mandate.
questions.answer: Identify consequences of variation: interoperability, security, support, learning, and innovation. Compare shared defaults, mandatory constraints, and exceptions. Explain decision ownership, adoption support, and how standards change when evidence shows they no longer help.
questions.failures: Uniformity as an end, autonomy without shared costs, or mandates that provide no migration/support path.
questions.intent: Examine justified boundaries for local technical choice.
questions.probes: Who pays for an exception? What justifies changing the standard?
questions.provenance: Editorial strategy synthesis informed by [L07](sources.md#will-larson) and [L08](sources.md#will-larson).

rubric.strong: Identifies material costs or risks of variation
Sets proportionate defaults, requirements, and exceptions
rubric.weak: Requires either complete uniformity or no constraints

rubric.strong: Supports adoption and evidence-based revision
rubric.weak: Treats a standard as permanently correct

questions.title: When should teams follow a shared standard rather than choose independently?
questions.variants: How do you balance technical consistency with autonomy?

questions.adaptation: Requirements, alternatives, costs, and decision role. IC: feasibility assessment. Leader: staffing and commercial constraints with responsible partners. Do not invent procurement authority.
questions.alternatives: A hybrid or temporary purchase can fit. Building can be rational without assuming all internal technology is differentiating.
questions.answer: Clarify the differentiating need and compare fit, time, total operating effort, integration, data/control concerns, and exit costs. Test consequential assumptions and explain ownership after adoption. Distinguish short-term acquisition cost from long-term obligations.
questions.failures: Comparing license cost only with initial coding time, vendor enthusiasm without diligence, or “we can build it” as sufficient rationale.
questions.intent: Examine the full responsibility attached to a technical option.
questions.probes: What would switching cost? Who maintains it two years later?
questions.provenance: Editorial decision scenario; contextual tradeoffs informed by [L07](sources.md#will-larson).

rubric.strong: Relates alternatives to actual requirements
Examines continuing obligations and material risks
Tests key assumptions and defines ownership

questions.title: How do you decide whether to build, buy, or reuse a capability?
questions.variants: Should we develop this internally or use a vendor?

questions.adaptation: Consumers, tasks, service boundaries, adoption, and costs. Platform IC: concrete improvements. Leader: mandate and product priorities. Mandatory usage is not proof that the platform is useful.
questions.alternatives: A smaller service, documentation, purchased tools, or discontinuation may beat a broad platform.
questions.answer: Understand consumer teams' tasks, constraints, and current alternatives. Define a useful service boundary and experience, account for migration/support costs, and prioritize consumer outcomes. Explain evidence of adoption, reduced burden, and continuing ownership.
questions.failures: Centralizing for prestige, treating consumers as difficult, or transferring work to teams while claiming reduced burden.
questions.intent: Examine an internal product rather than availability alone.
questions.probes: What work becomes easier? Why would a team choose this over its current approach?
questions.provenance: Practice extrapolation from platform-as-product in [TP01](sources.md#additional-topic-research).

rubric.strong: Identifies useful tasks and consumer constraints
rubric.weak: Starts with the platform team's preferred technology

rubric.strong: Creates a usable boundary, experience, and ownership
Examines adoption, benefit, and total consumer burden
rubric.weak: Equates mandate or availability with success

questions.title: How do you make an internal platform genuinely useful?
questions.variants: Teams avoid the platform your group has built.

questions.adaptation: Decision, participants, authority, and resolution. Staff IC: facilitate and contribute technical judgment. Leader: clarify authority and organizational tradeoffs without pretending to settle every detail.
questions.alternatives: Consensus, a designated owner, or escalation can fit. The right mechanism depends on consequences and reversibility.
questions.answer: State the decision, constraints, and responsible owner. Surface substantive alternatives and evidence, use a focused experiment if necessary, and set a proportionate route to closure. Record rationale and revisit conditions without requiring everyone to share the same preference.
questions.failures: Rank wins every time, endless voting, or writing an RFC after the decision solely to manufacture agreement.
questions.intent: Examine a decision process that uses expertise and reaches closure.
questions.probes: What evidence would resolve disagreement? When does discussion stop?
questions.provenance: Practice extrapolation from [R03](sources.md#michael-lopp) and [L13](sources.md#will-larson).

rubric.strong: Defines the choice, consequences, and useful alternatives
Incorporates relevant evidence and dissent
Establishes accountable closure and review conditions

questions.title: How do you make architecture decisions when senior engineers disagree?
questions.variants: An RFC attracts endless debate without a decision.

questions.adaptation: Workload definitions, measurements, system limits, and contribution. IC/staff: mechanism and evidence. Executive: capacity/investment decision without invented technical authorship.
questions.alternatives: Demand shaping, simpler architecture, capacity, or product limits may fit. Future scale does not always require immediate redesign.
questions.answer: Define workload, desired service behavior, and plausible growth. Use observations and suitable tests to locate limiting resources or coordination costs. Compare interventions, explain operating costs, and verify the change under relevant conditions.
questions.failures: Unqualified scale numbers, fashionable distributed systems, or a benchmark unrelated to real workload.
questions.intent: Examine measured constraints rather than speculative redesign.
questions.probes: Which measurement identified the limit? What might become the next bottleneck?
questions.provenance: Editorial technical scenario; contextual system quality in [L15](sources.md#will-larson).

rubric.strong: Defines meaningful load and service expectations
rubric.weak: Says “millions of users” without relevant demand

rubric.strong: Uses relevant evidence to locate constraints
Compares cost and verifies behavior under suitable conditions

questions.title: How do you identify and address a scaling bottleneck?
questions.variants: How would you prepare a system for substantially higher demand?

questions.adaptation: Existing complexity, actual pain, changes, and effects. IC: component simplification. Staff: interfaces or shared capability. Do not assume fewer lines mean lower complexity.
questions.alternatives: Retaining complexity can be correct when it serves a necessary requirement. Removing an abstraction is not always simplification.
questions.answer: Identify which complexity comes from the problem, scale, or avoidable design choices. Explain the concrete maintenance or user cost, compare changes, and preserve required behavior through a feasible transition. Describe what became easier and what tradeoff remained.
questions.failures: Aesthetic cleanup without value, deleting safeguards, or shifting complexity onto consumers and calling it removed.
questions.intent: Examine simplification that preserves necessary behavior.
questions.probes: Which requirement made complexity unavoidable? Who benefited from the change?
questions.provenance: Practice extrapolation from complexity distinctions in [L15](sources.md#will-larson).

rubric.strong: Separates necessary constraints from avoidable burden
Preserves needs through proportionate transition
rubric.weak: Simplifies by dropping required behavior silently

rubric.strong: Shows reduced cognitive or operating burden with limits

questions.title: Tell me about reducing unnecessary technical complexity
questions.variants: When did a simpler solution improve the system?

questions.adaptation: Problem, trial, costs, evidence, and authority. IC: evaluate a bounded use. Leader: investment and adoption conditions. A hypothetical plan must not imply a completed successful rollout.
questions.alternatives: Decline, wait, or experiment narrowly. An imperfect new technology can be worthwhile when it solves a material problem.
questions.answer: State the relevant problem and compare current alternatives. Identify consequential unknowns, design a bounded trial, and define evaluation and exit conditions. Account for operating skills, support, security, and switching burden before broader adoption.
questions.failures: Novelty as justification, pilots without decisions, or using a toy demonstration as proof of production readiness.
questions.intent: Examine exploration with a decision purpose and bounded cost.
questions.probes: Why now? What trial result would make you decline adoption?
questions.provenance: Editorial exploration framework informed by [L08](sources.md#will-larson).

rubric.strong: Connects exploration to a relevant need
Tests material unknowns with explicit decision criteria
rubric.weak: Has no meaningful comparison or exit

rubric.strong: Accounts for operations, skills, risk, and transition

questions.title: How do you evaluate an emerging technology without chasing hype?
questions.variants: A senior stakeholder wants the organization to adopt a new tool.

questions.adaptation: Time pressure, design choice, assumptions, and follow-up. IC: technical mechanism. Leader: capacity and future commitment. Avoid claiming a shortcut was temporary when no exit path existed.
questions.alternatives: A long-lived simple solution can be excellent. Some high-consequence decisions justify investing early despite uncertain demand.
questions.answer: Explain urgency, expected lifetime, consequences, and what makes the choice reversible or costly to change. Compare a bounded temporary approach with durable investment. Make limits and future ownership explicit, then check whether the expected revisit actually occurred.
questions.failures: Permanent “temporary” work without an owner, speculative future-proofing, or treating reversible choices as risk-free.
questions.intent: Examine reversibility and continuing obligations.
questions.probes: What would trigger replacement? Who pays the later transition cost?
questions.provenance: Editorial synthesis informed by decision inspection in [L10](sources.md#will-larson).

rubric.strong: Connects investment to realistic horizon and stakes
Explains exit cost, constraints, and consequences
rubric.weak: Calls a choice reversible without a mechanism

rubric.strong: Makes limits, ownership, and revisit conditions explicit
rubric.weak: Leaves future cleanup to unspecified others

questions.title: How do you choose between a temporary solution and a long-term investment?
questions.variants: When is a deliberate shortcut responsible?

questions.adaptation: Actual requirements, workload, service/data constraints, team capabilities, delivery horizon, technical options, and evidence. An IC should explain mechanisms within owned work. Staff/principal answers should include affected teams and adoption when relevant. Managers and executives should explain investment and technical accountability without claiming authorship or authority they lacked. Choose material criteria for the case; do not require every possible system concern in every answer.
questions.alternatives: Familiar technology, a novel tool, buying, reusing, repairing, or deliberately deferring work can all be justified. Simplicity is a useful default, not permission to omit needed behavior. Some choices are hard to reverse and can still be appropriate; describe their consequences rather than pretending every decision can be rolled back cheaply.
questions.answer: Begin with the problem and the behavior the system must provide for its users and business. Explain which constraints are decisive and compare credible options, including the current approach where viable. Connect the choice to actual technical mechanisms and relevant failure paths. Consider the effort to build, adopt, operate, change, and retire it, including costs shifted to other teams. Identify consequential unknowns, why any added complexity earns its cost, and how verification or a bounded experiment informs the choice. Make implementation and operating ownership usable. Explain what would justify revisiting the design and the real cost of doing so. Technical elegance, consensus, and a successful launch alone do not establish quality; a context-appropriate compromise may be better. Judge the original choice using its original context, while evaluating whether it remains appropriate today.

examples.body:
Synthetic principle answer:

“A good technical decision fits the problem and the team that must deliver and
operate it. I'd first identify the required behavior and the decisive
constraints, then compare plausible approaches on the costs and failure paths
that matter. The technically most elegant option can be worse if its migration
and operating burden outweigh the benefit. I'd make the important uncertainty
visible and explain how we would verify or revisit the choice.

“For a small team with one product, staying with an existing monolith could be
sound when it meets the workload, consistency, and release needs and lets the
team focus on the product. If later teams need independent changes or a measured
bottleneck emerges, that original choice is not automatically a mistake. We
would assess the new constraints and compare an incremental repair with stronger
separation. Conversely, a cheap initial build is not good if it leaves essential
recovery or data integrity requirements unsupported.”

| Dimension | What the answer demonstrates | Useful follow-up |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Problem and technical fit | Required behavior and relevant workload matter more than a fashionable architecture | Explain the mechanism behind a decisive requirement in your example. |
| Whole-system tradeoffs | Initial delivery and ongoing adoption/operation can point to different choices | Who bears the cost, and why is it acceptable? |
| Risk and evolution | Changed context differs from ignored original constraints | What concrete signal would trigger reconsideration, and how costly is the transition? |

Neither a monolith nor services receive automatic credit. In a real answer,
technical depth and evidence must support the claimed fit; this illustration
does not establish that any particular candidate has made that decision.

## Evaluation edge cases

These expected treatments are editorial fixtures for review, not measured
results from a model or an independent human panel.

| Case | Expected treatment |
| --- | --- |
| Strong answer with a previously unrecorded truthful outcome | Mark `new_user_statement`; assess content separately and request confirmation for canonical reuse |
| Accepted profile says contributor; answer says sole program owner | Mark `needs_clarification`; identify the exact ownership conflict rather than silently rewriting the profile |
| Candidate gives no exact metric for a concrete useful change | Assess the observation; do not invent a metric or automatically lower the result |
| Same reasoning expressed briefly or with imperfect grammar | Preserve substantive assessment; ask clarification if needed |
| Respectful, evidence-based decision differs from evaluator preference | Judge reasoning and constraints; do not deduct for choosing a different tool or organization shape |
| Good decision followed by an external setback | Examine information available at the time and response; do not equate bad outcome with bad judgment |
| Successful outcome after a reckless decision | Do not use the result to excuse the unaddressed risk |
| First-time manager describes a plausible performance plan | Label situational; management reasoning can be assessed while prior experience stays unestablished |
| Recruiter ends before candidate questions | C10 dimensions are `not_observed`, not zero or “not interested” |
| Candidate declines private career-gap details | Respect the boundary; grade only the relevant professional explanation supplied |
| Candidate asks for employer compensation range before naming theirs | C07 default: examine information seeking, package clarity, and professional persistence; never grade salary level or private needs |
| Candidate gives a deliberate target after the employer refuses disclosure | Examine the reasoning and truthful response; do not treat a chosen exception as a competency defect |
| Candidate answers a good-decision question with criteria and a hypothetical counterexample | Assess principle reasoning; do not demand or infer historical experience from the example |
| Confidential example uses anonymized roles and qualitative outcomes | Preserve abstraction; probe reasoning without demanding protected details |
| Model-generated story sounds compelling but adds unsupported authority | Require revision; presentation quality cannot establish factual support |
| Role-play starts with good feedback wording but ignores the response | Dialogue dimension remains weak; a framework recitation is insufficient |
| Candidate chooses a live conversation rather than async communication | Assess channel fit and access; do not penalize disagreement with a company's handbook default |
| Candidate cites a published AI productivity result from another setting | Assess whether its population, tasks, and limitations fit; do not transfer the percentage automatically |
| Candidate describes a humane reduction plan without naming employment-law steps | Assess leadership judgment and appropriate specialist involvement; do not invent jurisdictional requirements |
| Candidate changes career direction for priorities they decline to explain privately | Assess the disclosed professional reasoning; boundaries and priorities are ungraded |
| Manager-of-managers plan is strong but the candidate has only managed ICs | Assess situational reasoning and mark the experience boundary; do not promote it to demonstrated director experience |
| Internal platform usage is mandatory but consumer work becomes harder | Do not treat adoption count alone as value; examine consumer benefit and transferred burden |

See [calibration](evaluation.md#calibration-before-product-use) before treating
these intended behaviors as a reliable automated evaluator.
examples.title: A technically appropriate choice can later need replacement

questions.failures: Fashion or elegance as the whole rationale; listing quality attributes without choosing among them; speculative scale; comparing initial coding cost with only a vendor's license fee; “reversible” without an exit mechanism; no technical depth; or treating changed requirements as proof that the original engineers lacked judgment.
questions.intent: Establish the candidate's technical decision criteria, distinct from narrating one tradeoff in T02 or closing a disagreement in TS04.
questions.probes: Why not keep the existing approach? Which requirement makes your preferred option better? Where does complexity or operating burden move? Which failure could make the design unacceptable? If it worked at launch but became expensive two years later, does that make the original decision bad? What would change your recommendation?
questions.provenance: Practice extrapolation from [L20](sources.md#will-larson) on context and shared direction, [L21](sources.md#will-larson) on evolving quality requirements, and [DM01](sources.md#additional-topic-research) on whole-system technology costs. This definition and rubric are editorial; these sources do not endorse a particular architecture, technology, or universal right answer.

rubric.strong: Connects the choice to relevant system behavior, constraints, and technical evidence
rubric.weak: Chooses a technology without decisive requirements or mechanisms

rubric.strong: Compares viable approaches and material delivery, adoption, operating, and change costs
rubric.weak: Optimizes one property while hiding alternatives or transferred burden

rubric.strong: Explains consequential unknowns, proportionate checks, ownership, and credible conditions for revision
rubric.weak: Treats launch or claimed reversibility as permanent proof

questions.title: What makes a technical decision a good technical decision?
questions.variants: What is a good architecture decision? How do you distinguish a technically elegant solution from the right solution? When is a technical compromise sensible? How do you judge a past design that no longer fits?

questions.adaptation: Team context, actual behavior, authority, and response. IC: peer interactions. Leader: decision access and consequences. Do not infer people's internal psychological state from silence alone.
questions.alternatives: Written, private, or facilitated channels can help. Not every concern should be debated publicly.
questions.answer: Show how concerns can be raised, how leaders respond, and how expectations remain clear. Describe a concrete response to disagreement or a mistake, distinguish inquiry from avoiding consequences, and examine whether people could contribute information that improved the work.
questions.failures: “My door is open” without usable access, punishment for good-faith questions, or equating safety with universal agreement.
questions.intent: Examine psychological safety alongside accountability.
questions.probes: What happened when someone challenged you? Which standards still applied?
questions.provenance: Practice extrapolation from [AE01](sources.md#additional-topic-research).

rubric.strong: Creates practical routes for relevant concerns
rubric.weak: Assumes everyone can speak equally easily

rubric.strong: Demonstrates respectful inquiry and useful follow-up
Combines candor with clear work accountability

questions.title: How do you encourage candor while maintaining high standards?
questions.variants: People are afraid to raise mistakes or disagree with senior colleagues.

questions.adaptation: Barrier, user/colleague input, action, and observed effect. IC: review or meeting practice. Leader: operating policy/resources. No private identity disclosures are required to supply a useful example.
questions.alternatives: Small access improvements can matter. An unsuccessful change with honest learning is useful evidence.
questions.answer: Identify a concrete participation barrier using appropriate evidence. Describe an intervention shaped with affected people, check whether access or influence improved, and acknowledge remaining limits. Avoid speaking for an entire group from one person's experience.
questions.failures: Assuming inclusion from attendance, token consultation, or requiring marginalized colleagues to do all improvement work.
questions.intent: Examine inclusion as an operating change rather than a slogan.
questions.probes: How did affected people shape the change? What actually became more accessible?
questions.provenance: Editorial inclusion scenario informed by participation in [AE01](sources.md#additional-topic-research).

rubric.strong: Identifies a specific obstacle to participation
rubric.weak: Uses generic claims without an operating problem

rubric.strong: Addresses the barrier with appropriate involvement
rubric.weak: Chooses a symbolic action without input

rubric.strong: Examines access/influence changes and continuing limits

questions.title: Tell me about a change that made participation more inclusive
questions.variants: How have you improved whose input shapes decisions?

questions.adaptation: Assignment patterns, choice, authority, and outcomes. IC: raise patterns and share credit. Manager: allocate work and development. Do not infer discrimination from one assignment alone.
questions.alternatives: Different preferences and specialization can justify different work. Enabling work can be valuable when recognized and sustainable.
questions.answer: Understand who receives which work and why, including preferences, readiness, support, and recognition. Address recurring imbalance through transparent assignment, protected capacity, development, and credit. Check whether changes improve opportunity without simply rotating unsupported burdens.
questions.failures: Always asking the helpful person, invisible career penalties, or nominal rotation without training and support.
questions.intent: Examine access, workload, and career consequences of assignment.
questions.probes: Who gets time to learn? Does the promotion process value the assigned work?
questions.provenance: Practice extrapolation from [TR01](sources.md#other-contemporary-leaders).

rubric.strong: Examines access, burden, and recognition patterns
Makes defensible assignments with choice and development
Addresses credit, sustainability, and career effects

questions.title: How do you distribute valuable opportunities and enabling work fairly?
questions.variants: The same people receive visible projects while others do the coordination.

questions.adaptation: Reported facts, seriousness, authority, and available channels. IC: support and appropriate reporting. Manager: response within scope; formal investigations require the responsible specialists.
questions.alternatives: Different concerns require different paths. A direct conversation is not mandatory when power or safety makes it unsuitable.
questions.answer: Listen without dismissing or promising an outcome before understanding facts. Explain confidentiality limits and next steps, consider immediate protection needs, and involve the appropriate responsible process. Follow up within your role while avoiding retaliation or public adjudication.
questions.failures: Demanding proof before listening, gossip, absolute secrecy, or protecting a powerful person's reputation over appropriate inquiry.
questions.intent: Examine care, responsible inquiry, and appropriate escalation.
questions.probes: What would you say first? Which promises can you actually keep?
questions.provenance: Editorial conduct scenario; care and power informed by [U02](sources.md#other-contemporary-leaders). Not an investigative procedure.

rubric.strong: Listens and identifies appropriate immediate needs
rubric.weak: Dismisses the concern or pressures disclosure

rubric.strong: Uses proportionate inquiry and responsible channels
Explains next steps and monitors relevant ongoing risk
rubric.weak: Leaves the reporter unsupported or exposed

questions.title: How do you respond when someone reports harmful behavior?
questions.variants: A colleague says they were excluded or treated disrespectfully.

questions.adaptation: Values, actual decisions, role, and intervention. IC: attribution and raising evidence. Leader: reward/assignment decisions. Do not assume every inconsistency is deliberate deception.
questions.alternatives: Some competing values need explicit tradeoffs. A bounded local correction can help even when broader authority is absent.
questions.answer: Identify a concrete mismatch and its effects. Examine who controls recognition, allocation, and advancement. Change relevant decisions within authority or raise the discrepancy with evidence; check whether behavior and opportunity shift rather than just rewriting values.
questions.failures: More slogans, rewarding repeated rescue while ignoring prevention, or promising process changes outside authority.
questions.intent: Examine incentives as evidence of operating priorities.
questions.probes: Which decision sent the strongest signal? What would you reward differently?
questions.provenance: Practice extrapolation from the introductory principle in [H07](sources.md#other-contemporary-leaders); reward-system criteria are ours.

rubric.strong: Shows a concrete incentive/behavior discrepancy
Changes or challenges consequential decisions appropriately
Examines resulting behavior and continuing tradeoffs

questions.title: What do you do when stated values conflict with actual rewards?
questions.variants: Collaboration is praised, but promotions reward individual heroics.

questions.adaptation: Norm conflict, constraints, participation needs, and authority. Any role can contribute. Do not explain an individual's behavior using stereotypes about nationality, identity, or personality.
questions.alternatives: Different teams can use different norms when interfaces remain clear. Written clarification or facilitated dialogue can fit.
questions.answer: Describe concrete behavior and its work impact, ask about differing expectations, and distinguish necessary requirements from personal preferences. Agree usable norms with room for legitimate variation and revisit whether the agreement solves the problem.
questions.failures: “Professionalism” as undefined similarity, forced uniformity, or ignoring constraints because one style feels more familiar.
questions.intent: Examine explicit agreements rather than assumed cultural similarity.
questions.probes: Which norm is essential to the work? What did you learn about their expectations?
questions.provenance: Editorial synthesis informed by priorities in [H03](sources.md#other-contemporary-leaders) and clear norms in [GI01](sources.md#additional-topic-research).

rubric.strong: Examines specific behavior and differing expectations
Separates work needs from optional style
rubric.weak: Treats preference as a universal standard

rubric.strong: Establishes workable shared expectations and checks them

questions.title: How do you handle different expectations about working norms?
questions.variants: Colleagues disagree about responsiveness, disagreement, or meeting behavior.

questions.adaptation: Requested use, data sensitivity, authority, and controls. IC: raise concerns and implement permitted alternatives. Leader: accountable decisions with the responsible owners.
questions.alternatives: Synthetic, minimized, aggregated, or explicitly authorized data may fit. No particular technique guarantees appropriateness.
questions.answer: Clarify the purpose, required data, permissions, expectations, and uncertainty. Seek privacy/security or other responsible expertise, pause unsupported use, and compare safer ways to meet the objective. Explain authorization, auditability, and verification without claiming legal expertise.
questions.failures: Business urgency as permission, informal access sharing, or assuming de-identification removes all risk.
questions.intent: Examine boundaries, evidence, and appropriate risk ownership.
questions.probes: What data is truly needed? Who can authorize the use?
questions.provenance: Practice extrapolation from [L16](sources.md#will-larson); not a legal compliance checklist.

rubric.strong: Clarifies necessary use, sensitivity, and constraints
rubric.weak: Uses all available data by default

rubric.strong: Obtains appropriate responsible review and authorization
Compares feasible safer paths and auditable controls
rubric.weak: Frames safeguards as blocking the business

questions.title: What would you do with a request to use customer data in a questionable way?
questions.variants: A useful experiment needs data access beyond the team's current permissions.

questions.adaptation: Decision, power differences, contribution, and effect. Leader: create access and avoid premature anchoring. IC: provide evidence and help others participate without inventing authority.
questions.alternatives: Time-sensitive decisions may limit discussion. Listening does not require adopting every objection or perpetual consensus.
questions.answer: Invite independent perspectives before anchoring, make relevant evidence accessible, and seek omitted expertise. Show a case where dissent changed or refined a choice, or was considered and rejected with reasons. Clarify closure and continued routes for material new evidence.
questions.failures: Performative consultation after deciding, requiring dissenters to be charismatic, or treating objections as personal opposition.
questions.intent: Examine access to decision influence before authority closes discussion.
questions.probes: Whose input was missing? What happened to the strongest objection?
questions.provenance: Practice extrapolation from [R03](sources.md#michael-lopp) and [AE01](sources.md#additional-topic-research).

rubric.strong: Creates practical routes for independent relevant input
rubric.weak: Assumes assent means all expertise was heard

rubric.strong: Addresses substantive dissent and explains its effect
Reaches accountable closure with a path for material revision
rubric.weak: Silences new facts or never decides

questions.title: How do you ensure disagreement can improve a decision?
questions.variants: Everyone agrees with the most senior person immediately.

questions.adaptation: Work example, participants, constraints, and outcome. IC: practical channel choices. Leader: norms and access across teams. No universal remote policy is required.
questions.alternatives: A live conversation can be best; an asynchronous default can also work. Sensitive concerns may need private channels.
questions.answer: Consider urgency, complexity, ambiguity, access, and the decision needed. Explain how written context supports independent work and when live discussion helps resolve uncertainty. Capture useful conclusions so absent colleagues can act.
questions.failures: Meetings for every update, text-only dogma, or decisions trapped in a conversation inaccessible to affected people.
questions.intent: Examine communication suited to the work and participants.
questions.probes: What would make you switch channels? How do people learn what was decided?
questions.provenance: Practice extrapolation from selected [GI01](sources.md#additional-topic-research) communication policies.

rubric.strong: Chooses based on urgency, ambiguity, and access
rubric.weak: Uses one channel for every need

rubric.strong: Provides enough context for useful independent work
Records relevant decisions, owners, and next steps

questions.title: When do you use asynchronous communication and when do you meet?
questions.variants: How do you choose the right communication channel?

questions.adaptation: Locations, coverage needs, existing burdens, and authority. IC: handoff practice. Manager: schedules and expectations. Do not assume every person can shift personal hours equally.
questions.alternatives: Regional ownership, rotating live sessions, or limited overlap can fit. Rotation alone may not solve unequal decision access.
questions.answer: Identify overlap, required response coverage, and who bears current inconvenience. Use async work, clear handoffs, and deliberate scheduling to reduce burden. Agree exceptions for urgent work and examine whether influence and access remain equitable.
questions.failures: “Everyone is flexible,” permanent late-night attendance, or global availability as a performance expectation.
questions.intent: Examine coverage and collaboration without permanent unequal burden.
questions.probes: Which work truly requires overlap? Who misses decisions under this arrangement?
questions.provenance: Editorial distributed-work scenario informed by availability boundaries in [GI01](sources.md#additional-topic-research).

rubric.strong: Identifies coverage needs and unequal costs
Uses feasible ownership, handoffs, and scheduling
Checks decision influence and continuing burden

questions.title: How do you work fairly across time zones?
questions.variants: One region always attends meetings outside normal hours.

questions.adaptation: Location patterns, work/decision examples, authority, and effects. IC: document decisions and include peers. Leader: assignments and evaluation consistency.
questions.alternatives: Some work legitimately requires a location; explain the requirement and consequences rather than treating presence as dedication.
questions.answer: Investigate where decisions, recognition, and assignments depend on physical presence. Make relevant information and participation accessible, use work evidence in decisions, and check opportunity patterns. Avoid assuming equal access because remote attendance is technically possible.
questions.failures: Visibility as commitment, remote observers without influence, or rewarding attendance rather than contribution.
questions.intent: Examine location-independent access to consequential work.
questions.probes: What decisions happen in hallway conversations? Who gets high-value work?
questions.provenance: Editorial synthesis from communication access in [GI01](sources.md#additional-topic-research) and opportunity concerns in [TR01](sources.md#other-contemporary-leaders).

rubric.strong: Examines information, assignments, and recognition by location
Improves practical access and evidence-based decisions
Checks actual opportunities and decision participation

questions.title: How do you prevent proximity bias in a hybrid team?
questions.variants: People near leadership receive more information and opportunities.

questions.adaptation: Decision, readers, record, and use. IC: technical decision. Leader: shared operating choice. Confidential details should have appropriate access rather than being indiscriminately published.
questions.alternatives: A short note can suffice. Not every small decision needs a lengthy RFC or permanent archival process.
questions.answer: Capture the problem, relevant constraints, options, decision, rationale, owner, and important follow-up. Choose an accessible location, distinguish approved decisions from proposals, and keep material changes visible. Write for actual consumers rather than documenting every conversation.
questions.failures: Transcript dumps, missing ownership, obsolete decisions treated as current, or inaccessible private-channel conclusions.
questions.intent: Examine actionable context and institutional memory.
questions.probes: Can a newcomer act from the record? How will they know it changed?
questions.provenance: Practice extrapolation from written conclusions in [GI01](sources.md#additional-topic-research).

rubric.strong: Explains enough problem and constraints for the reader
rubric.weak: Gives the conclusion without needed rationale

rubric.strong: Identifies decision status, owner, and next steps
Provides findable, appropriately accessible current information
rubric.weak: Assumes everyone heard the original discussion

questions.title: What makes a written decision record useful?
questions.variants: How do you communicate a decision to people who were not in the meeting?

questions.adaptation: Meeting purpose, participant needs, changes, and observed effects. IC: propose improvements. Manager: team cadence. Do not remove listening/support channels merely because they lack status outputs.
questions.alternatives: Some meetings are valuable for relationships or sensitive discussion. Smaller, less frequent, or asynchronous formats can fit.
questions.answer: State the meeting's intended outcome and necessary participants. Examine whether it produces decisions, coordination, or valuable support; compare alternatives. Change format, attendance, cadence, or existence, then check effects on both work and participation.
questions.failures: Attendance as effectiveness, blanket meeting bans, or replacing coordination with invisible extra work.
questions.intent: Examine meeting purpose, access, and opportunity cost.
questions.probes: What breaks if it stops? Who can contribute under the new format?
questions.provenance: Editorial synthesis from [GI01](sources.md#additional-topic-research) and listening beyond status in [R06](sources.md#michael-lopp).

rubric.strong: Clarifies decision, coordination, or support need
Examines time, participation, and alternatives
Evaluates whether the revised arrangement still serves the need

questions.title: How do you decide whether a recurring meeting is useful?
questions.variants: Your team's calendar leaves little time for focused work.

questions.adaptation: Messages, relationship, stakes, role, and outcome. Any role can describe contribution. A synchronous conversation is optional, especially where access or safety makes it inappropriate.
questions.alternatives: Clear written clarification, mediation, or escalation may fit. Not every dispute is merely a tone misunderstanding.
questions.answer: Review concrete messages and work impact without assuming intent. Clarify missing context and choose a suitable private, written, or live conversation. Address the actual disagreement or conduct, agree next steps, and capture relevant conclusions for affected colleagues.
questions.failures: Assuming malicious intent from terse wording, forced calls, or resolving tone while leaving the work conflict unchanged.
questions.intent: Examine channel limitations and substantive repair.
questions.probes: What substantive concern remains after clarification? Why choose that channel?
questions.provenance: Editorial synthesis informed by observation-based feedback in [H01](sources.md#other-contemporary-leaders).

rubric.strong: Separates observed messages, impact, and unknown intent
Chooses an accessible, proportionate clarification path
rubric.weak: Continues escalation or forces an unsuitable format

rubric.strong: Agrees substantive next steps and usable communication
rubric.weak: Declares peace without addressing the issue

questions.title: How do you repair a conflict that escalated through remote messages?
questions.variants: A chat exchange is becoming increasingly hostile or ambiguous.

questions.adaptation: Newcomer needs, support relationship, actions, and observations. Buddy: bounded contribution. Manager: ownership and team practices. Do not diagnose loneliness from quietness alone.
questions.alternatives: Optional social interaction, pairing, written orientation, or small group sessions can work; mandatory socializing is unnecessary.
questions.answer: Ask what context and connections the newcomer needs. Provide explicit introductions, a usable help path, and supported collaboration on meaningful work. Make unwritten norms discoverable and check whether they can find information and participate without requiring a particular social style.
questions.failures: More tooling as the whole answer, forced camera participation, or expecting accidental conversations to supply all context.
questions.intent: Examine informal context and access beyond setup completion.
questions.probes: Who can they ask safely? What information was previously available only informally?
questions.provenance: Editorial remote adaptation of onboarding ownership in [L18](sources.md#will-larson).

rubric.strong: Asks about practical context and relationship gaps
Creates accessible relationships and useful collaboration
rubric.weak: Leaves introductions and help to chance

rubric.strong: Checks information access and participation without style penalties

questions.title: How do you help a remote newcomer build context and working relationships?
questions.variants: A new colleague is technically onboarded but still isolated from the team.

questions.adaptation: Communication need, preferences, action, and effect. Any role can adapt interactions; organizational accommodations require the responsible channel. Do not assume one solution fits everyone.
questions.alternatives: Plain-language notes, captions, advance material, or different channels can help when participants want them.
questions.answer: Ask about usable formats and constraints without demanding private diagnoses. Provide clear context, explain terms, allow preparation or written contributions where helpful, and check shared understanding respectfully. Preserve substantive standards while improving the route to participation.
questions.failures: Accent or speed as competence, unsolicited diagnoses, or simplifying the person's responsibilities instead of improving communication.
questions.intent: Examine comprehension without judging intelligence from presentation.
questions.probes: How did you check comprehension without embarrassment? What preference did you ask about?
questions.provenance: Editorial accessibility synthesis informed by clear communication in [GI01](sources.md#additional-topic-research); no medical inference or universal accommodation prescription.

rubric.strong: Respectfully asks about practical communication needs
rubric.weak: Assumes ability or demands protected detail

rubric.strong: Provides appropriate accessible ways to understand and contribute
rubric.weak: Requires everyone to use the same format

rubric.strong: Checks work understanding while preserving relevant expectations

questions.title: How do you communicate when people have different language or access needs?
questions.variants: Important decisions are difficult for some colleagues to follow.

questions.adaptation: Instructions, relationship, authority, choices, and outcome. IC: bounded priority clarification. Leader: broader mandate and cross-functional constraints.
questions.alternatives: Act on an explicit temporary assumption when delay is costly and authority permits. Escalation can fit a material unresolved risk.
questions.answer: Identify the ambiguity and consequences with concrete examples. Ask about intended outcomes and constraints, offer feasible choices, and agree a usable priority or decision path. Make unresolved uncertainty visible and keep your manager informed without requiring them to solve every detail.
questions.failures: Guessing silently, dismissing the manager as incompetent, or escalating before attempting proportionate clarification.
questions.intent: Examine clarification and influence within actual authority.
questions.probes: What would you ask first? What can you decide while awaiting clarity?
questions.provenance: Practice extrapolation from constraints and influence in [H05](sources.md#other-contemporary-leaders).

rubric.strong: Specifies expectations and practical consequences
Presents evidence and feasible choices respectfully
rubric.weak: Demands clarity without offering useful context

rubric.strong: Establishes priorities or explicit interim boundaries

questions.title: How do you manage up when priorities or expectations are unclear?
questions.variants: Your manager gives conflicting instructions.

questions.adaptation: Behavior, stakes, relationship, attempts, and outcomes. Any level can provide a bounded example. Do not require candidates to diagnose, reform, or remain indefinitely under a difficult manager.
questions.alternatives: Adjust collaboration, seek mediation, change roles, or leave. Serious conduct concerns need a different path from ordinary disagreement.
questions.answer: Describe observable decisions and their work impact, including what you may not know. Seek context, offer evidence and feedback through a suitable channel, and choose feasible next steps. Explain boundaries or appropriate escalation when the issue persists or exceeds your role.
questions.failures: Character attacks, blind obedience, or portraying resignation as proof the candidate lacked resilience.
questions.intent: Examine specific feedback, responsibility, and realistic options.
questions.probes: What information might you lack? Which part was within your influence?
questions.provenance: Editorial synthesis informed by [H01](sources.md#other-contemporary-leaders) and [H05](sources.md#other-contemporary-leaders); no assessment of the absent manager's character.

rubric.strong: Identifies decisions, consequences, and uncertainty
rubric.weak: Labels the manager without concrete impact

rubric.strong: Uses appropriate evidence, dialogue, and feasible choices
Recognizes authority limits and proportionate next steps
rubric.weak: Assumes the candidate must fix everything

questions.title: How do you work with a manager whose decisions are causing problems?
questions.variants: Tell me about disagreeing with a manager over a recurring issue.

questions.adaptation: Workload, choices, support, and observed effect. IC: personal commitments. Manager: own and team capacity. No diagnosis, family detail, or health disclosure is required.
questions.alternatives: Short exceptional periods can occur with explicit limits and recovery. Boundaries vary; no preferred personal schedule is graded.
questions.answer: Identify overload early using practical signals, clarify essential commitments, and communicate feasible tradeoffs. Stop, defer, delegate, or renegotiate work with appropriate owners. Explain how the arrangement became sustainable rather than treating repeated personal sacrifice as success.
questions.failures: Endless overtime as the only plan, unowned delegation, or judging a candidate's boundary as insufficient dedication.
questions.intent: Examine boundaries and workload decisions, not private health.
questions.probes: What did you stop? How did stakeholders learn what would change?
questions.provenance: Practice extrapolation from [R05](sources.md#michael-lopp) and [H04](sources.md#other-contemporary-leaders).

rubric.strong: Recognizes limits with concrete workload signals
Makes feasible priority and support decisions
rubric.weak: Promises all work through more effort

rubric.strong: Establishes workable commitments and review conditions

questions.title: How do you keep your work sustainable when demands exceed capacity?
questions.variants: What do you do when you cannot responsibly take on more?

questions.adaptation: Support sources, advice, action, and effects. Early-career candidates can use peers; executives can use appropriately scoped advisors. Famous mentors or paid coaching are not required.
questions.alternatives: Informal relationships, written reflection, or structured review can help. Advice can be rejected for a reason.
questions.answer: Describe how you obtain relevant challenge through peers, mentors, specialists, or feedback. Explain a specific insight, how you tested or used it, and where you retained responsibility for the decision. Protect confidential information when seeking external advice.
questions.failures: Name-dropping, seeking agreement only, outsourcing judgment, or sharing private employee/customer material indiscriminately.
questions.intent: Examine useful feedback relationships and independent judgment.
questions.probes: What challenge changed your behavior? What advice did you decide not to follow?
questions.provenance: Editorial synthesis informed by candid support in [R05](sources.md#michael-lopp) and reflection in [R02](sources.md#michael-lopp).

rubric.strong: Seeks perspectives relevant to a real blind spot
Tests or applies insight with concrete behavior
rubric.weak: Cannot show any consequence of advice

rubric.strong: Retains judgment and respects information boundaries
rubric.weak: Treats advice as authority to act

questions.title: How do you seek support and challenge your own thinking?
questions.variants: Who helps you notice blind spots in your leadership?

questions.adaptation: Domain, mandate, learning actions, and observations. IC: unfamiliar system. Manager: new leadership responsibility. Executive: business or functional context with qualified partners.
questions.alternatives: Hire or partner with expertise rather than becoming the expert. Some gaps require a narrower mandate or more time.
questions.answer: State the new responsibility, essential gaps, and what competent work requires. Learn from relevant people and actual artifacts, practice on bounded work, and obtain feedback. Explain a changed decision or capability without claiming mastery from superficial exposure.
questions.failures: Bluffing, course completion as proof of capability, or delegating without understanding enough to oversee the responsibility.
questions.intent: Examine a practical learning process and honest limits.
questions.probes: What did you initially misunderstand? How did you know your understanding improved?
questions.provenance: Practice extrapolation from changing role demands in [L14](sources.md#will-larson).

rubric.strong: Identifies relevant unknowns and responsibility boundaries
Uses suitable expertise, artifacts, and bounded application
rubric.weak: Lists resources without practice or feedback

rubric.strong: Shows a practical improvement and remaining limits

questions.title: How do you learn when your role moves into unfamiliar territory?
questions.variants: Tell me about becoming responsible for work you had not done before.

questions.adaptation: Promise, responsibility, affected people, actions, and subsequent observations. Match the commitment to actual role; personal accountability does not imply sole responsibility for every outcome.
questions.alternatives: Trust may remain damaged despite appropriate action. An honest unresolved outcome can still demonstrate responsible repair.
questions.answer: Name the commitment and effect on others, acknowledge your contribution, and communicate promptly without excuses. Agree feasible repair and future expectations. Explain subsequent behavior and any evidence of restored working trust without asserting the other person forgave you.
questions.failures: Apology without action, blaming others, or declaring trust restored solely because the candidate feels better.
questions.intent: Examine relationship repair, distinct from analyzing the project failure.
questions.probes: What did you say? What changed in your later commitments?
questions.provenance: Editorial repair question informed by concrete feedback in [H01](sources.md#other-contemporary-leaders).

rubric.strong: Recognizes specific responsibility and impact
Agrees concrete repair and realistic future expectations
Shows changed behavior and bounds claims about trust

questions.title: How have you repaired trust after breaking a commitment?
questions.variants: You promised something you could not deliver; what happened next?

questions.adaptation: Desired scope, observed capability, support, and trial outcomes. IC: greater technical ambiguity. Manager: larger or different leadership mandate. No obligation to choose management or ever-larger scope.
questions.alternatives: Deepen expertise, stay in the current role, or choose a narrower scope. Development is not a contest for maximum headcount.
questions.answer: Identify the new responsibility and relevant evidence from current work. Seek feedback, test suitable scope with support, and explain what must change in delegation or ownership. State gaps and conditions rather than equating tenure with readiness.
questions.failures: Title as evidence, hidden gaps, or accumulating responsibility while leaving every decision dependent on the candidate.
questions.intent: Examine capability and readiness for additional work, beyond title ambition.
questions.probes: What new decision could you handle? What would you stop owning personally?
questions.provenance: Editorial growth synthesis informed by [R02](sources.md#michael-lopp), [H02](sources.md#other-contemporary-leaders), and [J01](sources.md#other-contemporary-leaders).

rubric.strong: Identifies the responsibility and relevant capability
rubric.weak: Wants advancement without naming new work

rubric.strong: Offers concrete evidence, feedback, and bounded tests
Plans support, delegation, and limits sustainably

questions.title: How do you decide you are ready for broader responsibility?
questions.variants: How do you grow your scope without becoming a bottleneck?

questions.adaptation: Actual choices and user-owned disclosure boundaries. Any career stage qualifies. Compensation, location, caregiving, or health details are optional; the evaluator does not rank those preferences.
questions.alternatives: IC/management transitions, lateral moves, stability, or time away can all be valid. No prestigious employer or promotion is required.
questions.answer: Explain the professional choice, relevant priorities, feasible options, and uncertainty you are comfortable discussing. Describe what you gained, gave up, and learned. Distinguish expectations at the time from later outcomes without retroactively making the decision inevitable.
questions.failures: Requiring an ambition narrative, judging private priorities, or treating nonlinear careers as poor commitment.
questions.intent: Examine deliberate decision-making without grading personal priorities.
questions.probes: What was uncertain then? What would change your choice now?
questions.provenance: Practice extrapolation from career-track choice in [J01](sources.md#other-contemporary-leaders) and reflection in [R02](sources.md#michael-lopp); preferences themselves are ungraded.

rubric.strong: Describes relevant options and priorities within boundaries
Acknowledges meaningful costs and uncertainty
rubric.weak: Presents only benefits or false inevitability

rubric.strong: Separates expectations, results, and learning
rubric.weak: Rewrites later knowledge into the original decision

questions.title: Tell me about a consequential career choice and its tradeoffs
questions.variants: Why did you change tracks, take a smaller role, or turn down an opportunity?

questions.adaptation: Tasks, tools, permissions, users, and actual observations. IC: bounded workflow. Manager: support and team practices. Executive: investment decisions with accountable technical/risk partners.
questions.alternatives: Slow adoption, targeted use, or declining a use case can be reasonable. Enthusiasm and skepticism are not themselves quality signals.
questions.answer: Identify useful tasks, constraints, and current baselines. Choose a bounded pilot, provide learning/support, and define permitted use, review ownership, and decision criteria. Examine useful outcomes and costs before expanding, including cases where assistance is not appropriate.
questions.failures: Adoption targets without outcomes, universal tool mandates, or assuming generated code needs no human ownership.
questions.intent: Examine problem-led adoption with accountable learning.
questions.probes: What problem does the pilot solve? What would make you stop it?
questions.provenance: Practice extrapolation from selected [OS01](sources.md#additional-topic-research); adoption framework and anchors are ours.

rubric.strong: Connects bounded use to a relevant task and baseline
Provides practical support and accountable use boundaries
Uses outcomes and costs to decide whether to expand

questions.title: How would you introduce AI assistance into an engineering team?
questions.variants: Leadership asks you to accelerate AI adoption.

questions.adaptation: Baseline, task mix, adoption pattern, measures, and limitations. IC: own bounded comparison. Leader: team/system effects. No controlled experiment is required for every local decision.
questions.alternatives: Qualitative observations support limited conclusions. An inconclusive estimate can still justify continued bounded learning.
questions.answer: Define the task and useful outcome, including review, defects, rework, and operating cost. Compare reasonably similar work where feasible, consider who chooses which tasks/tools, and distinguish elapsed time from effort. Explain uncertainty and how evidence informs a bounded decision rather than claiming a universal uplift.

examples.body:
Synthetic facts: a manager's team piloted AI on routine test scaffolding. People
reported faster drafting; review effort and defects were not yet compared.

**Weak answer:** “AI increased our engineering productivity by 40%, so we can
deliver the same roadmap with fewer engineers.” The supplied facts support neither claim.

**Truthful revision:** “The team reported faster drafting for routine test
scaffolding. We haven't compared total effort, review work, or defects, so I
wouldn't translate that into a team-capacity gain. I'd examine similar tasks,
including which ones people chose to use AI on, and track the work through review.
We can continue the bounded pilot while gathering that evidence. Broader roadmap
or staffing assumptions need stronger support than the drafting observation.”

| Dimension | Proposed assessment | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Outcome | 2 | Names downstream quality and effort, but measurements remain future work |
| Comparison | 2 | Recognizes similar-task comparison and selection; details still need a probe |
| Inference | 3 | Explicitly bounds the claim and rejects unsupported capacity extrapolation |

**Factual support:** The pilot and reports are synthetic facts; the measurement
plan is hypothetical. These are example human judgments, not a model evaluation
result. **IC adaptation:** Discuss one's own bounded task comparison. **Executive
adaptation:** Explain what evidence supports investment choices without turning
this manager's pilot into a company-wide transformation.
examples.title: Bounding a productivity claim

questions.failures: Lines generated as productivity, self-report as causality, or copying another study's percentage into the team's forecast.
questions.intent: Examine measurement and causal uncertainty.

questions.adaptation: Task, sources, audience, claim consequences, and authority. IC: source-linked output. Manager: people-decision review. Executive: accountable systems rather than confidence in summary fluency.
questions.alternatives: Abstain, request clarification, or use a qualitative statement when evidence is incomplete. Missing documentation does not prove a user is lying.
questions.answer: Separate source facts, new user statements, hypotheses, and generated interpretations. questions.failures: Fabricated quotes, plausible metrics, automatic record updates, or treating an old accepted record as impossible to correct.
questions.intent: Examine provenance and correction in consequential information.

questions.title: How do you prevent an AI summary or draft from turning guesses into facts?

questions.adaptation: Forecast, local evidence, costs, responsibilities, and authority. Manager: realistic team planning. Executive: investment and people implications with appropriate partners. Predictions remain labeled.
questions.alternatives: Invest in training, redesign work, maintain staffing, or adjust capacity cautiously. No inevitable workforce outcome is presumed.
questions.answer: Separate observed task effects from forecasts about team capacity. Consider review, maintenance, learning, demand, and role changes. Use scenarios and bounded investments, preserve accountability, and define evidence that would justify changing commitments or staffing assumptions.
questions.failures: Extrapolating generation speed to headcount savings, ignoring downstream work, or making irreversible decisions from vendor claims.
questions.intent: Examine responsible planning when capability and adoption are changing.
questions.probes: What local evidence supports the forecast? How would the plan change if gains do not appear?
questions.provenance: Editorial planning synthesis informed by measurement limits in [ME01](sources.md#additional-topic-research) and leadership in [OS01](sources.md#additional-topic-research).
